   111	/- The nested sum is the fixed register order
   112	`V_X ⊕ V_Z ⊕ V_I ⊕ V_V ⊕ V_{R_X} ⊕ V_{R_Z}` from the blueprint. -/
   113	/-- The `V_X` block of an ambient Pauli vector (`def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   114	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
   115	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`). -/
   116	def pauliXBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   117	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl i)))))
   118	
   119	/-- The `V_Z` block of an ambient Pauli vector in `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   120	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   121	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   122	-/
   123	def pauliZBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   124	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))))
   125	
   126	/-- The scalar block `V_I` of an ambient Pauli vector in
   127	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   128	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   129	-/
   130	def pauliScalarBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   131	  z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr ()))))
   132	
   133	/-- The direction block `V_V` of an ambient Pauli vector in
   134	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   135	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   136	-/
   137	def pauliDirectionBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   138	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))
   139	
   140	/-- The `r_X` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
   141	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   142	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   143	-/
   144	def pauliRXBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   145	  z (.inl (.inr ()))
   146	
   147	/-- The `r_Z` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
   148	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   149	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   150	-/
   151	def pauliRZBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
   152	  z (.inr ())
   153	
   154	/-- Select the basis-dependent point block from a Pauli question content in
   155	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
   156	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   157	-/
   158	def pauliPointBlock (W : PauliKind) (z : PauliSpace P) :
   159	    Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
   160	  match W with
   161	  | .X => pauliXBlock z
   162	  | .Z => pauliZBlock z
   163	
   164	/-- Read the low-degree register selected by a basis from an ambient Pauli
   165	vector.  Lean-only coordinate plumbing for `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
   166	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   167	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   168	-/
   169	def pauliToLd (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind) (z : PauliSpace P) :
   170	    LdSpace P.toLdParams :=
   171	  fun i => match i with
   172	  | .inl (.inl j) => pauliPointBlock W z j
   173	  | .inl (.inr _) => pauliScalarBlock z
   174	  | .inr j => pauliDirectionBlock z j
   175	
   176	/-- Embed a low-degree vector into the basis-selected Pauli blocks, clearing the
   177	other basis and the two `r` registers.  This is Lean-only coordinate plumbing
   178	for `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
   179	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
   180	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   181	-/
   182	def embedLd (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
   183	    (u : LdSpace P.toLdParams) : PauliSpace P :=
   184	  fun i => match i with
   185	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) =>
   186	      match W with
   187	      | .X => u (.inl (.inl j))
   188	      | .Z => 0
   189	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) =>
   190	      match W with
   191	      | .X => 0
   192	      | .Z => u (.inl (.inl j))
   193	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => u (.inl (.inr ()))
   194	  | .inl (.inl (.inr j)) => u (.inr j)
   195	  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
   196	  | .inr _ => 0
   197	
   198	/-- The type-4 projection retaining `V_X`, `V_Z`, `V_{R_X}`, and `V_{R_Z}` from
   199	`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper
   200	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   201	-/
   202	def pauliSharedProjection (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliSpace P :=
   203	  fun i => match i with
   204	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))))
   205	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))))
   206	  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => 0
   207	  | .inl (.inl (.inr _)) => 0
   208	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   209	  | .inr _ => z (.inr ())
   210	
   211	/-- The source level attached to each typed Pauli CL map.  This records the
   212	exact levels in items 1--5 of `def:pauli-question-distribution`: point, line,
   213	and diagonal maps have levels 1, 2, and 3, the Pauli map has level 0, and the
   214	shared projection has level 1.  Blueprint
   215	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
   216	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
   217	-/
   218	def pauliCLLevel : PauliType → ℕ
   219	  | .point _ => 1
   220	  | .aline _ => 2

1	import Mathlib
     2	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Algebra.Pauli
     3	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Games.Defs
     4	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Games.Distance
     5	import MIPStarRE.QPBT.Test.PauliBasisTest
     6	
     7	/-!
     8	# Pauli basis test soundness
     9	
    10	The quantitative error function and the source-shaped soundness statement live
    11	here.  All analytic estimates are intentionally proof-level obligations in the
    12	stage-4.1 skeleton; the carriers below are concrete finite-dimensional vectors
    13	and matrices so that later proofs can use the existing Hilbert-space API.
    14	
    15	## References
    16	
    17	The main declaration is `thm:pauli` in
    18	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`, with paper origin
    19	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
    20	The distance functionals use `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` from
    21	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-220`.
    22	-/
    23	
    24	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    25	
    26	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    27	
    28	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    29	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    30	
    31	/-- The Pauli-test error scale.  The argument order is `(a, b, ε, m, d, q)`;
    32	the powers are real `rpow`s and the asymptotic constants are absorbed into `a`,
    33	as specified by `thm:pauli` (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`,
    34	paper `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`).
    35	-/
    36	noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
    37	  a * Real.rpow ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) a *
    38	    (Real.rpow ε b + Real.rpow (q : ℝ) (-b) +
    39	      Real.rpow 2 (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))
    40	
    41	/-- Matrix conjugation by a finite-dimensional linear isometry.  This is a
    42	Lean-only helper for the operator conclusion of `thm:pauli`; it uses the
    43	matrix representation of the isometry and its conjugate transpose.  Blueprint
    44	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`, paper origin
    45	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
    46	-/
    47	noncomputable def conjIsometry {ι ι' : Type*}
    48	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι']
    49	    (φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ ι')
    50	    (M : Op ι) : Op ι' :=
    51	  let U : Matrix ι' ι ℂ := Matrix.toEuclideanLin.symm φ.toLinearMap
    52	  U * M * Uᴴ
    53	
    54	/-- Reindex a finite Euclidean-space vector along an equivalence.  This is the
    55	coordinate form of the tensor-register shuffle used in the paper's ideal
    56	state (`def:EPR`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:513-523`),
    57	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`.
    58	-/
    59	noncomputable def reindexState {ι ι' : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    60	    [Fintype ι'] [DecidableEq ι'] (e : ι ≃ ι')
    61	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι' :=
    62	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv ι' ℂ).symm
    63	    (fun j => (EuclideanSpace.equiv ι ℂ ψ) (e.symm j))
    64	
    65	/-- Coordinate tensoring of two local maps on a bipartite state.  The formula
    66	is a genuine finite sum over the input coordinates; preservation of the norm
    67	is part of the later soundness proof for `thm:pauli`, blueprint
    68	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`, paper origin
    69	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
    70	-/
    71	noncomputable def isometryTensor
    72	    {ιA ιB ιA' ιB' R : Type*}
    73	    [Fintype ιA] [DecidableEq ιA] [Fintype ιB] [DecidableEq ιB]
    74	    [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA'] [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
    75	    [Fintype R] [DecidableEq R]
    76	    (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × R))
    77	    (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ] EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × R))
    78	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)) :
    79	    EuclideanSpace ℂ ((ιA' × R) × (ιB' × R)) :=
    80	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv ((ιA' × R) × (ιB' × R)) ℂ).symm
    81	    (fun p =>
    82	      ∑ i : ιA, ∑ j : ιB,
    83	        ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (ιA' × R) ℂ)
    84	            (φA ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ιA ℂ).symm (Pi.single i 1))) p.1) *
    85	          ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (ιB' × R) ℂ)
    86	            (φB ((EuclideanSpace.equiv ιB ℂ).symm (Pi.single j 1))) p.2) *
    87	          ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (ιA × ιB) ℂ) ψ (i, j)) )
    88	
    89	/-- The ideal auxiliary state `aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}` in the shuffled register
    90	ordering.  The EPR factor is the concrete `eprState` from
    91	`def:EPR` (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:513-523`; paper
    92	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`).
    93	-/
    94	noncomputable def idealState (P : AdmissibleParams)
    95	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
    96	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
    97	    (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')) :
    98	    EuclideanSpace ℂ ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
    99	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) ×
   100	      (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) ℂ).symm
   101	    (fun p =>
   102	      ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (ιA' × ιB') ℂ) aux (p.1.1, p.2.1)) *
   103	        ((EuclideanSpace.equiv (PauliRegister P × PauliRegister P) ℂ)
   104	          (eprState (PauliRegister P)) (p.1.2, p.2.2)))
   105	
   106	/-- The Pauli question carrying no additional coefficient data, as in
   107	`def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
   108	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1006-1008`.
   109	-/
   110	def pauliQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind) : PauliQuestion P :=
   111	  (.pauli W, 0)
   112	
   113	/-- The A-side ideal Pauli projector, with identities on the auxiliary and
   114	B-side registers.  This is a concrete matrix form of the operator comparison
   115	in `thm:pauli` (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`; paper
   116	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`).
   117	-/
   118	noncomputable def pauliProjOnA'' (P : AdmissibleParams)
   119	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   120	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB'] (W : PauliKind)
   121	    (u : PauliRegister P) :
   122	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   123	  fun p q =>
   124	    if p.1.1 = q.1.1 ∧ p.2 = q.2 then
   125	      pauliProj W u p.1.2 q.1.2
   126	    else 0
   127	
   128	/-- The symmetric B-side ideal Pauli projector from `thm:pauli`, blueprint
   129	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`, paper origin
   130	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   131	-/
   132	noncomputable def pauliProjOnB'' (P : AdmissibleParams)
   133	    {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   134	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB'] (W : PauliKind)
   135	    (u : PauliRegister P) :
   136	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   137	  fun p q =>
   138	    if p.1 = q.1 ∧ p.2.1 = q.2.1 then
   139	      pauliProj W u p.2.2 q.2.2
   140	    else 0
   141	
   142	/-- Lift a conjugated A-side effect to the full ideal register in `thm:pauli`,
   143	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`, paper origin
   144	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   145	-/
   146	noncomputable def liftedAEffect {P : AdmissibleParams} {G : Game}
   147	    (S : Strategy G) {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   148	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
   149	    (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   150	      EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
   151	    (M : Op S.ιA) :
   152	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   153	  fun p q =>
   154	    if p.2 = q.2 then
   155	      (conjIsometry φA M) p.1 q.1
   156	    else 0
   157	
   158	/-- Lift a conjugated B-side effect to the full ideal register in `thm:pauli`,
   159	blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`, paper origin
   160	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   161	-/
   162	noncomputable def liftedBEffect {P : AdmissibleParams} {G : Game}
   163	    (S : Strategy G) {ιA' ιB' : Type*} [Fintype ιA'] [DecidableEq ιA']
   164	    [Fintype ιB'] [DecidableEq ιB']
   165	    (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   166	      EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
   167	    (M : Op S.ιB) :
   168	    Op ((ιA' × PauliRegister P) × (ιB' × PauliRegister P)) :=
   169	  fun p q =>
   170	    if p.1 = q.1 then
   171	      (conjIsometry φB M) p.2 q.2
   172	    else 0
   173	
   174	/-- A finite witness packaging the auxiliary dimensions, isometries, and state
   175	from `thm:pauli`.  This structure is a Lean-only encoding of the existential
   176	data in the paper theorem; it introduces no extra hypothesis.  Blueprint
   177	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`, paper origin
   178	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   179	-/
   180	structure PauliSoundnessWitness (P : AdmissibleParams)
   181	    (S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P)) where
   182	  ιA' : Type
   183	  ιB' : Type
   184	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA']
   185	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB']
   186	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA']
   187	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB']
   188	  φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   189	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P)
   190	  φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
   191	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P)
   192	  aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')
   193	  aux_norm : ‖aux‖ = 1
   194	
   195	attribute [instance] PauliSoundnessWitness.ιAFintype PauliSoundnessWitness.ιBFintype
   196	  PauliSoundnessWitness.ιADecidableEq PauliSoundnessWitness.ιBDecidableEq
   197	
   198	/-- The A-side operator-distance quantity appearing in the soundness
   199	conclusion.  It is the finite-sum realization of `def:povm-distance` from
   200	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:201-220`, paper origin
   201	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`.
   202	-/
   203	noncomputable def pauliOperatorDistanceA
   204	    (P : AdmissibleParams) (S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P))
   205	    (w : PauliSoundnessWitness P S) (W : PauliKind) : ℝ :=
   206	  ∑ u : PauliRegister P,
   207	      ‖applyOperatorToState (liftedAEffect S w.φA
   208	        ((S.A (pauliQuestion P W)).effect (.pauliOutcome u)) -
   209	      pauliProjOnA'' P W u) (idealState P w.aux)‖ ^ 2
   210	
   211	/-- The symmetric B-side operator-distance quantity from `def:povm-distance`,
   212	blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:201-220`, paper origin
   213	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:258-271`.
   214	-/
   215	noncomputable def pauliOperatorDistanceB
   216	    (P : AdmissibleParams) (S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P))
   217	    (w : PauliSoundnessWitness P S) (W : PauliKind) : ℝ :=
   218	  ∑ u : PauliRegister P,
   219	      ‖applyOperatorToState (liftedBEffect S w.φB
   220	        ((S.B (pauliQuestion P W)).effect (.pauliOutcome u)) -
   221	      pauliProjOnB'' P W u) (idealState P w.aux)‖ ^ 2
   222	
   223	/-- `thm:pauli`: every sufficiently successful Pauli basis test strategy admits
   224	local isometries and an auxiliary unit state for which the state and both
   225	operator families are close at scale `deltaQld`.  The theorem is stated over
   226	the fixed self-dual-normal field model stored in `AdmissibleParams`, not over a
   227	freshly quantified field identification.  Blueprint
   228	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:386-403`; paper origin
   229	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1426-1447`.
   230	
   231	The paper's asymptotic constants are encoded by the explicit `deltaQld`
   232	functional; the squared operator distances use the quantitative convention of
   233	`def:povm-distance` (`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:201-220`).
   234	-/
   235	theorem pauli_soundness :
   236	    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧
   237	      ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) (ε : ℝ), 0 ≤ ε →
   238	        ∀ S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P), 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
   239	          ∃ w : PauliSoundnessWitness P S,
   240	            ‖isometryTensor w.φA w.φB S.ψ - idealState P w.aux‖ ≤
   241	                deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
   242	            (∀ W : PauliKind,
   243	              pauliOperatorDistanceA P S w W ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q) ∧
   244	            (∀ W : PauliKind,
   245	              pauliOperatorDistanceB P S w W ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q) := by
   246	  sorry
   247	
   248	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

1	\section{Classical and Quantum Low-degree Tests}
     2	\label{sec:ldt}
     3	
     4	In this section we introduce the classical and quantum low individual degree tests, that form the basis of our classical, quantum-sound and quantum PCP constructions. For quantum soundness of the classical test we refer to~\cite{ML20}. For the quantum test, we refer to~\cite{natarajan2018low} and its adaptation to the low individual degree test given in Appendix~\ref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
     5	The protocol in this work combines both of these tests, using the quantum
     6	low individual degree test for question reduction and the classical low individual degree test for
     7	answer reduction.
     8	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier} below introduces the classical test,
     9	and Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier} does the same for the quantum 
    10	test.
    11	Prior to doing this, we introduce the \emph{Magic Square game} in
    12	Section~\ref{sec:ms}, a key subroutine in the quantum test.
    13	
    14	
    15	\subsection{The classical low-degree test}
    16	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    17	
    18	We begin with a generalization of the classical low-degree test known as the
    19	``simultaneous individual low-degree test''.
    20	We sometimes refer to this as the ``classical low-degree test'' for short.
    21	The low-degree test is used as a subroutine in the Pauli Basis test (see
    22	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) as well as the answer-reduction normal form
    23	verifier (see Section~\ref{sec:ans}).
    24	We describe the test as a nonlocal game in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game} and show
    25	that the question distribution can be implemented as a (typed) conditionally
    26	linear distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL
    27	distributions).
    28	
    29	
    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99

   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898	
   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}

   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}

   231	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]
   232	  A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
   233	  subset of the standard basis of $V$.\footnote{The use of the term ``register''
   234	    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often

   241	\begin{definition}
   242	  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
   243	  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
   244	  define the \emph{dot product}
   245	  \begin{equation*}
   246	    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
   249	  \begin{equation*}
   250	    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
   251	    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
   252	  \end{equation*}
   253	  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
   254	  space will always be clear from context.

   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).

   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}

   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.

   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}

   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}

   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.

   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}

   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose

   359	  Write $A = U B$ where $U$ is invertible and $B$ is in reduced row echelon
   360	  form.
   361	  Let $J$ be the set of column indices of the leading 1 entries in
   362	  $B$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.  
   363	  Now, the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span the subpsace $S$, and the restriction of

   421	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   422	
   423	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ be a prime power.
   424	We denote the finite fields of $p$ and $q$ elements by $\Fp$ and $\Fq$
   425	respectively.
   426	The prime $p$ is the characteristic of field $\Fq$, and field $\Fp$ is the
   427	\emph{prime subfield} of $\Fq$.
   428	We sometimes omit the subscript and simply use $\F$ to denote the finite field
   429	when the size of the field is implicit from context.
   430	For general background on finite fields, and explicit algorithms for elementary
   431	arithmetic operations, we refer to~\cite{mullen2013handbook}.
   432	
   433	\subsubsection{Subfields and bases}
   434	\label{sec:subfields}
   435	Let $q$ be a prime power and $k$ an integer. 
   436	The field $\Fq$ is a subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of
   437	dimension $k$ over $\Fq$.
   438	Let $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ be a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ as a linear space over $\Fq$.
   439	Introduce a bijection $\downsize_q : \F_{q^k} \rightarrow \Fq^k$ between
   440	$\F_{q^k}$ and $\Fq^k$ defined with respect to the basis $\{ e_i \}_{i=1}^k$ by
   441	\begin{equation*}
   442	  \downsize_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k
   443	\end{equation*}
   444	where $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$.
   445	This map satisfies several nice properties.
   446	First, the map is an isomorphism of $\Fq$-vector spaces: it is $\Fq$-linear and addition in $\F_{q^k}$
   447	naturally corresponds to vector addition in $\Fq^k$.
   448	Namely, for all $a,b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   449	\begin{equation*}
   450		\downsize_q (a + b) = \downsize_q(a) + \downsize_q(b)\;.
   451	\end{equation*}
   452	Second, multiplication by a field element in $\F_{q^k}$ corresponds to a linear
   453	map on $\F_{q}^k$.
   454	For all $a \in \F_{q^k}$, there exists a matrix $K_a \in \Matrix_k (\Fq)$ such
   455	that for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$,
   456	\begin{equation*}
   457		\downsize_q (a b) = K_a \, \downsize_q(b)\;.
   458	\end{equation*}
   459	The matrix $K_a$ is called the \emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to
   460	  basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$}.
   461	
   462	We extend the map $\downsize_q$ to vectors, matrices and sets over $\F_{q^k}$.
   463	For $v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$, define
   464	\begin{equation*}
   465	  \downsize_q (v) = \bigl( \downsize_q (v_i) \bigr)_{i=1}^n \in \Fq^{kn}\;.
   466	\end{equation*}
   467	Similarly, for matrix $M = (M_{i, j}) \in \Matrix_{m, n}(\F_{q^k})$, define
   468	\begin{equation*}
   469	  \downsizem_q (M) = \bigl( K_{M_{i, j}} \bigr) \in \Matrix_{mk, nk} (\Fq)\;,
   470	\end{equation*}
   471	the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th block is the multiplication table $K_{M_{i,
   472	    j}}$ of $M_{i, j}$ with respect to basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$.
   473	For a set $S$ of vectors in $\F_{q^k}^n$, define
   474	\begin{equation*}
   475		\downsize_q(S) = \{ \downsize_q(v) : v \in S \}\;.
   476	\end{equation*}
   477	We omit the subscript and write $\downsize$ and $\downsizem$ for $\downsize_q$
   478	and $\downsizem_q$ respectively when $q$ equals to $p$, the characteristic of
   479	the field.
   480	
   481	The \emph{trace of\/ $\F_{q^k}$ over\/ $\Fq$} is defined as
   482	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   483	  \tr_{q^k \to q} :\; a \,\mapsto \, \Tr(K_a)
   484	\end{equation}
   485	for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $\Tr(K_a)$ is the trace of the multiplication table
   486	of $a$ with respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$.
   487	By definition, the trace is an $\Fq$-linear map from $\F_{q^k}$ to
   488	$\Fq$. The trace is in fact independent of the choice of basis, which
   489	can be seen from the following equivalent definition~\cite[Definition 2.1.80]{mullen2013handbook}:
   490	\[
   491		\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j = 0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   492	\]
   493	
   494	A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', e_2', \ldots, e_k' \}$ of $\{e_1, e_2, \ldots,
   495	e_k\}$ is a basis such that $\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for
   496	all $i, j \in \{1, 2, \ldots, k\}$.
   497	A \emph{self-dual basis} is one that is equal to its dual.
   498	If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set $\{ \alpha^{q^j} \}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a
   499	basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\Fq$, the basis is called a \emph{normal
   500	  basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not exist for all fields but are guaranteed to exist under
   501	certain conditions; in particular, if $q = 2$ and $k$ is odd, as will
   502	be shown in \Cref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   503	
   504	We record some convenient facts about the maps $\downsize(\cdot)$ and
   505	$\downsizem(\cdot)$ for self-dual bases.
   506	
   507	\begin{lemma}
   508	  \label{lem:downsize_field}
   509	  Let $q$ be a prime power, $k$ an integer and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual basis for
   510	  $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$.

   641	  Since $\downsize_q(\cdot)$ is a bijection, this implies that $z = \sum_i
   642	  \alpha_i v_i$, and therefore $z^V = \sum_{i=1}^m \alpha_i v_i$ (and similarly

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   820	\end{proof}

   822	\begin{remark}
   823	  \label{rmk:tm_fields}
   824	  Throughout this paper, whenever we refer to Turing machines that perform
   825	  computations with elements of a field $\F_q$ for an admissible field size $q =
   826	  2^k$, we mean that that the Turing machines are representing elements of
   827	  $\F_q$ as vectors in $\{0,1\}^{k}$ using the basis specified by the
   828	  algorithm of Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} and performing arithmetic as
   829	  described in Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   830	\end{remark}

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898

   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log

   905	\end{lemma}

   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}
  1004	
  1005	We will make frequent use of Naimark dilation. In our setting, it can be formulated as follows. For a proof, see~\cite[Theorem 5.1]{ML20}
  1006	
  1007	\begin{theorem}[Naimark dilation]\label{thm:naimark}
  1008	Let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in $\mH_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \mH_{\mathrm{B}}$.
  1009	Let $A = \{A^x_a\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\mH_{\mathrm{A}}$
  1010	and $B=\{B^y_b\}$ be a sub-measurement acting on $\mH_{\mathrm{B}}$.
  1011	Then there exists
  1012	\begin{enumerate}
  1013	\item Hilbert spaces $\mH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$ and $\mH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
  1014	\item a state $\ket{\mathsf{aux}} \in \mH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}} \ot \mH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
  1015	\item and two measurements  $\widehat{A} = \{\widehat{A}^x_a\}$ and $\widehat{B}=\{\widehat{B}^y_b\}$
  1016	acting on $\mH_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \mH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$
  1017	and $\mH_{\mathrm{B}} \ot \mH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$,
  1018	respectively,
  1019	\end{enumerate}
  1020	such that the following is true.
  1021	If we write $\ket{\widehat{\psi}} = \ket{\psi} \otimes \ket{\mathsf{aux}}$,
  1022	then for all $x,y, a, b$,
  1023	 \begin{equation*}
  1024	 \bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}
  1025	 = \bra{\widehat{\psi}} \widehat{A}^x_a \ot \widehat{B}^y_b \ket{\widehat{\psi}}.
  1026	 \end{equation*}
  1027	 In addition, $\ket{\mathsf{aux}}$ is a \emph{product state},
  1028	 meaning that we can write it as
  1029	 \begin{equation*}
  1030	 \ket{\mathsf{aux}}= \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A}}} \ot \ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B}}},
  1031	 \end{equation*}
  1032	for $\ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{A}}}$ in $\mH_{\mathrm{A}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$
  1033	and $\ket{\mathsf{aux}_{\mathrm{B}}}$ in $\mH_{\mathrm{B}_{\mathsf{aux}}}$.
  1034	\end{theorem}

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations
  1146	\begin{equation*}
  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,
  1149	\end{equation*}
  1150	where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \in \Fq$.
  1151	For $W\in\{X,Z\}$ and $e \in \Fq^n$ define the eigenstates
  1152	\[ \ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}\;, \]
  1153	and associated rank-$1$ projectors $\qp^W_e$. Analogous versions of \Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1154	and \Cref{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single} relate the multi-qubit observables
  1155	and projectors:
  1156	\begin{align}
  1157	  \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b \in \Fq^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}
  1158	  \qp^W_b\;, \label{eq:pauli-obs-proj} \\
  1159	    \E_{a\in \F_q^n} \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)} \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b'\in \F_q^n} \E_{a\in \F_q^n}
  1160	  \omega^{\tr(a\cdot (b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;. \label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
  1161	\end{align}
  1162	
  1163	Since we only consider finite fields $\F_q$ such that $q = 2^k$ the maximally
  1164	entangled state $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and the corresponding qudit Pauli
  1165	observables/projectors are isomorphic to a tensor product of maximally entangled
  1166	states $\ket{\EPR_2}$ and \emph{qubit} Pauli observables/projectors
  1167	respectively; this is shown in the next lemma.
  1168	This is used to argue that the Pauli basis test (described in
  1169	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) gives a self-test for Pauli observables and
  1170	maximally entangled states over qubits.

## (d) Statement sketch of `MIPStarRE.QPBT.pauli_soundness`

```lean
/-- Soundness function of the Pauli basis test; argument order (ε, m, d, q)
everywhere, per rem:delta-qld-argument-order. Real rpow throughout. -/
noncomputable def deltaQld (a b ε : ℝ) (m d q : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  a * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ) ^ a *
    (ε ^ b + (q : ℝ) ^ (-b) + (2 : ℝ) ^ (-(b * ((m * d : ℕ) : ℝ))))

/-- thm:pauli (qpbt-paper 08_…tex:1426-1447): soundness of the Pauli basis test. -/
theorem pauli_soundness :
    ∃ a b : ℝ, 1 ≤ a ∧ 0 < b ∧ b < 1 ∧
      ∀ (P : AdmissibleParams) [FieldModel P.q] (ε : ℝ), 0 < ε →
        ∀ S : Strategy (pauliBasisTest P), 1 - ε ≤ S.value →
          ∃ (ιA' ιB' : Type) (_ : Fintype ιA') (_ : DecidableEq ιA')
            (_ : Fintype ιB') (_ : DecidableEq ιB')
            (φA : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιA →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × PauliRegister P))
            (φB : EuclideanSpace ℂ S.ιB →ₗᵢ[ℂ]
                    EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
            (aux : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA' × ιB')), ‖aux‖ = 1 ∧
            -- item 1: ‖φA ⊗ φB ψ − aux ⊗ EPR_q^{⊗M}‖ ≤ δ_qld  (squared distance,
            -- via stateDistSq and deltaQld²; or state with ‖·‖ directly — either
            -- form is acceptable, document the choice)
            ‖isometryTensor φA φB S.ψ - idealState P aux‖
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
            -- item 2, for both players and both bases, summation over u ∈ F_q^M,
            -- w.r.t. the ideal state; O(·) constants absorbed into a (see (e)8)
            ∀ W : PauliKind,
              (∑ u : PauliRegister P,
                ‖(heteroKron
                    (conjIsometry φA ((S.A (pauliQuestion P W)).effect
                      (PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u) ...decoded))
                    (1 : Op (ιB' × PauliRegister P))
                  - pauliProjOnA'' P W u).mulVec (idealState P aux)‖ ^ 2)
                ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q ∧
              (symmetric B-side bound)
```

Supporting definitions in Soundness.lean (all NEW, Lean-only):
`idealState P aux := reindexState prodShuffle (vecTensor aux (eprState (PauliRegister P)))`;
`pauliQuestion P W : (pauliBasisTest P).QuestionA := (PauliType.pauli W, 0)` (the
`(Pauli, W)` question has content `0`, image of the 0-level CL function);
`pauliProjOnA'' P W u : Op ((ιA' × Reg) × (ιB' × Reg))` places `pauliProj W u` on the
`A''` factor, identity elsewhere (and the `B''` analogue). The A-side measurement
outcome family is the sub-family of `S.A` at outcomes `PauliAnswer.pauliOutcome u`
(other constructors carry no mass in the ideal comparison; define the family by
pattern-matching `PauliAnswer → Op` with `0` on the other constructors — this is the
faithful reading of "answer summation over `u ∈ F_q^M`").

## (e) Settled encoding decisions (do not re-derive)

1. **Polynomials — representative convention** (issue #0004, `def:polynomials-degree`):
   polynomial-valued objects are representatives, not function classes. Reuse
   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Preliminaries.polyFunc` where a polynomial *class* is quantified.
   Game *answers* are finite coefficient tuples exactly as printed in the paper
   ("given by its d+1 coefficients"): `Fin (d+1) → K`, resp. `Fin (m*d+1) → K`.
   Do not reuse `LDT.AxisLinePolynomial`/`DiagonalLineAnswer` (the LDT diagonal answer
   is function-encoded and `Parameters`-bundled; a bridge can come later).
   `def:ld-meas`/`PolyMeas` are NOT in this closure — do not build them now.
2. **Distributions — match LDT, not PMF**: the LDT question distributions use
   `MIPStarRE.LDT.Distribution` (Finset-supported, real weights, `Error := ℝ`) with
   `IsProbability`, `avgOver`, `map`, `uniformDistribution`, `uniformOnFinset`
   (`LDT/Basic/Distribution.lean`, `DistributionUniform.lean`; product combinators in
   `DistributionProduct.lean` — verify the exact name before use). All QPBT question
   distributions are `Distribution` values; `PMF` only ever via the existing
   `DistributionPMF` bridge, never in game-facing statements.
3. **Measurements**: use `MIPStarRE.Quantum.Measurement`/`Submeasurement`
   (`Quantum/Measurement.lean`) as the POVM carrier; marginals and the bracket
   notation are `Measurement.postprocess` (already `\leanok` for ch12 `def:bracket`).
   Projectivity via `MIPStarRE.Quantum.IsProj`.
4. **States**: pure states as unit vectors of `EuclideanSpace ℂ ι` (the theorem's
   conclusion needs vector norms, isometries `→ₗᵢ[ℂ]` — reuse
   `Quantum/FiniteHilbert.lean` patterns — and `eprState`). The density-matrix
   `LDT.QuantumState` layer is NOT used in the QPBT games layer.
5. **Field model**: reuse `MIPStarRE.LDT.FieldModel q` (bundled `K ≃ Fin q`). The χ
   map (eq:chi-func) interprets `s : K` as an integer through `FieldModel.equiv`;
   the finite-field trace is the basis-independent `Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K`
   (= Tr of `Algebra.leftMulMatrix`, i.e. eq:def-trace). The self-dual normal basis
   and `def:binary-representation` are NOT in the statement closure and are deferred
   (see OPEN-6). `canonicalComplement` is defined basis-freely by the pivot
   characterization — `j` is a pivot of `W` iff restricting to coordinates `≤ j`
   increases rank — which agrees with the source's RREF construction by the
   basis-independence noted in `def:canonical-complement` (equivalence proof deferred).
6. **Qudit indexing**: the `M = 2^m` qudits and the vectors `F_q^M` are indexed by
   `Cube m := Fin m → Bool`. Never introduce `Fin (2^m)`; `M` appears only as
   `Fintype.card (Cube m)` in docstrings.
7. **Prose claims inside blueprint definitions become companion lemmas**: CL-level
   assertions ("`L_ALine` is a 2-level CL function"), uniformity of `χ(s)`,
   well-definedness remarks — each a named `sorry` lemma next to the definition, not
   a definitional obligation. Definitions themselves are direct and computable-shaped.
8. **Asymptotic `≈`/O(·) → quantitative functionals**: `def:state-distance` /
   `def:povm-distance` are encoded as explicit real error quantities (`stateDistSq`,
   `opFamilyDistSq`), mirroring how the LDT track already quantifies `≃`/`≈`
   (cf. rem:asymptotic-distance). The implicit universal constants of the blueprint's
   `≈_δ` are absorbed into the existentially quantified constant `a` of
   `pauli_soundness`; record this in the theorem docstring.
9. **Win predicates are `Bool`-valued**, answer alphabets are sum types, and
   "answers not of the prescribed form are rejected" is a predicate clause (match on
   constructor shape). Question alphabets are `Type × ambient-space` pairs — contents
   are full ambient vectors `ι → K` (images of the CL maps), not per-type refined
   types; this matches the blueprint's `(t, L_t(z))` format.
10. **`deltaQld` argument order** is `(ε, m, d, q)` with `0 < b < 1` strict and
    prefactor `a(md)^a` — per rem:delta-qld-argument-order; do not copy the classical
    `δ_ld` shape.

     3	/-!
     4	# Basic finite-dimensional matrix operators
     5	
     6	This module contains the elementary trace and matrix-algebra facts used by the
     7	finite-dimensional quantum layer.  It introduces the local operator abbreviation
     8	`Op d = Matrix d d ℂ` and keeps the basic trace bookkeeping independent of the
     9	positive-semidefinite order and normalized-trace material.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	The declarations in this file are matrix facts for the LDT
    14	formalization of `references/ldt-paper/`.
    15	-/
    16	
    17	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder Matrix.Norms.Elementwise
    18	open WithLp
    19	
    20	namespace Matrix
    21	
    22	/-! ### Trace bookkeeping -/
    23	
    24	/-- Reindexing rows and columns by the same equivalence preserves matrix trace.
    25	
    26	This generic matrix lemma is used when moving between equivalent finite index
    27	presentations of the same operator. -/
    28	theorem trace_reindex {α β R : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    29	    [AddCommMonoid R] (e : α ≃ β) (M : Matrix α α R) :
    30	    Matrix.trace (Matrix.reindex e e M) = Matrix.trace M := by
    31	  classical
    32	  simp only [Matrix.trace, Matrix.diag_apply, Matrix.reindex_apply]
    33	  rw [← e.symm.sum_comp (fun i : α => M i i)]
    34	  rfl
    35	
    36	/-! ### Linear matrix maps -/
    37	
    38	/-- Taking a submatrix is linear in the ambient matrix.
    39	
    40	This packages the entrywise linearity of `Matrix.submatrix` in the same style
    41	as Mathlib's block-diagonal additive and linear maps. -/
    42	def submatrixLinearMap (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    43	    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    44	    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) :
    45	    Matrix m n α →ₗ[R] Matrix m' n' α where
    46	  toFun := fun A => Matrix.submatrix A row col
    47	  map_add' := by
    48	    intro A B
    49	    ext i j
    50	    rfl
    51	  map_smul' := by
    52	    intro c A
    53	    ext i j
    54	    rfl
    55	
    56	@[simp]
    57	theorem submatrixLinearMap_apply (R : Type*) {m n m' n' α : Type*}
    58	    [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid α] [Module R α]
    59	    (row : m' → m) (col : n' → n) (A : Matrix m n α) :
    60	    Matrix.submatrixLinearMap R row col A = Matrix.submatrix A row col :=
    61	  rfl
    62	
    63	/-- The trace pairing of two block-diagonal matrices is the sum of the trace
    64	pairings of the corresponding diagonal blocks. -/
    65	theorem trace_blockDiagonal_mul {o m R : Type*}
    66	    [Fintype o] [DecidableEq o] [Fintype m] [NonUnitalNonAssocSemiring R]
    67	    (B D : o → Matrix m m R) :
    68	    Matrix.trace (Matrix.blockDiagonal B * Matrix.blockDiagonal D) =
    69	      ∑ b : o, Matrix.trace (B b * D b) := by
    70	  rw [← Matrix.blockDiagonal_mul B D, Matrix.trace_blockDiagonal]
    71	
    72	end Matrix
    73	
    74	namespace MIPStarRE.Quantum
    75	
    76	/-! ### Basic operator type -/
    77	
    78	/-- Square complex matrices as the finite-dimensional operator algebra. -/
    79	abbrev Op (d : Type*) := Matrix d d ℂ
    80	
    81	/-! ### Kronecker product bookkeeping -/
    82	
    83	/-- Kronecker product is additive in the right factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
    84	theorem kronecker_sub_right
    85	    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A : Op d₁} {B₁ B₂ : Op d₂} :
    86	    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂ =
    87	      Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
    88	  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) = -Matrix.kronecker A B₂ := by
    89	    simpa using (Matrix.kronecker_smul (-1 : ℂ) A B₂)
    90	  calc
    91	    Matrix.kronecker A B₁ - Matrix.kronecker A B₂
    92	        = Matrix.kronecker A B₁ + Matrix.kronecker A (-B₂) := by
    93	            rw [hneg]
    94	            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
    95	    _ = Matrix.kronecker A (B₁ - B₂) := by
    96	          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.kronecker_add A B₁ (-B₂)).symm
    97	
    98	/-- Kronecker product is additive in the left factor, rewritten for subtraction. -/
    99	theorem kronecker_sub_left
   100	    {d₁ d₂ : Type*} {A₁ A₂ : Op d₁} {B : Op d₂} :
   101	    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B =
   102	      Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
   103	  have hneg : Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B = -Matrix.kronecker A₂ B := by
   104	    simpa using (Matrix.smul_kronecker (-1 : ℂ) A₂ B)
   105	  calc
   106	    Matrix.kronecker A₁ B - Matrix.kronecker A₂ B
   107	        = Matrix.kronecker A₁ B + Matrix.kronecker (-A₂) B := by
   108	            rw [hneg]
   109	            simp [sub_eq_add_neg]
   110	    _ = Matrix.kronecker (A₁ - A₂) B := by
   111	          simpa [sub_eq_add_neg] using (Matrix.add_kronecker A₁ (-A₂) B).symm
   112	
   113	end MIPStarRE.Quantum

    20	inductive Role where
    21	  | A
    22	  | B
    23	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    24
