    32	/-- Parameters for the `(m,q,d)` low individual degree test.
    33	
    34	Besides the usual positivity assumptions, we bundle the paper-faithful witness
    35	that `q = p^n` is a prime power. -/
    36	structure Parameters where
    37	  m : ℕ
    38	  q : ℕ
    39	  d : ℕ
    40	  hm : 0 < m
    41	  /-- Kept as a compatibility field so existing positivity proofs can continue
    42	  to use `params.hq`; it is derivable from `hqPrimePower`. -/
    43	  hq : 0 < q
    44	  /-- Paper-faithful witness that `q` is a prime power. -/
    45	  hqPrimePower : ∃ p n, Nat.Prime p ∧ 0 < n ∧ q = p ^ n
    46	
    47	deriving instance DecidableEq for Parameters
    48	
    49	namespace Parameters
    50	
    51	/-- Any number presented as a prime power is automatically positive. -/
    52	theorem q_pos_of_primePower {q : ℕ}
    53	    (hqPrimePower : ∃ p n, Nat.Prime p ∧ 0 < n ∧ q = p ^ n) : 0 < q := by
    54	  rcases hqPrimePower with ⟨p, n, hp, hn, rfl⟩
    55	  exact Nat.pow_pos hp.pos
    56	
    57	/-- Prime numbers are prime powers of exponent `1`. -/
    58	theorem prime_primePower {q : ℕ} (hqPrime : Nat.Prime q) :
    59	    ∃ p n, Nat.Prime p ∧ 0 < n ∧ q = p ^ n := by
    60	  exact ⟨q, 1, hqPrime, by decide, by simp⟩
    61	
    62	/-- Build parameters from explicit prime-power data `q = p^n`. -/
    63	def ofPrimePower (m q d p n : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m) (hp : Nat.Prime p) (hn : 0 < n)
    64	    (hq : q = p ^ n) : Parameters :=
    65	  { m := m
    66	    q := q
    67	    d := d
    68	    hm := hm
    69	    hq := q_pos_of_primePower ⟨p, n, hp, hn, hq⟩
    70	    hqPrimePower := ⟨p, n, hp, hn, hq⟩ }
    71	
    72	/-- Build parameters when `q` itself is prime. -/
    73	def ofPrime (m q d : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m) (hqPrime : Nat.Prime q) : Parameters :=
    74	  { m := m
    75	    q := q
    76	    d := d
    77	    hm := hm
    78	    hq := hqPrime.pos
    79	    hqPrimePower := prime_primePower hqPrime }
    80	
    81	/-- Convenience constructor for the ubiquitous binary field. -/
    82	def ofTwo (m d : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m) : Parameters :=

    84	
    85	/-- Paper finite fields have at least two elements: `q = p^n` with `p` prime
    86	and `0 < n` (see `preliminaries.tex`, lines 17--19 and 89--93). -/
    87	theorem two_le_q (params : Parameters) : 2 ≤ params.q := by
    88	  obtain ⟨p, n, hp, hn, hq⟩ := params.hqPrimePower
    89	  rw [hq]
    90	  exact le_trans hp.two_le (Nat.le_self_pow (Nat.ne_of_gt hn) p)
    91	
    92	/-- The field-size parameter is strictly larger than `1`. -/
    93	theorem one_lt_q (params : Parameters) : 1 < params.q :=
    94	  lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.one_lt_two params.two_le_q
    95	
    96	/-- Positivity of the field-size parameter after casting to the repository's
    97	real-valued error scalar type. -/
    98	theorem q_cast_pos (params : Parameters) : 0 < (params.q : Error) :=
    99	  Nat.cast_pos.mpr params.hq

   101	end Parameters

   106	/-- The successor test obtained by appending one coordinate. -/
   107	def Parameters.next (params : Parameters) : Parameters :=

   109	    q := params.q
   110	    d := params.d

   117	/-- The predecessor parameters obtained by removing the last coordinate from a
   118	non-base ambient dimension.
   119	
   120	This is the inverse construction to `Parameters.next` on the data fields.  The
   121	proof fields are inherited from the original parameter bundle, so the inverse is
   122	propositional rather than definitional. -/
   123	def previous (params : Parameters) (hm : 1 < params.m) : Parameters :=
   124	  { m := params.m - 1
   125	    q := params.q
   126	    d := params.d
   127	    hm := Nat.sub_pos_of_lt hm
   128	    hq := params.hq
   129	    hqPrimePower := params.hqPrimePower }
   130	
   131	/-- Removing the last coordinate and then applying `Parameters.next` recovers the
   132	original non-base parameters. -/
   133	theorem previous_next_eq (params : Parameters) (hm : 1 < params.m) :
   134	    (previous params hm).next = params := by
   135	  cases params with
   136	  | mk m q d hm0 hq hqPrimePower =>
   137	      have hsub : m - 1 + 1 = m := Nat.sub_add_cancel (le_of_lt hm)
   138	      simp [previous, Parameters.next, hsub]

   140	/-- A bundled predecessor for a parameter set known to be a successor dimension. -/
   141	structure SuccessorDecomposition (params : Parameters) where
   142	  /-- The predecessor parameter bundle. -/
   143	  pred : Parameters
   144	  /-- The predecessor's successor is the original parameter bundle. -/
   145	  next_eq : pred.next = params

   147	/-- Every parameter bundle of dimension strictly larger than one has a bundled
   148	predecessor whose successor is propositionally equal to the original bundle. -/

   152	  next_eq := previous_next_eq params hm

   163	  successorDecompositionOfOneLtM params (one_lt_m_of_ne_one params hm_ne_one)

   183	structure PrimePowerFieldSpec (params : Parameters) where
   184	  p : ℕ
   185	  n : ℕ
   186	  pPrime : Nat.Prime p
   187	  nPos : 0 < n
   188	  cardEq : params.q = p ^ n

   192	    (params : Parameters) : PrimePowerFieldSpec params :=
   193	  have : Nonempty (PrimePowerFieldSpec params) := by
   194	    obtain ⟨p, n, hp, hn, hq⟩ := params.hqPrimePower
   195	    exact ⟨{
   196	      p := p
   197	      n := n
   198	      pPrime := hp
   199	      nPos := hn

   201	    }⟩
   202	  this.some

   204	/-- An honest finite field of order `q`, obtained from the prime-power
   205	witness bundled in `Parameters`. -/
   206	noncomputable abbrev HonestFq (params : Parameters) (spec : PrimePowerFieldSpec params) :=
   207	  letI : Fact spec.p.Prime := ⟨spec.pPrime⟩
   208	  GaloisField spec.p spec.n

   210	/-- A bundled field model for the paper's `F_q`, together with a coding equivalence
   211	to the repository's finite carrier `Fin q`. -/
   212	class FieldModel (q : ℕ) where
   213	  K : Type*
   214	  instField : Field K
   215	  instFintype : Fintype K
   216	  instDecidableEq : DecidableEq K
   217	  equiv : K ≃ Fin q

   219	attribute [instance_reducible, instance] FieldModel.instField FieldModel.instFintype
   220	  FieldModel.instDecidableEq

   223	
   224	/-- The carrier bundled in a `FieldModel q` has exactly `q` elements, matching the
   225	paper's finite-field convention `|F_q| = q` (`preliminaries.tex`, lines 17--19). -/

   227	    Fintype.card (FieldModel.K q) = q := by
   228	  simpa using Fintype.card_congr (FieldModel.equiv (q := q))

   233	  Fintype.card_pos_iff.mpr ⟨0⟩
   234	
   235	/-- The finite cardinality of a bundled field model is nonzero. -/
   236	theorem card_ne_zero (q : ℕ) [FieldModel q] :
   237	    Fintype.card (FieldModel.K q) ≠ 0 :=
   238	  Nat.ne_of_gt (card_pos q)
   239	
   240	end FieldModel

     9	
    10	* `Submeasurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to at most the identity.
    11	* `Measurement` — a family of PSD matrices summing to exactly the identity.
    12	* `Submeasurement.postprocess` — data-processed submeasurements via answer relabeling.
    13	* `Measurement.postprocess` — the paper's postprocessing proposition for complete POVMs.
    14	* `inconsistency` — the off-diagonal mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`.
    15	* `diagOverlap` — the diagonal mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`.
    16	
    17	## References
    18	
    19	This file builds the project's finite-dimensional measurement layer on top of
    20	the normalized-trace and positive-operator facts in `MIPStarRE.Quantum.FiniteMatrix`
    21	for the quantum formalization in `references/ldt-paper/`.
    22	-/

    26	namespace MIPStarRE.Quantum
    27	
    28	/-! ## Submeasurements and measurements -/
    29	
    30	/--
    31	A submeasurement on a finite answer type `α` is a family of PSD matrices
    32	`M : α → Op d` with `∑ a, M a ≤ 1`.
    33	-/
    34	structure Submeasurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d] where
    35	  /-- The effect operators. -/
    36	  effect : α → Op d
    37	  /-- Each effect is positive semidefinite. -/
    38	  pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a
    39	  /-- The effects sum to at most the identity. -/
    40	  sum_le_one : ∑ a, effect a ≤ 1
    41	
    42	/--
    43	A measurement is a submeasurement whose effects sum exactly to the identity.
    44	-/
    45	structure Measurement (α : Type*) [Fintype α] (d : Type*) [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    46	    extends Submeasurement α d where
    47	  /-- The effects sum to the identity. -/
    48	  sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1
    49	
    50	/-! ## Totals and postprocessing -/
    51	
    52	namespace Submeasurement
    53	
    54	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    55	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
    56	
    57	/-! ### Totals and postprocessing -/
    58	
    59	/-- The total operator `∑ a, M_a`. -/
    60	noncomputable def total (M : Submeasurement α d) : Op d :=
    61	  ∑ a, M.effect a
    62	
    63	/--
    64	Data processing: relabel the answer set by `f : α → β`, summing the effects over
    65	fibers.
    66	-/
    67	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    68	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) : Submeasurement β d where
    69	  effect b := ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    70	  pos b := Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => M.pos a
    71	  sum_le_one := by
    72	    calc
    73	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
    74	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
    75	      _ ≤ 1 := M.sum_le_one
    76	
    77	/-- Restatement of `sum_le_one` in terms of the named total operator. -/
    78	theorem total_le_one (M : Submeasurement α d) :
    79	    M.total ≤ 1 := by
    80	  simpa [total] using M.sum_le_one
    81	
    82	/-- Postprocessing preserves the sum of all effects. -/
    83	theorem postprocess_sum_eq [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    84	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    85	    ∑ a, M.effect a = ∑ b, (M.postprocess f).effect b :=
    86	  (Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect).symm
    87	
    88	/-- Postprocessing preserves the named total operator. -/
    89	theorem postprocess_total [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    90	    (M : Submeasurement α d) (f : α → β) :
    91	    (M.postprocess f).total = M.total := by
    92	  simpa [total] using (M.postprocess_sum_eq f).symm
    93	
    94	end Submeasurement
    95	
    96	namespace Measurement
    97	
    98	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    99	variable {α β : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype β]
   100	
   101	/--
   102	Build a complete measurement from effects whose sum is exactly the identity.
   103	
   104	This constructor keeps the equality proof as the primary hypothesis and derives
   105	the inherited submeasurement inequality automatically.  It is useful at paper
   106	sites that are explicitly POVMs rather than relaxed sub-POVMs.
   107	-/
   108	def ofSumEqOne (effect : α → Op d) (pos : ∀ a, 0 ≤ effect a)
   109	    (sum_eq_one : ∑ a, effect a = 1) : Measurement α d where
   110	  effect := effect
   111	  pos := pos
   112	  sum_le_one := le_of_eq sum_eq_one
   113	  sum_eq_one := sum_eq_one
   114	
   115	/-- The named total of a complete measurement is the identity. -/
   116	theorem total_eq_one (M : Measurement α d) :
   117	    M.total = 1 :=
   118	  M.sum_eq_one
   119	
   120	/--
   121	Postprocess a complete measurement by relabeling outcomes.
   122	
   123	This formalizes `references/ldt-paper/preliminaries.tex:169--180`: regrouping
   124	the effects along the fibers of `f` preserves the total operator, so a POVM
   125	remains a POVM after postprocessing.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def postprocess [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   128	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) : Measurement β d where
   129	  toSubmeasurement := M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f
   130	  sum_eq_one := by
   131	    calc
   132	      ∑ b, ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a
   133	          = ∑ a, M.effect a := Finset.sum_fiberwise Finset.univ f M.effect
   134	      _ = 1 := M.sum_eq_one
   135	
   136	@[simp] theorem postprocess_effect [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   137	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) (b : β) :
   138	    (M.postprocess f).effect b =
   139	      ∑ a ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun a => f a = b), M.effect a :=
   140	  rfl
   141	
   142	@[simp] theorem postprocess_to_submeasurement [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
   143	    (M : Measurement α d) (f : α → β) :
   144	    (M.postprocess f).toSubmeasurement = M.toSubmeasurement.postprocess f :=
   145	  rfl
   146	
   147	end Measurement
   148	
   149	/-! ## Overlap definitions -/
   150	
   151	section Overlap
   152	
   153	variable {d : Type*} [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
   154	variable {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α]
   155	
   156	/-- The off-diagonal overlap mass `∑_{a ≠ b} τ(M_a N_b)`. -/
   157	noncomputable def inconsistency (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   158	  ∑ a, ∑ b ∈ Finset.univ.filter (fun b => b ≠ a), normalizedTrace (M a * N b)
   159	
   160	/-- The diagonal overlap mass `∑_a τ(M_a N_a)`. -/
   161	noncomputable def diagOverlap (M N : α → Op d) : ℂ :=
   162	  ∑ a, normalizedTrace (M a * N a)
   163	
   164	end Overlap
   165	
   166	end MIPStarRE.Quantum

     6	# Distribution infrastructure for the low individual degree test
     7	
     8	Shared distribution definitions: finite-support weighted distributions,
     9	a probability predicate, push-forward distributions, weighted-sum linear maps,
    10	averaging, uniform distribution, and outcome summation.

    12	Note: this module contributes declarations to the comparator statement closure
    13	of `mainFormal`, which must elaborate in the same environment as the
    14	Mathlib-only `Challenge.lean`.  Keep the full `import Mathlib`; do not narrow
    15	it.  See `docs/comparator.md`, "Environment alignment".

    18	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder

    20	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    21	
    22	/-- A finite-support weighted distribution with nonnegative real-valued weights. -/
    23	structure Distribution (α : Type*) where
    24	  support : Finset α := ∅
    25	  weight : α → Error := fun _ => 0
    26	  nonnegative : ∀ a, 0 ≤ weight a := by intro _; positivity
    27	  outsideSupport : ∀ a, a ∉ support → weight a = 0 := by intro _ _; rfl
    28	
    29	namespace Distribution
    30	
    31	/-- The total mass carried by the explicit support of a distribution. -/
    32	def totalWeight {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Error :=
    33	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a
    34	
    35	/-- A `Distribution` is probabilistic when its total mass is exactly `1`. -/
    36	def IsProbability {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Prop :=
    37	  𝒟.totalWeight = 1
    38	
    39	/-- Push a finite-support distribution forward along a map.
    40	
    41	This is the project `Distribution` analogue of `PMF.map`.  The support is the
    42	image of the original finite support, and each new weight is the sum of the
    43	weights in the corresponding fiber. -/
    44	noncomputable def map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    45	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) : Distribution β where
    46	  support := 𝒟.support.image e
    47	  weight := fun b => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a
    48	  nonnegative := fun _ => Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a
    49	  outsideSupport := fun _ hb =>
    50	    Finset.sum_eq_zero fun a ha =>
    51	      (hb (Finset.mem_image.mpr
    52	        ⟨a, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).1, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2⟩)).elim
    53	
    54	@[simp]
    55	theorem map_support {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    56	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    57	    (𝒟.map e).support = 𝒟.support.image e := rfl
    58	
    59	@[simp]
    60	theorem map_weight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    61	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (b : β) :
    62	    (𝒟.map e).weight b =
    63	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a := rfl
    64	
    65	/-- Push-forward preserves total mass. -/
    66	theorem map_totalWeight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    67	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    68	    (𝒟.map e).totalWeight = 𝒟.totalWeight := by
    69	  simpa [totalWeight, map] using
    70	    (Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    71	      (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    72	      (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩) 𝒟.weight)
    73	
    74	/-- A finite weighted sum over a push-forward distribution is the corresponding
    75	weighted sum of the pulled-back family.  This is the `Distribution` analogue of
    76	the finite-sum form of `PMF.map`. -/
    77	theorem map_sum_smul {α β M : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    78	    [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
    79	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → M) :
    80	    ∑ b ∈ (𝒟.map e).support, (𝒟.map e).weight b • f b =
    81	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    82	  classical
    83	  calc
    84	    ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    85	        (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a) • f b
    86	        = ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    87	            ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    88	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    89	          intro b _
    90	          rw [Finset.sum_smul]
    91	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    92	          intro a ha
    93	          exact congrArg (fun x => 𝒟.weight a • f x) (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2.symm
    94	    _ = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    95	          exact Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    96	            (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    97	            (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩)
    98	            (fun a => 𝒟.weight a • f (e a))
    99	
   100	end Distribution
   101	
   102	/-- On a finite ambient type, a summand that vanishes outside a distribution's
   103	explicit support has the same total sum over all ambient values as over that support.
   104	
   105	This is a project-local explicit-support adapter around Mathlib's `Finset.sum_subset`:
   106	Mathlib supplies the finite-sum theorem, while this lemma packages the common shape used
   107	when paper expressions sum over a whole question set but the repository stores a smaller
   108	`Distribution.support`.  It is not intended to replace Mathlib probability theory. -/
   109	theorem Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support {α β : Type*} [Fintype α]
   110	    [AddCommMonoid β] (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → β)
   111	    (hf : ∀ a, a ∉ 𝒟.support → f a = 0) :
   112	    (∑ a : α, f a) = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, f a := by
   113	  classical
   114	  simpa using
   115	    (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   116	      (fun a _ ha => hf a ha)).symm
   117	
   118	namespace Distribution.IsProbability
   119	
   120	/-- Unpack the equality form of the probability invariant. -/
   121	theorem weight_sum_eq_one {α : Type*}
   122	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   123	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   124	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.totalWeight] using h𝒟
   125	
   126	/-- On a finite ambient type, a probabilistic `Distribution` has total weight `1` even
   127	when its weights are summed over the whole ambient type.
   128	
   129	This packages the explicit-support bookkeeping in `Distribution` for downstream Lean
   130	statements that follow the paper's notation `𝔼_{x ∼ 𝒟}` over the question set rather
   131	than over a stored support finset. -/
   132	theorem weight_sum_univ_eq_one {α : Type*} [Fintype α]
   133	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   134	    (∑ a : α, 𝒟.weight a) = 1 := by
   135	  rw [Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support 𝒟 𝒟.weight 𝒟.outsideSupport]
   136	  exact h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   137	
   138	/-- A probability distribution has total weight at most `1`. -/
   139	theorem weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*}
   140	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   141	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a ≤ 1 :=
   142	  le_of_eq h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   143	
   144	/-- Push-forward preserves the probability invariant. -/
   145	theorem map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   146	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   147	    (𝒟.map e).IsProbability := by
   148	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.map_totalWeight] using h𝒟
   149	
   150	end Distribution.IsProbability
   151	
   152	namespace Distribution
   153	
   154	/-- The Mathlib probability mass function associated to a project `Distribution`
   155	whose total mass is one.
   156	
   157	The construction sends each nonnegative real weight to `ℝ≥0∞` by
   158	`ENNReal.ofReal`; the hypotheses of `PMF.ofFinset` are exactly the project
   159	probability invariant and the stored zero-off-support condition. -/
   160	noncomputable def toPMF {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   161	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) : PMF α :=
   162	  PMF.ofFinset (fun a => ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a)) 𝒟.support
   163	    (by
   164	      rw [← ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a),
   165	        h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one]
   166	      simp)
   167	    (by
   168	      intro a ha
   169	      rw [𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   170	      simp)
   171	
   172	@[simp]
   173	theorem toPMF_apply {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   174	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   175	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a) := rfl
   176	
   177	@[simp]
   178	theorem toPMF_apply_toReal {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   179	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (a : α) :
   180	    (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a).toReal = 𝒟.weight a := by
   181	  rw [toPMF_apply, ENNReal.toReal_ofReal (𝒟.nonnegative a)]
   182	
   183	/-- The associated PMF has zero mass outside the stored support of the project
   184	distribution. -/
   185	theorem toPMF_apply_of_notMem {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   186	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) {a : α} (ha : a ∉ 𝒟.support) :
   187	    𝒟.toPMF h𝒟 a = 0 := by
   188	  rw [toPMF_apply, 𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   189	  simp
   190	
   191	/-- The project push-forward agrees with Mathlib's push-forward of the
   192	associated probability mass function. -/
   193	theorem toPMF_map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   194	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   195	    (𝒟.map e).toPMF (h𝒟.map e) = (𝒟.toPMF h𝒟).map e := by
   196	  classical
   197	  ext b
   198	  rw [toPMF_apply, PMF.map_apply, map_weight]
   199	  rw [ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg
   200	    (s := 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b))
   201	    (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a)]
   202	  rw [tsum_eq_sum (s := 𝒟.support)]
   203	  · rw [Finset.sum_filter]
   204	    refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
   205	    intro a ha
   206	    by_cases hea : e a = b
   207	    · have hba : b = e a := hea.symm
   208	      rw [if_pos hea, if_pos hba, toPMF_apply]
   209	    · have hba : b ≠ e a := fun hba => hea hba.symm
   210	      rw [if_neg hea, if_neg hba]
   211	  · intro a ha
   212	    by_cases hba : b = e a
   213	    · rw [if_pos hba, toPMF_apply_of_notMem 𝒟 h𝒟 ha]
   214	    · rw [if_neg hba]
   215	
   216	end Distribution

   218	/-- Average a scalar function against the stored finite support of a distribution. -/
   219	def avgOver {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → Error) : Error :=
   220	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a * f a
   221	
   222	namespace Distribution
   223	
   224	/-- The module-valued weighted finite sum associated to a finite-support `Distribution`,
   225	as a linear map in the averaged family.
   226	
   227	This packages the finite-support expression underlying both scalar averages and
   228	operator averages.  It keeps the explicit support carried by `Distribution`,
   229	while exposing the `Error`-module structure of the weighted sum. -/
   230	noncomputable def weightedSumLinearMap (M : Type*) [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
   231	    {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : (α → M) →ₗ[Error] M where
   232	  toFun := fun f => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a
   233	  map_add' := fun f g => by
   234	    simp only [Pi.add_apply, smul_add, Finset.sum_add_distrib]
   235	  map_smul' := fun c f => by
   236	    simp only [Pi.smul_apply]
   237	    calc
   238	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • c • f a =
   239	          ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, c • (𝒟.weight a • f a) := by
   240	            refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
   241	            intro a _
   242	            rw [smul_smul, smul_smul, mul_comm]
   243	      _ = c • ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a := by
   244	            rw [Finset.smul_sum]
   245	
   246	@[simp]
   247	theorem weightedSumLinearMap_apply (M : Type*) [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
   248	    {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → M) :
   249	    𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap M f = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a :=
   250	  rfl
   251	
   252	/-- The scalar average is the weighted finite-sum linear map applied to a scalar
   253	family. -/
   254	theorem avgOver_eq_weightedSumLinearMap {α : Type*}
   255	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → Error) :
   256	    avgOver 𝒟 f = 𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap Error f := by
   257	  simp [avgOver, smul_eq_mul]
   258	
   259	/-- Averaging against a pushed-forward distribution is averaging the pulled-back
   260	function against the original distribution. -/
   261	theorem avgOver_map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   262	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → Error) :
   263	    avgOver (𝒟.map e) f = avgOver 𝒟 (fun a => f (e a)) := by
   264	  simpa [avgOver, smul_eq_mul] using
   265	    Distribution.map_sum_smul (𝒟 := 𝒟) e f
   266	
   267	end Distribution
   268	
   269	/-- Weighted sum of operators over a distribution's finite support, using the same
   270	`support`/`weight` data as the scalar `avgOver`.
   271	
   272	This is a project-local adapter around Mathlib finite sums for the LDT
   273	`Distribution` representation and `Quantum.Op` scalar action, not a replacement for
   274	Mathlib's probability theory APIs. -/
   275	noncomputable def averageOperatorOverDistribution {α : Type*}
   276	    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   277	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι :=
   278	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f a
   279	
   280	namespace Distribution
   281	
   282	/-- Operator averaging is the weighted finite-sum linear map applied to an
   283	operator-valued family. -/
   284	theorem averageOperatorOverDistribution_eq_weightedSumLinearMap {α : Type*}
   285	    (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   286	    {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   287	    (f : α → MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) :
   288	    averageOperatorOverDistribution 𝒟 f =
   289	      𝒟.weightedSumLinearMap (MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op ι) f :=

/-!
# Generalized Pauli operators and EPR states

The definitions here use finite matrix entries and rank-one projectors, so they
are usable by the later game statements without introducing an abstract
operator algebra.  The Fourier/orthogonality identities are retained as named
proof obligations for subsequent stages.

## References

The source-facing nodes are `def:lin-reg`, `def:EPR`, `def:generalized-pauli`,
and `lem:pauli-observable-expansion` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:494-652`.  The paper origin is
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:908-1161`.
-/

open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.Quantum

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
  [Algebra (ZMod 2) K]

/-- The two generalized Pauli bases used by the test in `def:generalized-pauli`,
blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
-/
inductive PauliKind where
  | X
  | Z
  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype

/-- The binary character used for generalized Pauli phases; see
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1081`.

It is public because the Fourier expansion declarations below expose this
character in their statement types. -/
noncomputable def phaseSign (t : ZMod 2) : ℂ :=
  if t = 0 then 1 else -1

/--
The shift operator `τ^X(a)`.  Blueprint `def:generalized-pauli`,
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
-/
noncomputable def tauShift (a : K) : Op K :=
  fun i j => if i = j + a then 1 else 0

/--
The phase operator `τ^Z(b)`, with the fixed binary trace in the phase.  It is
the second operator of `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 529-571; paper
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`).
-/
noncomputable def tauPhase (b : K) : Op K :=
  fun i j => if i = j then phaseSign (binTrace K (b * j)) else 0

/-- The single-qudit eigenvector coordinate used in the tensor-product basis;
see `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1126-1161`. -/
private noncomputable def singlePauliVec (W : PauliKind) (e x : K) : ℂ :=
  match W with
  | .Z => if x = e then 1 else 0
  | .X =>
      (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card K : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * phaseSign (binTrace K (e * x))

/--
The normalized single/multi-qudit eigenvector for a Pauli basis label.  For an
index type `ι`, the input `e : ι → K` labels the tensor-product basis vector.
This is the vector form of `def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:550-570`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`.
-/
noncomputable def pauliVec {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) (x : ι → K) : ℂ :=
  ∏ i : ι, singlePauliVec W (e i) (x i)

/--
The rank-one projector onto `pauliVec W e`.  This is the projective measurement
element `τ^W_e` in `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 562-570; paper
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`).
-/
noncomputable def pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
  Matrix.vecMulVec (pauliVec W e) (fun x => star (pauliVec W e x))

/-- A compact operator-valued form of a generalized Pauli observable from
`def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
-/
noncomputable def tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
  fun x y =>
    ∏ i : ι,
      match W with
      | .X => tauShift (a i) (x i) (y i)
      | .Z => tauPhase (a i) (x i) (y i)

/--
The EPR vector on a finite label space.  Blueprint `def:EPR`,
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:513-523`; paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`.
-/
noncomputable def eprState (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
    EuclideanSpace ℂ (V × V) :=
  (EuclideanSpace.equiv (V × V) ℂ).symm
    (fun p : V × V =>
      if p.1 = p.2 then (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card V : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ else 0)

/-- The EPR vector is normalized on a nonempty finite carrier; see
`def:EPR`, `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`. -/
theorem eprState_norm (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
    ‖eprState V‖ = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Fourier expansion of a generalized Pauli observable in the Pauli projectors.
This is `lem:pauli-observable-expansion`, equations `eq:pauli-obs-proj` and
`eq:pauli-inversion-0`, in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`;
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
Both directions are deliberately left as proof-level obligations in stage 4.1.
-/
theorem tauObservable_eq_sum_pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) :
    tauObservable W a =
      ∑ e : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • pauliProj W e := by
  sorry

/-- The inverse Fourier expansion of a Pauli projector
(`lem:pauli-observable-expansion`), blueprint
`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
-/
theorem pauliProj_eq_avg_tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) :
    pauliProj W e =
      (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ •
        ∑ a : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • tauObservable W a := by
  sorry

end MIPStarRE.QPBT

1	\chapter{Algebraic preliminaries for the Pauli basis test}
     2	\label{chap:qpbt-algebra}
     3	
     4	This chapter records the algebraic preliminaries needed for the quantum Pauli
     5	basis test, following the preliminaries of \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}: subspace
     6	machinery over finite fields (which underlies the conditionally linear question
     7	distributions of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}), field extensions, traces, and
     8	self-dual bases, the low-degree code, lines in $\F_q^m$, and the generalized
     9	Pauli observables together with the EPR states they act on. Measurements,
    10	strategies, and consistency relations for nonlocal games are treated in
    11	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the test itself is defined in
    12	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}.
    13	
    14	\section{Linear spaces and subspaces}
    15	% Paper label sec:linear-spaces kept for cross-reference fidelity.
    16	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
    17	
    18	Linear spaces are always of the form $V = \F^n$ for a finite field $\F$ and an
    19	integer $n \ge 1$, unless explicitly stated otherwise. We write $\hat{E} =
    20	\{\hat{e}_1, \dots, \hat{e}_n\}$ for the standard basis of $V$, where
    21	$\hat{e}_i$ has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere, and
    22	$\mathrm{End}(V)$ for the set of linear maps from $V$ to itself.
    23	
    24	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]\label{def:register-subspace}
    25		A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
    26		subset of the standard basis of $V$. Such a subspace is represented by an
    27		indicator vector $u \in \{0,1\}^s$, where $s = \dim(V)$, via
    28		$S = \mathrm{span}\{\hat{e}_i : u_i = 1\}$.
    29	\end{definition}
    30	
    31	\begin{definition}[Dot product and orthogonal subspace]\label{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    32		For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$ and
    33		$v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V = \F^n$, the \emph{dot product} is
    34		\[
    35			u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
    36		\]
    37		For a subspace $S$ of $V$, the \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
    38		\[
    39			S^\perp = \bigl\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0 \text{ for all } v \in S \bigr\}\;.
    40		\]
    41		The notation $S^\perp$ leaves the ambient space $V$ implicit.
    42	\end{definition}
    43	
    44	Over finite fields, orthogonality lacks some of the familiar properties it has
    45	over $\R$ or $\C$; for example, a nonzero subspace may be orthogonal to itself,
    46	as is $\mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ over $\F_2$. The following dimension identity
    47	nevertheless holds over every field.
    48	
    49	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perp_perp}
    50		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    51		Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) = \dim(V)$, and
    52		\[
    53			(S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
    54		\]
    55	\end{lemma}
    56	\begin{proof}
    57		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    58		The elements of $S^\perp$ are the solutions of a feasible linear system whose
    59		coefficient matrix has $\dim(S)$ linearly independent rows, so the solution
    60		space has dimension exactly $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$. Every $u \in S$ is
    61		orthogonal to every element of $S^\perp$, so $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
    62		Applying the dimension identity twice shows that
    63		$\dim\bigl((S^\perp)^\perp\bigr) = \dim(S)$, so the inclusion is an equality.
    64	\end{proof}
    65	
    66	\begin{definition}[Complementary subspaces]\label{def:complementary}
    67		Two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of a linear space $V$ form a pair of
    68		\emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
    69		\[
    70			S \cap T = \{0\}\;, \qquad S + T = V\;.
    71		\]
    72		In this case we write $V = S \oplus T$. Every $x \in V$ can be written
    73		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    74		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    75		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    76		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    77	\end{definition}
    78	
    79	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    80	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    81	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    82	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
    98		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
    99		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   100		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   101		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   102		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   103		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   104		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   105		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   106		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   107		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   108		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   109		$S^\perp$.
   110	\end{definition}
   111	
   112	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   113		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   114		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   115		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   116		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   117		\[
   118			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   119		\]
   120	\end{lemma}
   121	\begin{proof}
   122		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   123		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   124		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   125		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   126		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   127		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   128		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   129		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   130		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   131	\end{proof}
   132	
   133	\begin{definition}[Canonical linear map with prescribed kernel]\label{def:cl-canonical}
   134		\uses{def:canonical-complement, lem:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   135		Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors and let
   136		$F^\perp$ be its canonical complement. The \emph{canonical linear map
   137		$L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ with kernel basis $F$} is the projector onto $T$
   138		parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and
   139		$T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$; this is well defined by
   140		Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement}. Since the canonical complement
   141		depends only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$
   142		(Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}), so does $L$, and we also call
   143		it the \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$}. Note that
   144		$\ker(L) = S$.
   145	\end{definition}
   146	
   147	\begin{definition}[The map $L^\perp$]\label{def:Lperp}
   148		\uses{def:cl-canonical, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   149		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map and let $F$ be a basis for
   150		$\ker(L)^\perp$. Define $L^\perp : V \to V$ as the canonical linear map with
   151		kernel basis $F$. (By the basis-independence noted in
   152		Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}, the map $L^\perp$ depends only
   153		on $\ker(L)$ and not on the chosen basis $F$.)
   154	\end{definition}
   155	
   156	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   157		\uses{def:Lperp}
   158		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map, $F$ a basis for
   159		$\ker(L)^\perp$, and $L^\perp$ as in Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}. Then
   160		$\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   161	\end{lemma}
   162	\begin{proof}
   163		\uses{def:Lperp, def:cl-canonical, lem:canonical-complement}
   164		Set $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$;
   165		by Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement} every $v \in V$ decomposes uniquely
   166		as $v = v^S + v^T$, and by definition $L^\perp v = v^T$. If
   167		$L^\perp v = 0$ then $v = v^S \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$. Conversely, if
   168		$v \in S$ then $v^T = 0$, so $L^\perp v = 0$.
   169	\end{proof}

   171	\section{Finite fields, traces, and self-dual bases}
   172	% Paper labels sec:finite-fields, sec:subfields, sec:ff-representations kept
   173	% for cross-reference fidelity.
   174	\label{sec:finite-fields}
   175	\label{sec:subfields}
   176	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   177	
   178	Let $p$ be a prime and $q = p^k$ a prime power. We write $\F_p$ and $\F_q$ for
   179	the finite fields with $p$ and $q$ elements; $p$ is the characteristic of
   180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.

180	$\F_q$, and $\F_p$ is its prime subfield.
   181	
   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists
   184		% only for k >= 1, so that domain condition is made explicit here.
   185		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a
   186		subfield of $\F_{q^k}$ and $\F_{q^k}$ is a linear space of dimension $k$
   187		over $\F_q$.
   188		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   189		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   190		\[
   191			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   192			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   193		\]
   194		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   195		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   196		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   197		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   198		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   199		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   200		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   201		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   202		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   203		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   204		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   205		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   206		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   207		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.
   208	\end{definition}
   209	
   210	\begin{definition}[Admissible field size]\label{def:admissible-size}
   211		A field size $q$ is \emph{admissible} if $q = 2^k$ for an odd integer $k$.
   212	\end{definition}
   213	
   214	Only fields $\F_{2^k}$ with $k$ odd are used in the analysis of the Pauli basis
   215	test.
   216	
   217	\begin{definition}[Trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$]\label{def:subfield-trace}
   218		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size}
   219		The \emph{trace of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$} is the map
   220		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   221		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-trace}
   222			\tr_{q^k \to q} : a \mapsto \Tr(K_a)
   223		\end{equation}
   224		for $a \in \F_{q^k}$, where $K_a$ is the multiplication table of $a$ with
   225		respect to the basis $\{e_i\}$. The trace is an $\F_q$-linear map from
   226		$\F_{q^k}$ to $\F_q$, and it is independent of the choice of basis, as can
   227		be seen from the equivalent formula
   228		\[
   229			\tr_{q^k \to q}(a) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} a^{q^j}\;.
   230		\]
   231		For admissible $q = 2^k$ we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q \to 2}$.
   232	\end{definition}
   233	
   234	\begin{definition}[Dual, self-dual, and normal bases]\label{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   235		\uses{def:subfield-trace}
   236		A \emph{dual basis} $\{e_1', \dots, e_k'\}$ of a basis
   237		$\{e_1, \dots, e_k\}$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$ is a basis such that
   238		$\tr_{q^k \to q}(e^{}_i e'_j) = \delta_{i,j}$ for all
   239		$i, j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$. A \emph{self-dual basis} is one equal to its own
   240		dual. If for some $\alpha \in \F_{q^k}$ the set
   241		$\{\alpha^{q^j}\}_{j=0}^{k-1}$ forms a basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$, that
   242		basis is called a \emph{normal basis}. Self-dual and normal bases do not
   243		exist for every field extension, but for $q = 2$ and odd $k$ a self-dual
   244		normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ always exists; \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}
   245		exhibits one through an explicit construction.
   246	\end{definition}
   247	
   248	\begin{lemma}[Coordinate maps of self-dual bases]\label{lem:downsize_field}
   249		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace,
   250			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   251		Let $q$ be a prime power, $k \ge 1$ an integer, and $\{e_i\}$ a self-dual
   252		basis of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The map $\kappa_q$ corresponding to
   253		$\{e_i\}$ satisfies:
   254		\begin{enumerate}
   255			\item for all $x \in \F_{q^k}$,
   256			      $\kappa_q(x) = \bigl(\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_1), \dots,
   257			      \tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_k)\bigr)$;
   258			\item for all $x, y \in \F_{q^k}$,
   259			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
   260			\item for all $M \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ and $v \in \F_{q^k}^n$,
   261			      $\chi_q(M)\, \kappa_q(v) = \kappa_q(Mv)$.
   262		\end{enumerate}
   263		Items 1 and 2 use self-duality; item 3 holds for an arbitrary basis.
   264	\end{lemma}
   265	\begin{proof}
   266		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   267		For item 1, write $x = \sum_i x_i e_i$, multiply both sides by $e_j$, and
   268		take traces: $\tr_{q^k \to q}(x e_j) = \sum_i x_i \tr_{q^k \to q}(e_i e_j)
   269		= x_j$ by self-duality. For item 2, expand
   270		$xy = \sum_{i,j} x_i y_j e_i e_j$ and take traces; self-duality retains
   271		exactly the diagonal terms, giving $\sum_i x_i y_i = \kappa_q(x) \cdot
   272		\kappa_q(y)$. For item 3, the $i$-th block of $\kappa_q(Mv)$ equals
   273		$\sum_j \kappa_q(M_{i,j} v_j) = \sum_j K_{M_{i,j}}\, \kappa_q(v_j)$, which
   274		is the $i$-th block row of $\chi_q(M)$ applied to $\kappa_q(v)$.
   275	\end{proof}
   276	
   277	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:one}
   278		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:subfield-trace, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   279		Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ a self-dual normal basis of
   280		$\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$. Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and the
   281		representation $\kappa(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all-ones
   282		vector in $\F_2^k$.
   283	\end{lemma}
   284	\begin{proof}
   285		\uses{lem:downsize_field}
   286		Normality gives $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$ (indices taken cyclically), and
   287		$\tr(b^2) = \tr(b)$ for every $b \in \F_{2^k}$ because squaring permutes the
   288		terms of $\tr(b) = \sum_{j=0}^{k-1} b^{2^j}$, using $b^{2^k} = b$. Hence all
   289		the values $\tr(e_i)$ coincide. If the common value were $0$, then $\tr$
   290		would vanish identically on $\F_{2^k}$ by linearity; but then item 1 of
   291		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} would give $\kappa(b) =
   292		(\tr(b e_1), \dots, \tr(b e_k)) = 0$ for every $b$, contradicting the
   293		bijectivity of $\kappa$. Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and item 1 of
   294		Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_field} gives
   295		$\kappa(1) = (\tr(e_1), \dots, \tr(e_k)) = (1, \dots, 1)$.
   296	\end{proof}
   297	
   298	\begin{definition}[Binary representation of field elements]\label{def:binary-representation}
   299		\uses{def:subfields-kappa, def:admissible-size,
   300			def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}
   301		Let $q = 2^k$ be an admissible field size. For each odd $k$ we fix, once and
   302		for all, a self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   303		$\F_2$ together with its multiplication tables
   304		$\{K_{e_i}\}_{i=1}^k$ (Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis});
   305		the maps $\kappa$ and $\tr$ always refer to this basis. The \emph{binary
   306		representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is the $k$-bit string
   307		$\kappa(a) \in \F_2^k$, the \emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}; the two are
   308		freely identified. Addition of representations is bitwise addition modulo
   309		$2$, and multiplication is determined by the multiplication tables through
   310		\begin{equation}\label{eq:eq-mult}
   311			\kappa(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i\, \kappa(e_i b)
   312			= \sum_{i=1}^k a_i \bigl(K_{e_i}\, \kappa(b)\bigr)\;,
   313		\end{equation}
   314		where $\kappa(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$.
   315	\end{definition}

   317	\section{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   318	% Paper label sec:ld-encoding kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   319	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   320	
   321	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree]\label{def:polynomials-degree}
   322		\uses{def:polyfunc}
   323		An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   324		\[
   325			f(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m}
   326			c_\alpha\, x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   327		\]
   328		with coefficients $c_\alpha \in \F_q$; the coefficients are uniquely
   329		determined by $f$, since the $q^m$ monomial functions indexed by
   330		$\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m$ span the $q^m$-dimensional space of all
   331		functions $\F_q^m \to \F_q$ and are therefore linearly independent. The
   332		polynomial $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if
   333		$c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when $\alpha_i \le d$ for all $1 \le i \le m$, and
   334		\emph{total degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when
   335		$\sum_i \alpha_i \le d$. (Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are those
   336		of individual degree $1$.
   337		% Relationship to def:polyfunc: polyfunc keeps polynomial representatives,
   338		% so evaluation identifies it with the function classes above only for
   339		% d <= q-1.
   340		Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc} introduces the set $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ of
   341		polynomials in $\F_q[x_1, \dots, x_m]$ of degree at most $d$ in each
   342		variable, identified by their polynomial representatives rather than by the
   343		functions they induce. Evaluation maps $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ onto the set of
   344		$m$-variate polynomials of individual degree at most $\min(d, q-1)$ in the
   345		sense above; for $d \le q-1$ this map is a bijection, while for $d \ge q$
   346		distinct representatives, such as $x_1^q$ and $x_1$, induce the same
   347		function. Statements phrased in terms of $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ retain the
   348		representative convention of Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}.
   349	\end{definition}
   350	
   351	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz--Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]\label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   352		% Restatement of lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree under the source's label.
   353		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   354		Let $f, g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials of total degree at
   355		most $d$. Then
   356		\[
   357			\Prb_{\bx \sim \F_q^m}[f(\bx) = g(\bx)] \le \frac{d}{q}\;.
   358		\]
   359	\end{lemma}
   360	\begin{proof}

360	\begin{proof}
   361		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   362		This is Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, stated and proved in
   363		Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries}; it is restated here under the label used
   364		by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   365	\end{proof}
   366	
   367	\begin{remark}\label{rem:schwartz-zippel-restated}
   368		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel} restates the total-degree bound of
   369		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} under the label used by
   370		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. The individual-degree consequence,
   371		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-individual}, shows that distinct elements of
   372		$\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ agree on at most an $md/q$ fraction of the points of
   373		$\F_q^m$; the analysis of the Pauli basis test uses the bound in this
   374		individual-degree form.
   375	\end{remark}
   376	
   377	The Schwartz--Zippel lemma implies that low-degree polynomials form an
   378	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   379	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).
   380	
   381	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   382		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   383		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   384		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   385		\[
   386			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   387			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   388		\]
   389		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   390		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   391		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   392		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   393		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   394		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   395		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   396		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   397			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   398		\end{equation}
   399		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   400		degree at most $m$.
   401	\end{definition}
   402	
   403	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   404		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   405		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   406		\[
   407			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   408			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   409		\]
   410		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   411		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   412		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   413		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   414			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   415		\end{equation}
   416		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   417	\end{definition}
   418	
   419	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   420	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   421	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   422	
   423	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   424		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   425		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   426		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   427		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   428		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   429		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   430		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   431	\end{definition}

   433	\section{Lines}
   434	
   435	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   436	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   437	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   438	
   439	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   440		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   441		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   442		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   443			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   444		\end{equation}
   445		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   446		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   447		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   448		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   449		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   450		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   451		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   452		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   453	\end{definition}
   454	
   455	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   456		\uses{def:line}
   457		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   458		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   459	\end{proposition}
   460	\begin{proof}
   461		\uses{def:line}
   462		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   463		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   464		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   465		inclusion.
   466	\end{proof}
   467	
   468	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   469	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   470	representation is obtained as follows.
   471	
   472	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   473		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   474		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   475		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   476		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   477		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   478		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   479		\[
   480			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   481		\]
   482		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   483		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   484		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   485		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   486		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   487		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   488		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   489		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   490		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   491		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   492	\end{definition}

   494	\section{Quantum registers and EPR states}
   495	% Paper label sec:lin-reg kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   496	\label{sec:lin-reg}
   497	
   498	\begin{definition}[State space of a linear register]\label{def:lin-reg}
   499		\uses{def:complementary}
   500		For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension
   501		$|V|$, endowed with the canonical orthonormal basis
   502		$\{\ket{x}\}_{x \in V}$. A \emph{quantum state on $V$} is a unit vector
   503		$\ket{\psi}_V \in \C^V$. If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_i$ is a direct sum of
   504		subspaces over $\F$, then $\C^V$ is identified with
   505		$\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{V_i}$ by identifying
   506		$\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus x_k}$ with
   507		$\ket{x_1} \ot \dots \ot \ket{x_k}$. In particular, a basis $\{e_i\}$ of
   508		$V$ yields the decomposition $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k (\F e_i)$ and hence
   509		$\C^V = \bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{|\F|}$; the factors $\C^{|\F|}$ are called
   510		the \emph{qudits} of $\C^V$.
   511	\end{definition}
   512	
   513	\begin{definition}[EPR state]\label{def:EPR}
   514		\uses{def:lin-reg}
   515		For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, the \emph{EPR state} on
   516		$\C^V \ot \C^V$ is
   517		\[
   518			\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_V
   519			= \frac{1}{\sqrt{|V|}} \sum_{x \in V} \ket{x} \ot \ket{x}\;.
   520		\]
   521		We write $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}_{\F_q}$ and
   522		$\ket{\mathrm{EPR}}$ for $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_2}$.
   523	\end{definition}
   524	
   525	\section{Generalized Pauli observables}
   526	% Paper label sec:generalized-pauli kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   527	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
   528	
   529	\begin{definition}[Generalized Pauli observables]\label{def:generalized-pauli}
   530		\uses{def:subfield-trace, def:lin-reg}
   531		Let $p$ be a prime and $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$. The \emph{generalized Pauli
   532		observables over $\F_p$} are the unitaries on $\C^{\F_p}$ given by
   533		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-fp}
   534			\sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   535			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   536			\sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_p} \omega^{bj} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   537		\end{equation}
   538		for $a, b \in \F_p$, with arithmetic over $\F_p$. For $q = p^k$, the
   539		\emph{generalized Pauli observables over $\F_q$} are the unitaries on
   540		$\C^{\F_q}$
   541		\[
   542			\tau^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \ket{j + a}\bra{j}
   543			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   544			\tau^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \F_q} \omega^{\tr(bj)} \ket{j}\bra{j}
   545		\]
   546		for $a, b \in \F_q$, where $\tr$ here denotes $\tr_{q \to p}$
   547		(Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}); for admissible $q$ this agrees with
   548		the standing shorthand, $p = 2$, and $\omega = -1$, so that all phases are
   549		signs. All the $\tau^X$ operators commute with one another, as do all the
   550		$\tau^Z$ operators. Their common eigenbases consist of the vectors
   551		$\ket{e_W}$, labeled by $e \in \F_q$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
   552		\[
   553			\ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{j \in \F_q}
   554			\omega^{-\tr(ej)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
   555			\ket{e_Z} = \ket{e}\;;
   556		\]
   557		the Fourier transform
   558		\begin{equation}\label{eq:fourier-f}
   559			F = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b \in \F_q}
   560			\omega^{-\tr(ab)} \ket{a}\bra{b}
   561		\end{equation}

   567			\tau^W(a) = \tau^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \tau^W(a_n)\;, \qquad
   568			\ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}

   573	\begin{lemma}[Product and twisted commutation relations]\label{lem:twisted-commutation}
   574		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   575		Let $q = p^k$, let $n \ge 1$ be an integer, and let $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   576		\begin{enumerate}
   577			\item For all $a, a' \in \F_q$ and $b \in \F_p$,
   578			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
   579				      \tau^W(a)\, \tau^W(a') = \tau^W(a + a')
   580				      \qquad \text{and} \qquad
   581				      \bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^b = \tau^W(ab)\;;
   582			      \end{equation}
   583			      in particular $\bigl(\tau^W(a)\bigr)^p = \Id$, so each
   584			      $\tau^W(a)$ is a unitary with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots
   585			      of unity.
   586			\item For all $a, b \in \F_q^n$,
   587			      % Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   588			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fq}
   589				      \tau^X(a)\, \tau^Z(b)
   590				      = \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^Z(b)\, \tau^X(a)\;,
   591			      \end{equation}
   592			      where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i \in \F_q$. The case
   593			      $q = p$, $n = 1$ reads
   594			      \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-fp}
   595				      \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b)
   596				      = \omega^{-ab}\, \sigma^Z(b)\, \sigma^X(a)
   597				      \qquad \text{for all } a, b \in \F_p\;.
   598			      \end{equation}
   599		\end{enumerate}
   600	\end{lemma}
   601	\begin{proof}
   602		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   603		All identities are verified on computational basis states. For the product
   604		relations with $W = X$, shifting twice by $a'$ and $a$ equals shifting by
   605		$a + a'$; with $W = Z$, the phases $\omega^{\tr(aj)}\omega^{\tr(a'j)}$
   606		combine by $\F_q$-linearity of the trace, and the power relation follows by
   607		iterating. For the scalar twisted commutation,
   608		$\tau^X(a)\tau^Z(b)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$, while
   609		$\tau^Z(b)\tau^X(a)\ket{j} = \omega^{\tr(b(j+a))}\ket{j + a} =
   610		\omega^{\tr(ab)}\,\omega^{\tr(bj)}\ket{j + a}$. The multi-qudit relation
   611		follows by applying the scalar relation factor by factor and summing the
   612		exponents, using $\tr(a \cdot b) = \sum_i \tr(a_i b_i)$. For $q = p$ the
   613		trace is the identity map, which gives \eqref{eq:twisted-fp}.
   614	\end{proof}

   616	\begin{lemma}[Fourier cancellation over a subspace]\label{lem:cancellation}
   617		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal, def:subfield-trace}
   618		Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F_q^k$ and let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/p}$, where
   619		$p$ is the characteristic of $\F_q$ and $\tr = \tr_{q \to p}$. For all
   620		$v \notin V^\perp$,
   621		\[
   622			\E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr(\bu \cdot v)} = 0\;,
   623		\]
   624		where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $\bu$ in $V$.
   625	\end{lemma}
   626	\begin{proof}
   627		This is Fact 3.2 of \cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Since $v \notin V^\perp$,
   628		the $\F_q$-linear functional $u \mapsto u \cdot v$ is not identically zero
   629		on $V$, hence surjective onto $\F_q$; composing with the nonzero map $\tr$
   630		shows that there is $u_0 \in V$ with $\tr(u_0 \cdot v) \neq 0$. Writing $C$
   631		for the expectation, translation invariance of the uniform distribution on
   632		$V$ gives
   633		$C = \E_{\bu \sim V}\, \omega^{\tr((\bu + u_0) \cdot v)}
   634		= \omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)}\, C$, and $\omega^{\tr(u_0 \cdot v)} \neq 1$
   635		forces $C = 0$.
   636	\end{proof}

   638	\begin{lemma}[Fourier expansion of Pauli observables]\label{lem:pauli-observable-expansion}
   639		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, def:subfield-trace}
   640		For every integer $n \ge 1$, all $W \in \{X, Z\}$, and all $a \in \F_q^n$,
   641		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   642		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj}
   643			\tau^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \F_q^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}\, \tau^W_b\;,
   644		\end{equation}
   645		and conversely
   646		\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
   647			\E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\, \omega^{-\tr(\ba \cdot b)}\, \tau^W(\ba)
   648			= \sum_{b' \in \F_q^n} \E_{\ba \sim \F_q^n}\,
   649			\omega^{\tr(\ba \cdot (b' - b))}\, \tau^W_{b'}
   650			= \tau^W_b\;.
   651		\end{equation}
   652	\end{lemma}
   653	\begin{proof}
   654		\uses{def:generalized-pauli, lem:cancellation}
   655		Each $\ket{b_W}$ is an eigenvector of $\tau^W(a)$ with eigenvalue
   656		$\omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}$: for $W = Z$ this is immediate from the
   657		definition, and for $W = X$ it follows from the single-qudit computation
   658		$\tau^X(a)\ket{e_X} = \omega^{\tr(ae)}\ket{e_X}$, applied factor by factor.
   659		Expanding $\tau^W(a)$ in the orthonormal eigenbasis
   660		$\{\ket{b_W}\}_{b \in \F_q^n}$ gives the first display. For the inversion,
   661		substitute the first display and exchange the order of summation; by
   662		Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation} applied with $V = \F_q^n$ (so that
   663		$V^\perp = \{0\}$), the inner expectation vanishes unless $b' = b$, where
   664		it equals $1$.
   665	\end{proof}

  1073	\paragraph{Conditional linear functions for the Pauli basis test.}
  1074	The CL functions corresponding to the Pauli basis test question distribution are
  1075	parameterized by the parameter tuple $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$.
  1076	Let $V^\pauli$ denote the linear space $(\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m
  1077	\times (\F_q)^2$.
  1078	The space $V^\pauli$ is decomposed into a direct sum of the following register
  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
  1080	$1$-dimensional), $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is $m$-dimensional), and
  1081	$V_{\rxpt},V_{\rzpt}$ (which are $1$-dimensional).
  1082	We identify elements of $V^\pauli$ as tuples $(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1083	\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m \times (\F_q)^2$.
  1084	We define CL functions $L_\tvar: V^\pauli \to V^\pauli$ for every type $\tvar
  1085	\in \type^\pauli$:
  1086	\begin{enumerate}
  1087	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Point,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1088	  = L_\Point(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\Point$ is the $1$-level CL function defined in
  1089	  \Cref{eq:cl-ptf}.\footnote{The range $V_{\xpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus
  1090	    V_{\dir{}}$ or $V_{\zpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ of $L_\Point$ is
  1091	    embedded in $V^\pauli$ in the natural way.
  1092	    The same convention is used also in Item 2 and 3 for $L_\ALine$ and
  1093	    $L_\DLine$.}
  1094	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\ALine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1095	  = L_\ALine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\ALine$ is the $2$-level CL function defined in
  1096	  \Cref{eq:cl-alnf}.
  1097	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\DLine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1098	  = L_\DLine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\DLine$ is the $3$-level CL function defined in
  1099	  \Cref{eq:cl-dlnf}.
  1100	\item For $\tvar \in \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair, (\Pair,X), (\Pair,Z) \}$,
  1101	  $L_{\tvar}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) =
  1102	  (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,0,0,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, i.e., it projects onto $V_\xpt \oplus
  1103	  V_\zpt \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$.
  1104	  Thus $L_{\tvar}$ is a $1$-level CL function.
  1105	  
  1106	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Pauli,W} = 0$ as the identically $0$
  1107	  function.
  1108	  Thus it is a $0$-level CL function.
  1109	
  1110	\end{enumerate}
  1111	We note that the maps $L_{\Point,W}, L_{\ALine,W}, L_{\DLine,W}$ act as the zero function

  1113	if $W = Z$ and $\overline{W} = Z$ if $W = X$.

178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238	
   239	
   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   274	For later convenience we make the following definition. 
   275	
   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   312	    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=

   320	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
   321	            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   322	        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   323	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
