30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   274	For later convenience we make the following definition. 
   275	
   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   320	\paragraph{Decision procedure} The decision procedure $\decider^\ld$ for the
   321	game $\game^\ld$ is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}.
   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   433	\section{Lines}
   434	
   435	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   436	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   437	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   438	
   439	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   440		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   441		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   442		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   443			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   444		\end{equation}
   445		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   446		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   447		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   448		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   449		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   450		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   451		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   452		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   453	\end{definition}
   454	
   455	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   456		\uses{def:line}
   457		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   458		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   459	\end{proposition}
   460	\begin{proof}
   461		\uses{def:line}
   462		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   463		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   464		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   465		inclusion.
   466	\end{proof}
   467	
   468	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   469	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   470	representation is obtained as follows.
   471	
   472	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   473		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   474		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   475		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   476		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   477		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   478		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   479		\[
   480			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   481		\]
   482		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   483		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   484		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   485		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   486		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   487		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   488		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   489		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   490		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   491		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   492	\end{definition}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}
   727	
   728	For $q=2^k$ for $k$ odd (i.e.\ $q$ is an admissible field size) we use the shorthand $\tr$ for $\tr_{q\to 2}$.
   729	
   730	\begin{lemma}
   731	  \label{lem:one}
   732	  Let $k$ be an odd integer and $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ be a self-dual normal basis of
   733	  $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   734	  Then $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i$, and furthermore the representation
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   735	  $\downsize(1)$ of the unit $1 \in \F_{2^k}$ is the all ones vector in
   736	  $\F_2^k$.
   737	\end{lemma}
   738	
   739	\begin{proof}
   740	  Since $\{e_i \}$ is a normal basis, $e_i = \alpha^{2^i}$ for some element
   741	  $\alpha \in \F_{2^k}$.
   742	  Furthermore, for every element $b \in \F_{2^k}$, we have that $\tr(b^2) =
   743	  \tr(b)$.
   744	  This is because
   745	  \[
   746	    \tr(b^2) = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} b^{2^{i+1}} =
   747	    \sum_{i = 0}^{k-1} b^{2^i} = \tr(b)\;,
   748	  \]
   749	  where we use that $b^{2^k} = b$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   750	  Since $e_{i+1} = e_i^2$, we get that $\tr(e_i) = \tr(e_j)$ for all $i,j$.
   751	  It cannot be the case that $\tr(e_i) = 0$ for all $i$.
   752	  Suppose that this were the case.
   753	  This would imply that $\tr(b) = 0$ for all $b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   754	  But then for all $j \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ and for some $b \neq 0$, we would
   755	  also have by item 1 of \Cref{lem:downsize_field} that $b_j = \tr(b e_j) = 0$ where $b = \sum_j b_j e_j$ with $b_j \in
   756	  \F_2$.
   757	  This implies that $b$ is the all zero element of $\F_{2^k}$, which is a
   758	  contradiction.
   759	  Thus $\tr(e_i) = 1$ for all $i=1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   760	
   761		The ``furthermore'' part follows item 1 of
   762	        \Cref{lem:downsize_field}:
   763	        \begin{equation*}
   764	          \downsize(1) = (\tr(1 \cdot e_1), \dots, \tr(1 \cdot e_k))
   765	          = (1, \dots, 1).
   766	        \end{equation*}
   767	\end{proof}
   768	
   769	\begin{lemma}
   770	  \label{lem:efficient_arithmetic}
   771	  For any odd integer $k$, let $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ denote the self-dual normal basis
   772	  of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ that is returned by the algorithm specified in
   773	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} on input $k$.
   774	  Then the following can be computed in time $\poly(k)$ on input $k$:
   775	  \begin{enumerate}
   776	  \item The representation $\downsize(a+b)$ of the sum $a+b$ given the
   777	    representations $\downsize(a)$ and $\downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   778		\item The representation $\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ given the
   779	    representations $\downsize(a)$ and $\downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$.
   780	  \item The multiplication table $K_a \in \Matrix_k(\F_2)$ given the
   781	    representation $\downsize(a)$ of  $a\in \F_{2^k}$.
   782	  \item The representation $\downsize(a^{-1})$ of the multiplicative inverse of
   783	    $a \in \F_{2^k}$, given the representation $\downsize(a)$.
   784		\item The trace $\tr(a)$ given the multiplication table $K_a$ of $a \in \F_{2^k}$.
   785	  \end{enumerate}
   786	  Furthermore, for all integers $n$, the representations of projections
   787	  $\downsize(x^S)$ and $\downsize(x^T)$ of $x \in \F_{2^k}^n$ for complementary
   788	  subspaces $S,T$ of $\F_{2^k}^n$ can be computed in $\poly(k,n)$ time, given
   789	  the representations $\downsize(x)$, $\{\downsize(v_1), \downsize(v_2), \ldots,
   790	  \downsize(v_m)\}$ and $\{\downsize(w_1), \downsize(w_2), \ldots,
   791	  \downsize(w_{n - m})\}$ where $\{v_i\}$ and $\{w_j\}$ are bases for $S$ and
   792	  $T$ respectively.
   793	\end{lemma}
   794	
   795	\begin{proof}
   796	  Given an odd integer $k$ as input, by Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} it is
   797	  possible to compute the self-dual normal basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ together with the
   798	  multiplication tables $K_{e_i}$ for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, k$.
   799	  Addition is performed component-wise, and multiplication is done
   800	  using Eq.~\eqref{eq:eq-mult}.
   801	  For the multiplication table $K_a$ it suffices to compute the $k$ products
   802	  $\downsize(a e_i)$ for $i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$.
   803	  To compute inverses, observe that $\downsize(1) = \downsize(aa^{-1}) = K_a
   804	  \downsize(a^{-1})$.
   805	  The matrices $K_a$ are invertible over $\F_2$, so therefore $\downsize(a^{-1}) =
   806	  K_a^{-1} \downsize(1)$; moreover, $\kappa(1)$ is the all-ones vector
   807	  by Lemma~\ref{lem:one} and can thus be efficiently computed.
   808	  Inverting the matrix can be done in $\poly(k)$ time via Gaussian elimination.
   809	  The trace of an element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is by definition the trace of the
   810	  multiplication table $K_a$.
   811	
   812	  For the ``Furthermore'' part, we observe that since $\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m
   813	  \} \cup \{w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_{n-m} \}$ forms a basis for $\F_{2^k}^n$, there
   814	  is a unique way to write $x$ as a $\F_{2^k}$ linear combination of $\{ v_i\}$
   815	  and $\{w_j\}$.
   816	  Via Gaussian elimination over $\F_{2^k}$, the $\F_2$-representation of the
   817	  coefficients of this linear combination can be computed in $\poly(n,k)$ time.
   818	  Here we use that addition, multiplication and division over $\F_{2^k}$ can be
   819	  performed in time $\poly(k)$ using the previous items of the Lemma.
   820	\end{proof}
   821	
   822	\begin{remark}
   823	  \label{rmk:tm_fields}
   824	  Throughout this paper, whenever we refer to Turing machines that perform
   825	  computations with elements of a field $\F_q$ for an admissible field size $q =
   826	  2^k$, we mean that that the Turing machines are representing elements of
   827	  $\F_q$ as vectors in $\{0,1\}^{k}$ using the basis specified by the
   828	  algorithm of Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis} and performing arithmetic as
   829	  described in Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}.
   830	\end{remark}

    28	inductive MsType where

    33	/-- The cell incident to a constraint and one of its three positions in

    37	def msConstraintVars (i : Fin 6) (j : Fin 3) : Fin 9 :=
    38	  ⟨if i.val < 3 then i.val * 3 + j.val else i.val - 3 + j.val * 3, by

   103	/-- The Magic Square consistency predicate.  Constructor mismatches are
   104	rejected, as required by `def:ms-game` (blueprint lines 188-203; paper
   105	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`).
   106	-/
   107	def msWinPredicate :
   108	    MsType → MsType → MsAnswer → MsAnswer → Bool
   109	  | .constraint i, .constraint j, .triple β, .triple β' =>
   110	      decide (i = j ∧ β = β')
   111	  | .var i, .var j, .bit γ, .bit γ' =>
   112	      decide (i = j ∧ γ = γ')
   113	  | .constraint i, .var j, .triple β, .bit γ =>
   114	      decide
   115	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   116	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   117	  | .var j, .constraint i, .bit γ, .triple β =>
   118	      decide
   119	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   120	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   121	  | _, _, _, _ => false
   122	
   123	/-- The Magic Square game as a finite `Game`.  This is `def:ms-game` in
   124	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
   125	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def msGame : Game where
   128	  QuestionA := MsType
   129	  QuestionB := MsType
   130	  AnswerA := MsAnswer
   131	  AnswerB := MsAnswer
   132	  μ := graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty
   133	  μ_prob := by sorry
   134	  decide := msWinPredicate

   880	\subsection{The Pauli basis test}
   881	\label{sec:pauli-verifier}
   882	
   883	We introduce the quantum low-degree test of~\cite{natarajan2018low} in the form
   884	of a slight modification to it by~\cite{NW19} known as the \emph{Pauli basis
   885	  test}.
   886	Informally, the quantum low-degree test asks the players to measure a large
   887	number of qubits and return a highly compressed version of the measurement
   888	outcome.
   889	The Pauli basis test simply asks that the players return their uncompressed
   890	measurement outcomes, and it is designed by direct reduction to the quantum
   891	low-degree test.
   892	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-game} we describe the Pauli basis test as a nonlocal
   893	game $\game^\pauli$ and show that its question distribution is implementable via
   894	a CL distribution, as we did with the classical low-degree test in
   895	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   896	In Section~\ref{sec:qld-complexity} we exhibit canonical parameters for the
   897	Pauli basis test and give bounds on the time complexity of executing the test.
   898

   900	\label{sec:qld-game}

  "number": 5,
  "title": "feat(QPBT): minimal skeleton — thm:pauli statement and definition closure",
  "body": "### Motivation

- Repair the 17 findings from the round-1 review of local issue #0006, published
  as GitHub issue #4, for the QPBT statement skeleton.
- Restore the source-facing definitions to the Pauli basis test and its
  definition closure.  The primary sources are
  `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384,433-502,653-728,832-897,946-1161`,
  `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:10-57,219-230,258-271`,
  `references/qpbt-paper/07_types.tex:65-82`, and
  `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391,512-610,908-1225,1426-1447`.

### Description

- Encode `FixedFieldModel` with an actual `ZMod 2` algebra, a basis, its
  self-duality and normality witnesses, and derive the binary representation
  from the basis coordinates.  The model is fixed in `AdmissibleParams`, as the
  paper requires; no fresh field identification is added to `pauli_soundness`.
- Define `tauObservable` independently from the single-qudit shift and phase

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex-15-The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line. If the players share a polynomial $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$ and answer with $g(u)$ and with the restriction $g|_\ell$, they win with probability $1$; the soundness theorem below states that the converse approximately holds. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex-267-The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

    59	\section{Key theorem forms}
    60	
    61	Throughout, $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size, the tuple
    62	$(q,m,d)$ is admissible when moreover $d \ge 1$ and $m \mid q$, and
    63	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ denotes the $m$-variate polynomial representatives
    64	over $\F_q$ of individual degree at most $d$.  The comparison involves four
    65	theorem forms.
    66	\begin{enumerate}
    67	  \item \textbf{Source theorem form} (the polynomial-pair measurement).  There
    68	  is a function $\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$,
    69	  for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that for every
    70	  admissible $(q,m,d)$ and every projective strategy for the Pauli basis test
    71	  succeeding with probability at least $1-\eps$, there is a projective
    72	  measurement $\{\hat S_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ with outcomes pairs of polynomials in
    73	  $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ whose evaluations are $\delta_S$-consistent, on
    74	  average over a uniform point $u \in \F_q^m$ and in both bases
    75	  $W \in \{X,Z\}$, with the corresponding points measurements
    76	  $\{\hat M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\}$ of the strategy, together with the
    77	  symmetric counterpart of this relation.
    78	  \item \textbf{Missing instantiation obligation.}  The classical low
    79	  individual degree game with parameter tuple $(q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)$ is well
    80	  defined, and the combined point and line measurements assembled in the
    81	  analysis constitute a strategy for it of value at least
    82	  $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$.  The game's question distribution draws
    83	  its axis and diagonal indices through an index function
    84	  $\chi_{2m+2}\colon \F_q \to \{1,\ldots,2m+2\}$ with classes of equal size
    85	  $q/(2m+2)$, so the game exists only when $2m+2$ divides $q$.
    86	  \item \textbf{Restricted form supported by the present route.}  The source
    87	  theorem form under the additional hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$.  Among
    88	  admissible tuples this hypothesis holds exactly when $m = 1$ and
    89	  $q \ge 8$; it fails for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ and for
    90	  $(q,m) = (2,1)$.
    91	  \item \textbf{Repaired import form} (recommended target).  Quantum
    92	  soundness of the directly indexed variant of the classical low individual
    93	  degree game over $\F_q^{m'}$, for every dimension $m' \ge 1$ and
    94	  admissible $q$, with no divisibility hypothesis: the question
    95	  distribution samples the axis index, and the diagonal prefix index,

   108	\section{The source assertion and the obstruction}
   109	
   110	We examine the final step of the subsection ``Applying the classical
   111	low-degree test'' in the analysis of the Pauli basis test in the compression
   112	paper of Ji, Natarajan, Vidick, Wright, and Yuen (MIP$^{*}$=RE,
   113	arXiv:2001.04383), whose quantum soundness component builds on the low
   114	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}.%
   115	\footnote{Tracked in \localissue{0002}.  In the mirror of the source
   116	consulted here, the polynomial-pair lemma and its proof are at
   117	\path{references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex},
   118	lines~1267--1288; the sub-line lemma is at lines~1063--1116 and the combined
   119	line lemma at lines~1020--1034 of the same file.  The game parametrization
   120	with its divisibility, the index function, the soundness statement with its
   121	proof, and admissibility are at
   122	\path{references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex},
   123	lines~33--35, 214--219, 413--458, and 958--961.}
   124	There, the combined point measurements
   125	$\{\hat Q^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_c\}$ and combined line measurements
   126	$\{\hat Q^{\ell}_f\}$, indexed by points of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and lines in
   127	$\F_q^{2m+2}$, are asserted to form a strategy for the classical low
   128	individual degree game with parameters
   129	\[
   130	  \mathsf{ldparams} = (q,\, 2m+2,\, d,\, 1)
   131	  \tag{\path{lem:qld-4-7}}
   132	\]
   133	of value $1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$, and the quantum soundness theorem
   134	for that game is applied to produce the global polynomial-pair measurement.
   135	The two lemmas feeding this step are stated for the line-point distribution
   136	over $\F_q^{2m+2}$.
   137	
   138	The game, however, is parametrized by tuples $(q,m',d,k)$ with $q$ an
   139	admissible field size \emph{and $m'$ dividing $q$}.  The divisibility is not
   140	incidental: the question distribution is a conditionally linear distribution
   141	in which a uniform seed coordinate $s \in \F_q$, read as an integer in
   142	$\{0,\ldots,q-1\}$, determines the axis or diagonal index through the unique
   143	$\chi(s)$ with
   144	\[
   145	  s = (\chi(s)-1)\,\frac{q}{m'} + r, \qquad 0 \le r < \frac{q}{m'},
   146	  \tag{\path{eq:chi-func}}
   147	\]
   148	so that the $m'$ classes $\chi^{-1}(i)$ partition $\F_q$ into sets of equal
   149	size $q/m'$ and the index is uniform.  For $m' \nmid q$ neither the index
   150	function nor the line-point distribution built from it is defined.
   151	
   152	Admissibility of $(q,m,d)$ supplies only $m \mid q$.  Since an admissible $q$
   153	is a power of two, $m \mid q$ forces $m = 2^j$.  For $j \ge 1$ the integer
   154	$m+1 \ge 3$ is odd, so $2m+2 = 2(m+1)$ has an odd factor exceeding $1$ and
   155	divides no power of two; for $m = 1$ the condition $4 \mid q$ holds for every
   156	admissible $q$ except $q = 2$.  Thus the instantiation at dimension $2m+2$ is
   157	undefined for every admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$: for instance
   158	$(q,m,d) = (8,2,1)$ is admissible, while $6 \nmid 8$.  The source performs
   159	the instantiation without addressing the divisibility, so its proof route
   160	establishes the polynomial-pair lemma, and with it the soundness theorem for
   161	the Pauli basis test that rests on it, only for $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.

   163	\section{What the cited soundness theorem requires: the import obligations}
   164	\label{sec:import-obligations}
   165	
   166	The quantum soundness theorem for the classical game inherits the constraint
   167	$m' \mid q$ solely because it is stated for the game just described; its
   168	proof fixes an admissible $q$ with $m' \mid q$, asserts that the game with
   169	simultaneity parameter $1$ is \emph{identical} to the two-prover tensor-code
   170	test for the Reed--Solomon tensor code $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$ of the same
   171	authors' \emph{Quantum soundness of testing tensor codes} (arXiv:2111.08131)
   172	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, and concludes by Theorem~4.7 there, instantiated with
   173	that theorem's auxiliary integer parameter --- denoted $k$ in that source,
   174	and written $K$ here to avoid clashing with the field exponent and the
   175	simultaneity parameter --- chosen as $(m')^3 d$.  Neither
   176	the asserted identity nor the instantiation is complete as stated, so the
   177	import carries two verification obligations, which this section details and
   178	which the blueprint's proof node for the soundness statement records as
   179	open.  Both obligations are independent of the divisibility question: they
   180	arise at every dimension, for the $\chi$-based game where it is defined and
   181	equally for the directly indexed variant proposed under the candidate
   182	repairs.
   183	
   184	\paragraph{The cited test.}
   185	In the two-prover tensor-code test (Figures~1 and~2 of
   186	\cite{Ji2021Quantum}; the two-prover strategy format and the goodness
   187	measure are Definitions~4.5 and~4.6 there), the referee performs one of
   188	three subtests with probability $1/3$ each, assigning the two roles of each
   189	subtest to the two provers uniformly at random.  \emph{Axis-parallel lines
   190	test}: sample a uniform point $u \in [n]^{m'}$ and a uniform axis
   191	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$; send the axis-parallel line $\ell$ through $u$ in
   192	direction $j$ to one prover, who answers a codeword $g \in \mathcal C$;
   193	send $u$ to the other, who answers a field value $a$; accept iff
   194	$g(u_j) = a$.  \emph{Subcube commutation test}: sample
   195	$j \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$ and a subcube $H \subseteq [n]^{m'}$ by fixing the
   196	last $j-1$ coordinates uniformly; sample $u, v$ independently and uniformly
   197	in $H$ and a uniform order bit; send the ordered pair $(u,v)$ or $(v,u)$ to
   198	one prover, who answers a pair $(b_u, b_v)$ of field values; send $u$ to
   199	the other, who answers $a$; accept iff $b_u = a$.  \emph{Synchronicity
   200	test}: send one identical question --- a line, a point, or an ordered
   201	pair, with probability $1/3$ each --- to both provers and accept iff their
   202	answers agree.  Theorem~4.7 supposes a two-prover strategy passing this
   203	test with probability $1-\eps$ together with an integer parameter
   204	$K \ge 12 m' t$, where $t$ is the interpolation parameter of the base code
   205	--- for the degree-$d$ Reed--Solomon code, of blocklength $n = q$ and
   206	distance $q-d$, one has $t = d+1$ --- and produces projective measurements
   207	$\{G_c\}$ and $\{\tilde G_c\}$ with outcomes in $\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$,
   208	consistent with one prover's points measurements, with the other prover's
   209	lines measurements, and with each other, up to
   210	$\eta'(m',t,K,\eps,n^{-1}) = \mathrm{poly}(m',t,K) \cdot
   211	\mathrm{poly}(\eps, n^{-1}, e^{-K/(m')^2})$.
   212	
   213	\paragraph{Obligation 1: the game correspondence.}
   214	The source asserts that the $\chi$-based game at parameters $(q,m',d,1)$
   215	is this test.  It is not, in four respects.
   216	(i)~The game has no pair questions.  A pair question of the test reveals
   217	two points of a \emph{hidden} subcube --- the subcube itself is not sent
   218	--- and is answered by two field values, while the game's diagonal-line
   219	question reveals a full line description and is answered by a degree-$m'd$
   220	polynomial.  A reduction must construct the pair measurements from the
   221	diagonal-line measurements by post-processing (measure a line through $u$
   222	and $v$ and evaluate the answered polynomial at the two parameters), and
   223	both directions of the information mismatch matter: the game's line
   224	description carries an index and a seed, neither of which is a function of
   225	the pair $(u,v)$, so the constructed measurement must average over the
   226	compatible indices and seeds; and the game's diagonal lines fix the
   227	\emph{first} $i-1$ coordinates where the test's subcubes fix the
   228	\emph{last} $j-1$, so the coordinate conventions must be aligned.  The
   229	construction must preserve projectivity and must match the law of the
   230	hidden-subcube pair with the law induced by the game's diagonal sampling.
   231	(ii)~The game's line questions carry the seed $s \in \F_q$; the test's
   232	carry only the line.  A strategy may depend on the seed beyond its class
   233	$\chi^{-1}(i)$, and removing this dependence runs into the fiber-averaging
   234	difficulty made explicit under the candidate repairs: averaging preserves
   235	the line-versus-point branches exactly but not the synchronicity branches.
   236	(iii)~The branch weights differ: each nontrivial cross-test has mass $1/3$
   237	in the test against $2/9$ in the game.  Once the per-branch predicates are
   238	matched, the intended bookkeeping bound is that the constructed strategy's
   239	rejection probability in the test is at most $\tfrac32$ times the game's
   240	rejection probability, up to the $O(1/(m'q))$ of item~(iv); this bound is
   241	the target of the obligation, not an established fact.
   242	(iv)~The game's predicate fixes an acceptance convention on diagonal
   243	questions with zero direction --- an event of probability at most
   244	$2/(m'q)$, recorded in the blueprint's remark on zero directions --- for
   245	which the test has no counterpart branch.
   246	Finally, the displayed conclusions of Theorem~4.7 pair one prover's points
   247	measurements with the other prover's tensor-codeword measurement, and the
   248	first prover's tensor-codeword measurement with the second prover's lines
   249	measurements, while the game-level statement asserts the point consistency
   250	in both directions; deriving the stated form uses the role symmetrization
   251	of the test and belongs to the correspondence.  None of these steps is
   252	difficult to state, but none is carried out in the source, and together
   253	they replace the asserted one-line identity by a reduction carrying its
   254	own value bound.
   255	
   256	\paragraph{Obligation 2: the parameter bound.}
   257	Theorem~4.7 requires $K \ge 12 m' t = 12 m' (d+1)$.  The source
   258	instantiates $K = (m')^3 d$, which meets the bound iff
   259	$(m')^2 d \ge 12(d+1)$: this holds for all $d \ge 1$ when $m' \ge 5$,
   260	holds at $m' = 4$ exactly when $d \ge 3$, and fails for every $d$ when
   261	$m' \le 3$.  In the game's parameter domain the dimension divides the
   262	admissible field size and is therefore a power of two, so the source's
   263	instantiation violates the hypothesis exactly at $m' \in \{1,2\}$ for
   264	every $d$ and at $m' = 4$ for $d \in \{1,2\}$ --- in particular, in the
   265	multilinear regime $d = 1$, at every dimension $m' \le 4$.  A candidate
   266	repair is to instantiate $K = \max((m')^3 d,\, 12 m'(d+1))$; the open
   267	obligation is then to re-absorb the error, that is, to check that
   268	$\mathrm{poly}(m',t,K)$ and $e^{-K/(m')^2}$ still collapse to the form
   269	$a(dm')^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bm'd})$ in the small-$m'$ cases where the
   270	maximum is $12m'(d+1)$ --- plausible, since there
   271	$e^{-K/(m')^2} = e^{-12(d+1)/m'}$ decays in $d$ at a rate comparable to
   272	$2^{-m'd}$ for $m' \le 4$, but not checked here.
   273	
   274	In the correspondence of Obligation~1, the only role of the divisibility
   275	$m' \mid q$ is to make the $\chi$-sampled index uniform.  The underlying
   276	mathematics does not need the divisibility.  The low
   277	individual degree test of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} samples its axis
   278	index $i$ uniformly from $\{1,\ldots,m'\}$ directly, with no index function
   279	on $\F_q$ and no divisibility hypothesis,%
   280	\footnote{See the test figure in \path{references/ldt-paper/test_definition.tex}.}
   281	and the tensor-code test is likewise a test about the code
   282	$\mathcal C^{\ot m'}$, not about an encoding of indices into $\F_q$.  The
   283	$\chi$-based packaging exists so that the question distribution is
   284	conditionally linear, which the introspection machinery requires for the
   285	game the players actually play --- the Pauli basis test at dimension $m$,
   286	where admissibility does supply the divisibility.  The game at dimension
   287	$2m+2$ never appears in a verifier; it is an internal analysis device in the
   288	proof of the polynomial-pair lemma, so nothing there requires its question
   289	distribution to be conditionally linear.

   291	\section{Candidate repairs}
   292	
   293	\paragraph{Direct index sampling (candidate direction, recommended).}
   294	Define, for arbitrary $m' \ge 1$, the line-point distribution over
   295	$\F_q^{m'}$ that samples the uniform point, the uniform axis index
   296	$i \in \{1,\ldots,m'\}$, and the diagonal direction with vanishing first
   297	$i-1$ coordinates, directly; define the \emph{directly indexed game} with
   298	this question distribution, whose line questions carry the index $i$ (and,
   299	for diagonal lines, the projected direction) in place of the seed
   300	$s \in \F_q$; and state the imported soundness theorem for that game
   301	(form~4 above).  This removes the divisibility obstruction and nothing
   302	else: the directly indexed game still asks for polynomials on revealed
   303	lines, has no pair questions, and weighs its branches as the present game
   304	does, so establishing form~4 carries the same two import obligations as
   305	the $\chi$-based import (Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}), now at
   306	arbitrary dimension.
   307	
   308	The relation to the present game when $m' \mid q$ must moreover be proved
   309	at the level of games, not merely of question distributions, because the
   310	two games have different question alphabets: an $\mathsf{ALine}$ question
   311	of the $\chi$-based game is a pair $(u_0, s)$ and a $\mathsf{DLine}$
   312	question a triple $(u_0, s, v')$, so a strategy may select different
   313	measurements for seeds $s \ne s'$ with $\chi(s) = \chi(s')$, and equality
   314	of the induced laws of the geometric data does not by itself transport
   315	such a strategy.  The transport layer decomposes into the following
   316	obligations, none of which is carried out here.
   317	\begin{itemize}
   318	  \item \emph{Distribution lemma.}  When $m' \mid q$, the image of the
   319	  conditionally linear question distribution under the parsing map
   320	  $(u_0,s) \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s))$, $(u_0,s,v') \mapsto (u_0,\chi(s),v')$
   321	  is the direct distribution, and conditioned on the parsed question the
   322	  seed is uniform on the class $\chi^{-1}(i)$, independently of everything
   323	  else.
   324	  \item \emph{Parsing pullback.}  A strategy for the directly indexed game
   325	  composed with the parsing map is a seed-oblivious strategy for the
   326	  $\chi$-based game.  Since the win predicate depends on the question only
   327	  through the parsed data, and a seed-oblivious strategy answers
   328	  identically across each fiber --- in particular on the synchronicity
   329	  branches, where both players hold the same seed --- the value should be
   330	  preserved exactly on every branch, and projectivity is preserved.  This
   331	  is the direction the combining subtree needs.
   332	  \item \emph{Seed-fiber averaging: what it preserves and what it does
   333	  not.}  In the opposite direction, average each line measurement over its
   334	  seed fiber: attach to a direct question $(u_0,i)$, respectively
   335	  $(u_0,i,v')$, the average over uniform $s \in \chi^{-1}(i)$ of the
   336	  measurements attached to $(u_0,s)$, respectively $(u_0,s,v')$, leaving
   337	  the points measurements unchanged.  By the conditional uniformity of the
   338	  seed this preserves the value of every \emph{line-versus-point} branch
   339	  exactly: there the paired question carries no seed, so the branch value
   340	  is an average over the fiber of per-seed values, which the averaged
   341	  measurement computes.  It does \emph{not} preserve the synchronicity
   342	  branches.  There both players hold the same seed, so the $\chi$-based
   343	  branch value is the diagonal average
   344	  $\E_{s}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s)}_f
   345	  \rangle$, while the averaged strategy realizes the double average
   346	  $\E_{s,s'}\sum_f \langle M^{(u_0,s)}_f \ot \widetilde M^{(u_0,s')}_f
   347	  \rangle$ over independent seeds in the fiber; the two differ whenever
   348	  the players' measurements vary across a fiber in a correlated way (if
   349	  both apply a common seed-dependent relabelling, every diagonal term is
   350	  large and the cross terms are not), and neither quantity dominates the
   351	  other in general.  An earlier revision of this note claimed that the
   352	  averaging preserves the exact value, and with it synchronicity; that
   353	  claim was wrong and is withdrawn.  What needs proof is control of the
   354	  synchronicity branches under de-seeding.  Candidate approaches: show
   355	  that a strategy of value $1-\eps$ in the $\chi$-based game is, with
   356	  polynomial loss, close to a seed-oblivious one; or state form~4 with a
   357	  synchronicity hypothesis in the doubled-average form and re-derive it on
   358	  the tensor-code side.  Choosing and proving one of these is an open
   359	  obligation.
   360	  \item \emph{Projectivity round trip.}  The averaged strategy is a POVM
   361	  strategy even when the given one is projective, while the imported
   362	  theorem, like the present one, takes projective strategies.  The
   363	  intended round trip is: dilate the averaged strategy to a projective one
   364	  (Naimark preserves all product correlations
   365	  $\langle X \ot Y \rangle$ of the given strategy against the dilated
   366	  state --- hence the value of every branch the averaging preserved ---
   367	  but nothing restores the diagonal seed correlations once the averaging
   368	  has been performed); apply form~4; and compress the resulting polynomial
   369	  measurement along the dilation isometry back to a POVM in the required
   370	  measurement class on the original space.  That this compression
   371	  preserves the consistency conclusions must itself be proved; it is
   372	  stated here as an obligation, not established.  (Alternatively, form~4
   373	  may be stated for POVM strategies outright, moving the dilation inside
   374	  the import.)
   375	\end{itemize}
   376	
   377	The combining subtree would then be reread with the direct distribution
   378	and the directly indexed game at dimension $2m+2$: every statement becomes
   379	well defined for all admissible tuples, and the expectation is that the
   380	proofs survive unchanged, because the measurements constructed there are
   381	indexed by the geometric data --- points, lines, and polynomials on them
   382	--- and so constitute a strategy for the directly indexed game outright,
   383	with no fiber averaging.  Verifying, lemma by lemma, that those proofs use
   384	only the laws of the sampled objects and never the conditional linearity
   385	of the sampling is part of this direction's obligations.  This follows the
   386	subtree protocol for a definition-level mismatch: the definition is
   387	corrected at the lowest point rather than each downstream lemma acquiring
   388	a hypothesis.  The transport layer costs one parsing-map definition, the
   389	distribution lemma, the pullback lemma, whichever synchronicity control is
   390	chosen, and the dilation--compression lemma; the first three are an
   391	estimated one to two hundred lines on top of the restated import, with the
   392	blueprint's existing Naimark interface supplying the dilation, while the
   393	synchronicity control is the step whose weight is genuinely uncertain.
   394	The external check that the tensor-code test of arXiv:2111.08131 samples
   395	its axes and subcubes directly has been made against that source: Figure~1
   396	there draws the axis index and the subcube data uniformly and directly,
   397	with no index encoding into $\F_q$.
   398	
   399	\paragraph{Padding the dimension.}
   400	Alternatively, embed the combined polynomial into
   401	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,\bar m}(\F_q)$ for $\bar m = 4m$, the least power of two
   402	with $\bar m \ge 2m+2$, ignoring the $2m-2$ dummy variables.  Then
   403	$\bar m \mid q$ holds whenever $q \ge 4m$, and the existing game applies at
   404	dimension $\bar m$.  In the complementary regime $m \in \{q/2,\, q\}$ the
   405	conclusion is vacuous: $md \ge q/2$ gives
   406	$\delta_S \ge a(md)^a q^{-b} \ge a\,2^{-a} q^{a-b} \ge a\,2^{-b} \ge 1$
   407	for $a \ge 2$, while the consistency quantities bounded by the theorem never
   408	exceed $1$.  This route stays inside the present definitions but reworks the
   409	sub-line distribution (a fourth coordinate block of dummies), the combining
   410	map, and the wrong-block Schwartz--Zippel analysis, and it moves the
   411	combining lemmas away from their source statements at dimension $2m+2$.
   412	
   413	\paragraph{Unequal index classes.}
   414	One could instead define an index function at dimension $2m+2$ with classes
   415	of sizes $\lfloor q/(2m+2)\rfloor$ and $\lceil q/(2m+2)\rceil$.  The index
   416	is then only approximately uniform, the identification with the external
   417	test fails exactly, and every distributional identity in the sub-line
   418	analysis acquires an error term; this amounts to re-proving the imported
   419	soundness theorem for a perturbed game and is not recommended.
   420	
   421	\section{Comparison with the blueprint}
   422	
   423	The blueprint \cite{MIPStarREBlueprint} keeps the sub-line lemma, the
   424	combined line lemma, and the polynomial-pair lemma in their source-shaped
   425	statements, with no divisibility hypothesis.  Their proofs retain the source
   426	constructions and mark the unresolved obligation at the exact steps: the
   427	first sampling step of the sub-line construction, where $\chi_{2m+2}$ and
   428	the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$ are invoked, and the
   429	instantiation step of the polynomial-pair proof, where $(q,2m+2,d,1)$ is
   430	used as a game parameter tuple.  A chapter remark records the divisibility
   431	arithmetic and cites this note; the final soundness theorem for the Pauli
   432	basis test remains open modulo this obligation.  The blueprint's proof node
   433	for the classical soundness import itself states the source's route --- the
   434	identification with the two-prover tensor-code test and the application of
   435	Theorem~4.7 --- and enumerates the two obligations of
   436	Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations} as open, citing this note for the
   437	detailed comparison and the case arithmetic.  An earlier revision had
   438	instead added the hypothesis $2m+2 \mid q$ to the three lemmas; that was
   439	statement drift in the sense of the proof-gap protocol, since the hypothesis
   440	excludes all admissible $m \ge 2$ and does not appear in the source.
   441	
   442	\section{Conclusion}
   443	
   444	There is a theorem-level gap in the source proof route: the classical low
   445	individual degree game invoked at dimension $2m+2$ is undefined for every
   446	admissible tuple with $m \ge 2$ (and for $(q,m) = (2,1)$), because its
   447	question distribution requires $2m+2 \mid q$ while admissibility supplies
   448	only $m \mid q$.  The cited route therefore does not establish the
   449	polynomial-pair lemma, nor the soundness of the Pauli basis test that
   450	depends on it, beyond $m = 1$ and $q \ge 8$.  Independently of the
   451	divisibility, the import of the classical game's quantum soundness carries
   452	the two open verification obligations of
   453	Section~\ref{sec:import-obligations}: the asserted identity with the
   454	two-prover tensor-code test must be replaced by a reduction carrying a
   455	value bound, and the source's instantiation of the auxiliary parameter
   456	violates the theorem's lower bound at the small dimensions listed there.
   457	We do not assert that any conclusion is false: the underlying tensor-code
   458	soundness is insensitive to how the axis index is sampled, and both import
   459	obligations concern verification, not counterexample.  For the divisibility
   460	repair, the recommended candidate direction is direct index sampling ---
   461	restate the imported soundness theorem for the directly indexed game at
   462	arbitrary dimension; prove the distribution and parsing-pullback lemmas;
   463	settle the synchronicity control for de-seeding together with the
   464	dilation--compression round trip, so that the present soundness statement
   465	would follow from the repaired import; and reread the combining subtree
   466	against the directly indexed game --- a direction whose open obligations
   467	are enumerated under the candidate repairs, not an established route, with
   468	dimension padding as the fallback confined to the present game definition.

references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:6:Our results establish the existence of transformations on \emph{families} of nonlocal games $\{\game_n\}_{n\in \N}$ having certain properties. In order to keep track of efficiency (and ultimately, computability) properties it is important to have a way to specify such families in a {uniform} manner. Towards this we introduce the following formalism. A \emph{uniformly generated family of games} is specified through a pair of Turing machines $\verifier = (\sampler,\decider)$ that satisfy certain conditions, in which case the pair is called a \emph{normal form verifier}. The Turing machine $\sampler$ (called a \emph{sampler}) takes as input an index $n \in \N$ and returns the description of a procedure that can be used to sample questions $(x,y)$ in the game (this procedure itself obeys a certain format associated with ``conditionally linear'' distributions, defined below). The Turing machine $\decider$ (called a \emph{decider}) takes as input an index $n$, questions $(x,y)$, and answers $(a,b)$, and returns a single-bit decision. For the sake of this proof overview we assume that the sampling and decision procedures run in time polynomial in the index $n$; we refer to the running time of these procedures as the \emph{complexity} of the verifier. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:71:	To overcome these difficulties we identify a natural class of question distributions, called \emph{conditionally linear distributions}, that generalize the low-degree test distribution. We show that conditionally linear distributions can be ``introspected'' using conditionally linear distributions only, enabling recursive introspection. (In particular, they are a rich enough class to capture the types of question distributions produced by the compression scheme of~\cite{NW19}.) We define normal form verifiers by restricting their sampling procedure to generate conditionally linear question distributions, and this allows us to obtain the compression procedure on normal form verifiers described in Theorem~\ref{thm:compression-informal}. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:73:	Conceptually,  the identification of a natural class of distributions that is ``closed under introspection'' is a key step that enables the introspection technique to be applied recursively. (As we will see later, other closure properties of conditionally linear distributions, such as taking direct products, play an important role as well.) Since conditionally linear distributions are central to our construction we describe them next. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:78:Fix a vector space $V$ that is identified with $\F^m$, for a finite field $\F$ and integer $m$. Informally (see Definition~\ref{def:cl-func} for a precise definition), a function $L$ on $V$ is \emph{conditionally linear} (CL for short) if it can be evaluated by a procedure that takes the following form: (i) read a substring $z^{(1)}$ of $z$; (ii) evaluate a linear function $L_1$ on $z^{(1)}$; (iii) repeat steps (i) and (ii) with the remaining coordinates $z\backslash z^{(1)}$, such that the next steps are allowed to depend in an arbitrary way on $L_1(z^{(1)})$ but not directly on $z^{(1)}$ itself. What distinguishes a function of this form from an arbitrary function is that we restrict the number of iterations of (i)---(ii) to a constant number (at most $9$, in our case). (One may also think of CL functions as ``adaptively linear'' functions, where the number of ``levels'' of adaptivity is the number of iterations of (i)---(ii).) A distribution $\mu$ over pairs $(x,y) \in V\times V$ is called {conditionally linear}  if it is the image under a pair of {conditionally linear functions} $L^\alice,L^\bob: V\to V$ of the uniform distribution on $V$, i.e.\ $(x,y)\sim (L^\alice(z),L^\bob(z))$ for uniformly random $z\in V$. 
references/qpbt-paper/03_proof_overview.tex:80:An important class of CL distributions are low-degree test distributions, which are distributions over question pairs $(x,y)$ where $y$ is a randomly chosen affine subspace of $\F^m$ and $x$ is a uniformly random point on $y$. We explain this for the case where the random subspace $y$ is one-dimensional (i.e.\ a line). Let $V = V_\xpt \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ where $V_\xpt = V_{\dir{}} = \F^m$. Let $L^\alice$ be the projection onto $V_\xpt$ (i.e. it maps $(x,v) \to (x,0)$ where $x \in V_\xpt$ and $v \in V_{\dir{}}$). Define $L^\bob: V \to V$ as the map $(x,v) \mapsto (L^\lnf_v(x),v)$ where $L^\lnf_v: V_\xpt \to V_\xpt$ is a linear map that, for every $v \in V_{\dir{}}$, projects onto a complementary subspace to the one-dimensional subspace of $V_\xpt$ spanned by $v$ (one can think of this as an ``orthogonal subspace'' to the span of $\{ v \}$). $L^\bob$ is conditionally linear because it can be seen as first reading the substring $v \in V_{\dir{}}$ (which can be interpreted as specifying the \emph{direction} of a line), and then applying a linear map $L^\lnf_v$ to $x \in V_\xpt$ (which can be interpreted as specifying a canonical point on the line $\ell = \{ x + tv : t \in \F \}$). It is not hard to see (and shown formally in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game}) that the distribution of $(L^\alice(z),L^\bob(z))$ for $z$ uniform in $V$, is identical (up to relabeling) to the low-degree test distribution $(x,\ell)$ where $\ell$ is a uniformly random affine line in $\F^m$, and $x$ is a uniformly random point on $\ell$.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:445:Conditionally linear functions specify the question distributions of the games considered in the following chapters in a form that can be ``introspected''. Intuitively, a conditionally linear function takes as input an element $x \in V = \F^n$ and applies linear maps $L_j$ sequentially to $x^{V_j}$, where $V_1, V_2, \dots$ is a sequence of complementary register subspaces such that both the linear map $L_j$ and the subspace $V_j$, for $j \ge 2$, may depend on the values taken by the previous linear maps $L_1(x^{V_1})$, $L_2(x^{V_2})$, and so on.
blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:447:Throughout this section $V$ denotes the linear space $\F^n$ for some integer $n \ge 0$, and all the distinguished subspaces of $V$ are register subspaces (Definition~\ref{def:register-subspace}). If $V_1, V_2, \dots, V_\ell$ are fixed subspaces of $V$ and $k \in \{1, 2, \dots, \ell\}$, we use the subscript range notation
blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:451:and $V_{\le k}$, $V_{\ge k}$ are understood to be $V_{<k+1}$ and $V_{>k-1}$, respectively. For a register subspace $V'$ of $V$, the symbol $x^{V'}$ denotes the projection of $x$ onto $V'$ parallel to the complementary register subspace (Definition~\ref{def:complementary}). Moreover, if $F \colon V' \to V'$ is a function and $x \in V$, we write $x^F$ for $F(x^{V'})$; for example, in the following definition $x^{L_1}$ is shorthand for $L_1(x^{V_1})$.
