A repair\nshould therefore appear as a construction or as a theorem discharging the\ncorresponding obligation.  If a theorem assumes the output of the repair instead\nof constructing it, that theorem is conditional on the repair.\n\n\\paragraph{Obligation structure.}\nAn obligation structure is a record whose fields are the data and estimates\nneeded by a later construction.  This is acceptable only as an internal target\nor as a hypothesis of a conditional helper.  Such a structure becomes statement\ndrift if it is added to a paper-facing theorem instead of being constructed\ninside the proof.  The review question is whether every load-bearing field is\nproved from the source hypotheses or is explicitly tracked as a missing\nobligation.\n\n\\section{The main failure mode}\n\nSuppose the paper proves\n\\[\n  H \\Longrightarrow C.\n\\]\nDuring formalization, the proof may need an intermediate assertion \\(B\\).  The\npaper theorem should be represented as\n\\[\n  H \\Longrightarrow B \\Longrightarrow C\n  \\quad\\text{inside the proof,}\n\\]\nwhere \\(B\\) is obtained by a lemma or theorem from \\(H\\).  The following\npublic statement is a different theorem:\n\\[\n  H \\land B \\Longrightarrow C.\n\\]\nIt is not unsound in \\Lean{}, but it is not the paper theorem.  It says that the\nconclusion follows if the missing bridge data is supplied.  Such a theorem is a\nconditional helper, even if its conclusion looks exactly like the paper's\nconclusion.\n\nThis is the situation colloquially described as ``adding a bridge\nhypothesis''.  More precisely, an unproved intermediate step has been promoted\nfrom the proof body to the theorem's assumptions.  The correction is not to hide\nthe hypothesis under a different structure name.  The correction is to keep a\npaper-facing theorem with the source statement and move the missing step to a\nnamed internal proof obligation.\n\n\\section{Faithful boundary hypotheses}\n\nNot every extra formal hypothesis is a theorem drift.  Some hypotheses are\nfaithful boundary conditions introduced by formal encoding.  Examples include\nnonnegativity needed for a real power, positivity needed to divide by a\nquantity, finiteness and nonemptiness of an index type, a field-model instance,\nor decidability instances required by \\Lean{}.  Such hypotheses are acceptable\nwhen they express part of the mathematical ambient setting or make explicit a\ncondition used implicitly in the paper.\n\nThe distinction is load-bearing.  A faithful boundary hypothesis describes the\ndomain in which the paper's objects live.  A proof-debt hypothesis supplies a\nmathematical step that the proof should derive.  If removing the hypothesis\nleaves an unproved construction or estimate from the paper proof, then the\nhypothesis is proof debt, not a boundary condition.\n\n\\section{Definition drift and subtree repair}\n\nDefinition drift is especially dangerous because it propagates.  If a\ndefinition is changed so that it no longer denotes the object in the paper,\nthen every downstream theorem using that definition may continue to compile\nwhile proving statements about the wrong object.  Downstream theorem statements\ncan then be repaired piecemeal, but the development remains unstable because\nthe wrong definition is still upstream.\n\nWhen a definition mismatch is found, the repair should proceed by a subtree\nprotocol.\n\n\\begin{enumerate}\n  \\item Identify the source object and the formal object precisely.\n  \\item Freeze a source-faithful definition or state an adapter theorem\n  relating the existing definition to the source object.\n  \\item Recheck the downstream theorem chain against that definition or adapter.\n  \\item Re-formalize the affected subtree from the corrected interface, rather\n  than adding local hypotheses to each downstream theorem.\n  \\item If a downstream proof cannot be completed, record the missing obligation\n  at the lowest point where the paper proof needs it.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nThis is slower than editing a final theorem signature, but it prevents a local\ndefinition error from becoming a global theorem-statement error.\n\n\\section{Allowed shapes}\n\n\\begin{center}\n\\begin{tabular}{p{0.24\\linewidth}p{0.31\\linewidth}p{0.32\\linewidth}}\n\\textbf{Shape} & \\textbf{Allowed use} & \\textbf{Forbidden use} \\\\\n\\hline\nPaper-facing theorem & Matches the source statement up to faithful encoding &\nCarries non-paper bridge, residual, repair, input, obligation-structure, or\nproof-obligation hypotheses \\\\\nSource-shaped theorem with a tracked \\verb|sorry| & Default repair when the\nsource proof is blocked but the statement is known & Replaced by a strengthened\ntheorem statement merely to keep Complements\nthe lean-conventions `PROOF_INTEGRITY` reference, which covers the kernel-level\nblockers; this file covers patterns where the Lean code *compiles and the\ntrick is at the level of what the statement says or what the definitions\nbake in*.\n\nEvery pattern here is **castle-in-the-air in spirit**: a theorem named after a\npaper result that doesn't actually prove it. A theorem can:\n\n- Be marked `\\leanok` in the blueprint,\n- Have a sorry-free proof body,\n- Have a clean axiom closure (`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` only),\n\nand still prove **nothing that the paper actually claims**, if the proof\nobligation has been displaced into a hypothesis, a definition, or a sentinel\nbranch. The proof body\nis a trivial `rcases`/`exact`/`.trans`/`simpa using h` and does no\nmathematical work. A variant wraps the hypothesis in a named bundle\n(`*BridgePackage`, `*Statement`); see issues [#449], [#451], [#477] for the\ncatalogue, and [#493] for the inline-existential mutation triggered by\nPR [#491].\n\n### Why it's bad\n\nThe theorem's named mathematical content is never derived from prior lemmas;\nthe caller (who supplies the hypothesis) has to discharge it. In practice the\ncaller then has the same problem, pushing the obligation further up the\nstack. The theorem is true under a vacuous hypothesis and the `\\leanok` tag\nmisrepresents the actual state of the proof.\n\n### How to spot it\n\n- The hypothesis type contains, up to `∃` / `∧` / a coercion, the theorem's\n  conclusion.\n- The proof body is one of:\n  - `rcases h with ⟨...⟩; exact ⟨...⟩`\n  - `exact h.fieldName` / `exact h.a.trans h.b`\n  - `by simpa using h.fieldName`\n- The hypothesis is a bundle named `*BridgePackage`, `*Witness`, `*Package`,\n  `*Output`, with a field whose type matches the conclusion structure.\n- Consumers of the bundle are trivial (field projection + return).\n\n### Concrete example\n\nHistorical example (before the MainInductionStep cleanup):\n\n```lean\ntheorem mainInduction\n    (params : Parameters) [FieldModel params.q]\n    (strategy : SymStrat params ι)\n    (eps delta gamma : Error) (k : ℕ)\n    (hbridge : MainInductionBridgePackage params strategy eps delta gamma k) :\n    ∃ G : Measurement (Polynomial params) ι,\n      ConsRel strategy.state ...\n        (mainInductionError params k eps delta gamma) := by\n  rcases hbridge.witness with ⟨error, G, hG, herror⟩\n  refine ⟨G, ?_⟩\n  exact ⟨le_trans hG.offDiagonalBound herror⟩\n```\n\nHere `MainInductionBridgePackage.witness` has type\n`∃ error, ∃ G, ConsRel ... error ∧ error ≤ mainInductionError ...` — literally\nthe conclusion. Games, strategies, values, conditionally linear (CL) functions and distributions, typed distributions sampled from the edges of a graph, and the state-dependent approximation $\\\\approx_\\\\delta$ between families of measurement operators are as in Chapter~\\\\ref{chap:qpbt-games}; the algebraic material on lines, canonical linear maps, the low-degree encoding, and generalized Pauli observables is from Chapter~\\\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}.\\n     9\\t\\n    10\\t\\\\section{The classical low individual degree game}\\n    11\\t% Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.\\n    12\\t\\\\label{sec:ld-verifier}\\n    13\\t\\\\label{sec:ld-game}\\n    14\\t\\n    15\\tThe classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the simultaneous version, the players' answers are $k$-tuples, checked coordinatewise against a $k$-tuple of low individual degree polynomials.\\n    16\\t\\n    17\\t\\\\begin{definition}[The classical low individual degree game: parameters and registers]\\\\label{def:ld-game}\\n    18\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:game, def:admissible-size}\\n    19\\t\\tThe game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$ is parametrized by a tuple $\\\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$, where $m,d,k \\\\in \\\\N$, $q \\\\in \\\\N$ is an admissible field size (Definition~\\\\ref{def:admissible-size}), and $m$ divides $q$. Define $L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \\\\in V$,\\n    29\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    30\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:cl-ptf}\\n    31\\t\\t\\tL_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\\\\;.\\n    32\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    33\\t\\tFor $s \\\\in \\\\F_q$, let $\\\\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that\\n    34\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    35\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:chi-func}\\n    36\\t\\t\\ts = (\\\\chi(s)-1)\\\\,\\\\frac{q}{m} + r\\n    37\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    38\\t\\tfor some $0 \\\\le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\\\\{0,1,\\\\ldots,q-1\\\\}$ under the identification of $\\\\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\\\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}. Define $L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$ by\\n    39\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    40\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:cl-alnf}\\n    41\\t\\t\\tL_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}(u,s,v) = \\\\bigl(L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u),\\\\, s,\\\\, 0\\\\bigr)\\\\quad\\\\text{for all } (u,s,v) \\\\in V\\\\;,\\n    42\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    43\\t\\twhere $i = \\\\chi(s)$ and $L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ denotes the canonical linear map with one-dimensional kernel spanned by $v$, used to compute canonical representatives of lines (Definition~\\\\ref{def:line-representative}). Define $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ by\\n    44\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    45\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:cl-dlnf}\\n    46\\t\\t\\tL_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}(u,s,v) = \\\\bigl(L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),\\\\, s,\\\\, \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)\\\\bigr)\\\\;,\\n    47\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    48\\t\\twhere $i = \\\\chi(s)$ and $\\\\pi_{i-1}$ zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input. The function $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the concatenation of (i) the identity on $V_I$, (ii) for each $i$ the $1$-level CL function $v \\\\mapsto \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ on $V_V$, and (iii) for each pair $(s,v') \\\\in V_I \\\\oplus V_V$ the $1$-level CL function $L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{v'}$ on $V_X$; thus $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is a $3$-level CL function.\\n    49\\t\\n    50\\t\\tThe question distribution of $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$ is the typed CL distribution obtained as follows: sample a type pair $(t_{\\\\mathrm A}, t_{\\\\mathrm B})$ uniformly from $\\\\mathcal T^{\\\\mathrm{ld}} \\\\times \\\\mathcal T^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$, sample $z = (u,s,v)$ uniformly from $V$, and send each player $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$ the question $(t_w, L_{t_w}(z))$.\\n    51\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n    52\\t\\n    53\\tThe next two lemmas show that the CL functions $L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}$, $L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$, $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ give rise to the axis-parallel and diagonal line-versus-point distributions.\\n    54\\t\\n    55\\t\\\\begin{lemma}\\\\label{lem:alnf}\\n    56\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\\n    57\\t\\tConsider the pair $(\\\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\\\bigl((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0)\\\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\\\ell = \\\\ell(u_0, e_i)$ where $i = \\\\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\\\F_q^m$, and $\\\\ell$ is a line that goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$.\\n    58\\t\\\\end{lemma}\\n    59\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n    60\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:line-representative}\\n    61\\t\\tSince $s$ is uniformly random in $\\\\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$, the index $i = \\\\chi(s)$ is uniformly random in $\\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$, so $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$. Since $u_0 = L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u)$ is the canonical representative of the line through $u$ in direction $e_i$, we have $u \\\\in \\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$.\\n    62\\t\\\\end{proof}\\n    63\\t\\n    64\\t\\\\begin{lemma}\\\\label{lem:dlnf}\\n    65\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\\n    66\\t\\tConsider the pair $(\\\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\\\bigl((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0)\\\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\\\ell = \\\\ell(u_0, v)$ where $i = \\\\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\\\F_q^m$, and $\\\\ell$ is a random diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares its first $i-1$ coordinates with $u$, for uniformly random $i \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$.\\n    67\\t\\\\end{lemma}\\n    68\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n    69\\t\\t\\\\uses{lem:alnf}\\n    70\\t\\tThe proof is identical to that of Lemma~\\\\ref{lem:alnf}: uniformity of $s$ makes $i = \\\\chi(s)$ uniform, the direction component of the sampled tuple is $\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ for uniform $v$ (so its first $i-1$ coordinates vanish), and $u_0 = L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u)$ places $u$ on the line $\\\\ell(u_0,\\\\pi_{i-1}(v))$.\\n    71\\t\\\\end{proof}\\n    72\\t\\n    73\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]\\\\label{def:line-point-dist}\\n    74\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}\\n    75\\t\\tThe \\\\emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\\\ell = (u_0,e_i),\\\\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity. The \\\\emph{diagonal line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\\\ell = (u_0,s,v),\\\\, u)$. The \\\\emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{Line}}$ is the equal mixture of the two: with probability $\\\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$, and with probability $\\\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$.\\n    76\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n    77\\t\\n    78\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the classical low individual degree game]\\\\label{def:ld-win-predicate}\\n    79\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:line, def:polyfunc}\\n    80\\t\\tFix $\\\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$. Answers in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.\\n    81\\t\\t\\\\begin{itemize}\\n    82\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\\\\F_q^k$.\\n    83\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\\\\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.\\n    84\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{DLine}$, question content $(u_0,s,v) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q \\\\times \\\\F_q^m$, specifying the diagonal line $\\\\ell(u_0,v')$ with $v' = \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple of univariate polynomials of degree at most $md$.\\n    85\\t\\t\\\\end{itemize}\\n    86\\t\\tThe win predicate $D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\\\\mathrm A}, x_{\\\\mathrm A}, t_{\\\\mathrm B}, x_{\\\\mathrm B}, a_{\\\\mathrm A}, a_{\\\\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts.\\n    87\\t\\t\\\\begin{enumerate}\\n    88\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Consistency test}) If $t_{\\\\mathrm A} = t_{\\\\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\\\\mathrm A} = a_{\\\\mathrm B}$.\\n    89\\t\\t\\t% The source phrases both clauses with \\\"the\\\" t such that x = u_0 + tv; that phrase\\n    90\\t\\t\\t% does not determine t on diagonal questions with direction v' = 0, which the\\n    91\\t\\t\\t% question distribution samples with positive probability. The universal\\n    92\\t\\t\\t% quantification over t used here is the local correction; see the remark below.\\n    93\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Axis-parallel line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\\\mathsf{ALine}$ and $t_{\\\\overline w} = \\\\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$ and all $t \\\\in \\\\F_q$ such that $x_{\\\\overline w} = u_0 + t e_i$, where $i = \\\\chi(s)$.\\n    94\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Diagonal line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\\\mathsf{DLine}$ and $t_{\\\\overline w} = \\\\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$ and all $t \\\\in \\\\F_q$ such that $x_{\\\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$, where $v' = \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\\\chi(s)$.\\n    95\\t\\t\\\\end{enumerate}\\n    96\\t\\tThe game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the typed game with type set $\\\\mathcal T^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$, the question distribution of Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution}, and win predicate $D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$.\\n    97\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n    98\\t\\n    99\\t\\\\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\\\\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}\\n   100\\t\\tThe source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \\\\in \\\\F_q$ such that $x_{\\\\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\\\\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \\\\mapsto u_0 + t \\\\cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$.\\n   101\\t\\\\end{remark}\\n   102\\t\\n   103\\tThe soundness properties of the low individual degree game are expressed in terms of the following class of measurements.\\n   104\\t\\n   105\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]\\\\label{def:ld-meas}\\n   106\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:polyfunc, def:polymeasurements, def:polynomials-degree}\\n   107\\t\\tLet $\\\\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ denote the set of POVM measurements indexed by $\\\\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, the polynomial representatives of individual degree at most $d$ in each variable; this is the notion of Definition~\\\\ref{def:polymeasurements}, and the argument order $(m,q,d)$ follows that definition (the paper orders the arguments as $(m,d,q)$). By Definition~\\\\ref{def:polynomials-degree}, evaluation identifies these representatives with the corresponding polynomial functions $g\\\\colon \\\\F_q^m \\\\to \\\\F_q$, bijectively whenever $d \\\\le q-1$; the parameter regimes of this chapter (Definition~\\\\ref{def:introparams} fixes $d = 1$, and admissibility gives $q \\\\ge 2$) always satisfy this. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\\\\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\\\\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\\\\ldots,d_k)$, let $\\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \\\\{G_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\}$ such that for each $i \\\\in \\\\{1,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\\\\colon \\\\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \\\\to \\\\F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.\\n   108\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n   109\\t\\n   110\\tQuantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \\\\emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. Instead, the construction relies on the low \\\\emph{individual} degree test, whose quantum soundness is proved in~\\\\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} and generalized in~\\\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.\\n   111\\t\\n   112\\t% The paper states this result in a theorem environment with the label lem:ld-soundness.\\n   113\\t% We keep both the environment and the label verbatim for cross-reference fidelity.\\n   114\\t\\\\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\\\\label{lem:ld-soundness}\\n   115\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:povm-distance, def:bracket}\\n   116\\t\\tThere exists a function\\n   117\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   118\\t\\t\\t\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps, q, m, d, k) = a\\\\,(dmk)^a \\\\bigl(\\\\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\\\\bigr)\\n   119\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   120\\t\\tfor universal constants $a \\\\ge 1$ and $0 < b \\\\le 1$ such that the following holds. For all $\\\\eps > 0$ and every parameter tuple $\\\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ as in Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-game} (so $q$ is an admissible field size and $m$ divides $q$), and for all projective strategies $(\\\\psi, A, B)$ that succeed with probability at least $1-\\\\eps$ in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$, there exist measurements\\n   121\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   122\\t\\t\\tG^w \\\\in \\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)\\n   123\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   124\\t\\ton $\\\\hilb_w$ for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$, where by slight abuse of notation $m$, $q$, $d$ denote the constant tuples $(m,\\\\ldots,m)$, $(q,\\\\ldots,q)$, $(d,\\\\ldots,d)$ of length $k$, such that\\n   125\\t\\t\\\\begin{align*}\\n   126\\t\\t\\tA^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   127\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   128\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   129\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   130\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   131\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot B^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   132\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   133\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   134\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\;,\\n   135\\t\\t\\\\end{align*}\\n   136\\t\\twhere $\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = \\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps,q,m,d,k)$, all three approximations are with respect to the state $\\\\ket{\\\\psi}$, and the bracket notation for post-processed outcomes is that of Definition~\\\\ref{def:bracket}. The first two approximations hold on average over the uniform distribution on $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$; no question distribution is associated with the third.\\n   137\\t\\\\end{theorem}\\n   138\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n   139\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:povm-distance}\\n   140\\t\\tLet $\\\\Sigma = \\\\F_q$ and let $\\\\code \\\\subseteq \\\\Sigma^q$ be the Reed--Solomon code of degree $d$: the set of all $(p(x_1),\\\\ldots,p(x_q))$ where $p\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\\\\ldots,x_q$ enumerate $\\\\F_q$. We may assume $d < q$. In the opposite regime the statement is immediate: for $k \\\\ge 1$ and $d \\\\ge q$ the prefactor gives $\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}} \\\\ge a\\\\,(dmk)^a\\\\, q^{-b} \\\\ge q^{a-b} \\\\ge 1$, while the quantity bounded in Definition~\\\\ref{def:povm-distance} never exceeds $2$ for families of POVM elements, so the three approximations hold for an arbitrary choice of $G^w \\\\in \\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$; and for $k = 0$ every answer tuple is empty, all measurements involved are single-outcome, and the approximations hold with error zero. With the\\n   142\\t\\t% intended value n = q the printed distance q-d+1 exceeds the true minimum distance\\n   143\\t\\t% q-d of the degree-d evaluation code, and the dimension claim d+1 requires d < q.\\n   144\\t\\t% Both points are corrected above; the regime d >= q, which the parameter tuple of\\n   145\\t\\t% Definition def:ld-game permits, is handled by the triviality argument.\\n   146\\t\\tThe two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\\\\code^{\\\\ot m}$, as described in Figures~1 and~2 of~\\\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, coincides with the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$ with parameters $\\\\mathsf{ldparams}$ and $k=1$: the axis-parallel line-versus-point test is their axis-parallel lines test, with the roles of the two players chosen uniformly at random, which is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor-code test from Section~4.1 there; the diagonal line-versus-point test is their subcube commutation test, again with the added symmetrization between the players; and the consistency test is their synchronicity test. Define $L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \\\\in V$,\\n    29\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    30\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:cl-ptf}\\n    31\\t\\t\\tL_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\\\\;.\\n    32\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    33\\t\\tFor $s \\\\in \\\\F_q$, let $\\\\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that\\n    34\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    35\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:chi-func}\\n    36\\t\\t\\ts = (\\\\chi(s)-1)\\\\,\\\\frac{q}{m} + r\\n    37\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    38\\t\\tfor some $0 \\\\le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\\\\{0,1,\\\\ldots,q-1\\\\}$ under the identification of $\\\\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\\\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\\\F_q^m$, and $\\\\ell$ is a random diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares its first $i-1$ coordinates with $u$, for uniformly random $i \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$.\\n    67\\t\\\\end{lemma}\\n    68\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n    69\\t\\t\\\\uses{lem:alnf}\\n    70\\t\\tThe proof is identical to that of Lemma~\\\\ref{lem:alnf}: uniformity of $s$ makes $i = \\\\chi(s)$ uniform, the direction component of the sampled tuple is $\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ for uniform $v$ (so its first $i-1$ coordinates vanish), and $u_0 = L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u)$ places $u$ on the line $\\\\ell(u_0,\\\\pi_{i-1}(v))$.\\n    71\\t\\\\end{proof}\\n    72\\t\\n    73\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]\\\\label{def:line-point-dist}\\n    74\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}\\n    75\\t\\tThe \\\\emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\\\ell = (u_0,e_i),\\\\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity. Answers in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.\\n    81\\t\\t\\\\begin{itemize}\\n    82\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\\\\F_q^k$.\\n    83\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\\\\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.\\n    84\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{DLine}$, question content $(u_0,s,v) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q \\\\times \\\\F_q^m$, specifying the diagonal line $\\\\ell(u_0,v')$ with $v' = \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple of univariate polynomials of degree at most $md$.\\n    85\\t\\t\\\\end{itemize}\\n    86\\t\\tThe win predicate $D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\\\\mathrm A}, x_{\\\\mathrm A}, t_{\\\\mathrm B}, x_{\\\\mathrm B}, a_{\\\\mathrm A}, a_{\\\\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts.\\n    87\\t\\t\\\\begin{enumerate}\\n    88\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Consistency test}) If $t_{\\\\mathrm A} = t_{\\\\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\\\\mathrm A} = a_{\\\\mathrm B}$.\\n    89\\t\\t\\t% The source phrases both clauses with \\\"the\\\" t such that x = u_0 + tv; that phrase\\n    90\\t\\t\\t% does not determine t on diagonal questions with direction v' = 0, which the\\n    91\\t\\t\\t% question distribution samples with positive probability. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\\\\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\\\\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\\\\ldots,d_k)$, let $\\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \\\\{G_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\}$ such that for each $i \\\\in \\\\{1,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\\\\colon \\\\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \\\\to \\\\F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.\\n   108\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n   109\\t\\n   110\\tQuantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \\\\emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.\\n   111\\t\\n   112\\t% The paper states this result in a theorem environment with the label lem:ld-soundness.\\n   113\\t% We keep both the environment and the label verbatim for cross-reference fidelity.\\n   114\\t\\\\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\\\\label{lem:ld-soundness}\\n   115\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:povm-distance, def:bracket}\\n   116\\t\\tThere exists a function\\n   117\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   118\\t\\t\\t\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps, q, m, d, k) = a\\\\,(dmk)^a \\\\bigl(\\\\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\\\\bigr)\\n   119\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   120\\t\\tfor universal constants $a \\\\ge 1$ and $0 < b \\\\le 1$ such that the following holds. For all $\\\\eps > 0$ and every parameter tuple $\\\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ as in Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-game} (so $q$ is an admissible field size and $m$ divides $q$), and for all projective strategies $(\\\\psi, A, B)$ that succeed with probability at least $1-\\\\eps$ in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$, there exist measurements\\n   121\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   122\\t\\t\\tG^w \\\\in \\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)\\n   123\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   124\\t\\ton $\\\\hilb_w$ for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$, where by slight abuse of notation $m$, $q$, $d$ denote the constant tuples $(m,\\\\ldots,m)$, $(q,\\\\ldots,q)$, $(d,\\\\ldots,d)$ of length $k$, such that\\n   125\\t\\t\\\\begin{align*}\\n   126\\t\\t\\tA^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   127\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   128\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   129\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   130\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   131\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot B^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   132\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   133\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   134\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\;,\\n   135\\t\\t\\\\end{align*}\\n   136\\t\\twhere $\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = \\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps,q,m,d,k)$, all three approximations are with respect to the state $\\\\ket{\\\\psi}$, and the bracket notation for post-processed outcomes is that of Definition~\\\\ref{def:bracket}. The first two approximations hold on average over the uniform distribution on $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$; no question distribution is associated with the third.\\n   137\\t\\\\end{theorem}\\n   138\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n   139\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:povm-distance}\\n   140\\t\\tLet $\\\\Sigma = \\\\F_q$ and let $\\\\code \\\\subseteq \\\\Sigma^q$ be the Reed--Solomon code of degree $d$: the set of all $(p(x_1),\\\\ldots,p(x_q))$ where $p\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\\\\ldots,x_q$ enumerate $\\\\F_q$. /-!
# Conditionally linear functions and graph distributions

The question distributions in the Pauli basis test are generated by a finite
graph of types and a shared seed, with each type applying a conditionally linear
map to that seed.  The inductive predicate below records the level structure
needed by later formalization stages.

## References

The source-facing nodes are `def:cl-func`, `def:cl-dist`, `lem:cl-concat`, and
`def:graph-distribution` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-535`.
The paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`
and `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1010`.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT

open MIPStarRE.LDT

variable {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]

/--
The source definition is recursive in the residual map.  A direct inductive
predicate with that recursive occurrence under a dependent finite-set index is
rejected by Lean's strict-positivity checker.  We therefore expose the same
public predicate through a positive syntax tree (`CondLinearTerm`), together
with its support invariant and evaluation function.  This is a representation
deviation forced by Lean, not an additional mathematical hypothesis.  It encodes
`def:cl-func`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-463`,
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
-/
inductive CondLinearTerm (K : Type*) [Field K] {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    [DecidableEq ι] : ℕ → Type _ where
  | zero : CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) 0
  | succ {ell : ℕ}
      (S₁ : Finset ι)
      (L₁ : (ι → K) →ₗ[K] (ι → K))
      (hSupport : ∀ x i, i ∉ S₁ → L₁ x i = 0)
      (rest : (ι → K) → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell) :
      CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) (ell + 1)

/-- Restrict a coordinate vector to a register, zeroing the complementary
coordinates.  This is Lean-only support for the projections in `def:cl-func`,
blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:441-463`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
-/
def coordinateRestriction (S : Finset ι) (x : ι → K) : ι → K :=
  fun i => if i ∈ S then x i else 0

/-- Evaluation of a conditionally-linear syntax term.  Lean-only support for
`def:cl-func`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
-/
def CondLinearTerm.eval {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    {K : Type*} [Field K] :
    {ell : ℕ} → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell → (ι → K) → (ι → K)
  | _, .zero => fun _ => 0
  | _, .succ S₁ L₁ _ rest =>
      fun x =>
        let x₁ := coordinateRestriction S₁ x
        L₁ x₁ + CondLinearTerm.eval (rest (L₁ x₁)) x

/-- The support invariant for a conditionally-linear syntax term.  This is a
Lean-only companion to `def:cl-func`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
-/
def CondLinearTerm.supportedOn {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    {K : Type*} [Field K] :
    {ell : ℕ} → CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell → Finset ι → Prop
  | _, .zero, _ => True
  | _, .succ S₁ _ _ rest, S =>
      S₁ ⊆ S ∧ ∀ y, CondLinearTerm.supportedOn (rest y) (S \ S₁)

/-- The public conditionally-linear predicate.  Its positive syntax-tree
encoding is the Lean representation of `def:cl-func`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
-/
def IsCondLinearOn (K : Type*) [Field K] {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    [DecidableEq ι] (S : Finset ι) (ell : ℕ)
    (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) : Prop :=
  ∃ t : CondLinearTerm K (ι := ι) ell,
    CondLinearTerm.supportedOn t S ∧ CondLinearTerm.eval t = L

/--
`IsCondLinear` abbreviates the full-coordinate predicate.  Blueprint
`def:cl-func`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:453-463`; paper
`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:35-57`.
-/
def IsCondLinear (ell : ℕ) (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) : Prop :=
  IsCondLinearOn K Finset.univ ell L

/--
The distribution obtained by applying two conditionally linear maps to a common
uniform seed.  This is `def:cl-dist` in
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:467-470`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:132-138`.
-/
noncomputable def clDistribution [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
    (L R : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) :
    Distribution ((ι → K) × (ι → K)) :=
  (uniformDistribution (ι → K)).map (fun z => (L z, R z))

/-- The direct-sum map used to encode the paper's CL concatenation.  The left
coordinates carry `L`, while the right coordinates carry the family member
`R u v` selected by the left input `u`.  This is Lean-only coordinate
infrastructure for `lem:cl-concat`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:498-505`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`.
-/
def condLinearConcat {ιU ιV : Type*} [Fintype ιU] [DecidableEq ιU]
    [Fintype ιV] [DecidableEq ιV] (L : (ιU → K) → (ιU → K))
    (R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K))
    (x : ιU ⊕ ιV → K) : ιU ⊕ ιV → K :=
  let u : ιU → K := fun i => x (.inl i)
  let v : ιV → K := fun j => x (.inr j)
  Sum.elim (L u) (R (L u) v)

/--
Concatenating an outer and an indexed inner CL map adds their levels.  This is
`lem:cl-concat` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:498-505`, with
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`.
The direct-sum coordinate bookkeeping is represented by `condLinearConcat`; the
level proof remains deferred in this skeleton.
-/
theorem IsCondLinearOn.concat {ιU ιV : Type*} [Fintype ιU] [DecidableEq ιU]
    [Fintype ιV] [DecidableEq ιV] {ell k : ℕ}
    {L : (ιU → K) → (ιU → K)}
    {R : (ιU → K) → (ιV → K) → (ιV → K)}
    (hL : IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιU) k L)
    (hR : ∀ u : ιU → K, u ∈ Set.range L →
      IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset ιV) ell (R u)) :
    IsCondLinearOn K (Finset.univ : Finset (ιU ⊕ ιV)) (k + ell)
      (condLinearConcat L R) := by
  sorry

/--
The graph distribution samples an ordered endpoint pair whose unordered edge
`s(a,b)` lies in `E`, including self-loops.  It is the inlined graph sampler of
`def:graph-distribution` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:553-563`;
paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:984-1009`.
The underlying graph-distribution definition is
`references/qpbt-paper/07_types.tex:65-82`.
-/
noncomputable def graphDistribution {T : Type*} [Fintype T] [DecidableEq T]
    (E : Finset (Sym2 T)) (_hE : E.Nonempty) : Distribution (T × T) :=
  Distribution.uniformOnFinset
    (Finset.univ.filter fun ab : T × T => Sym2.mk ab.1 ab.2 ∈ E)

/-- The graph sampler has unit mass whenever its edge set is nonempty. -/
theorem graphDistribution_isProbability {T : Type*} [Fintype T] [DecidableEq T]
    (E : Finset (Sym2 T)) (hE : E.Nonempty) :
    (graphDistribution E hE).IsProbability := by
  sorry

    84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
    98		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
    99		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   100		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   101		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   102		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   103		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   104		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   105		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   106		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   107		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   108		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   109		$S^\perp$.
   110	\end{definition}
   111	
   112	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   113		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   114		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   115		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   116		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   117		\[
   118			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   119		\]
   120	\end{lemma}
   121	\begin{proof}
   122		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   123		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   124		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   125		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   126		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   127		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   128		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   129		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   130		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   131	\end{proof}

   133	\begin{definition}[Canonical linear map with prescribed kernel]\label{def:cl-canonical}
   134		\uses{def:canonical-complement, lem:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   135		Let $F \subseteq V$ be a set of linearly independent vectors and let
   136		$F^\perp$ be its canonical complement. The \emph{canonical linear map
   137		$L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ with kernel basis $F$} is the projector onto $T$
   138		parallel to $S$, where $S = \mathrm{span}(F)$ and
   139		$T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$; this is well defined by
   140		Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement}. Since the canonical complement
   141		depends only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$
   142		(Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}), so does $L$, and we also call
   143		it the \emph{canonical linear map with kernel $S$}. Note that
   144		$\ker(L) = S$.
   145	\end{definition}
   146	
   147	\begin{definition}[The map $L^\perp$]\label{def:Lperp}
   148		\uses{def:cl-canonical, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   149		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map and let $F$ be a basis for
   150		$\ker(L)^\perp$. Define $L^\perp : V \to V$ as the canonical linear map with
   151		kernel basis $F$. (By the basis-independence noted in
   152		Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}, the map $L^\perp$ depends only
   153		on $\ker(L)$ and not on the chosen basis $F$.)
   154	\end{definition}
   155	
   156	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:L_perp_perp}
   157		\uses{def:Lperp}
   158		Let $L \in \mathrm{End}(V)$ be a linear map, $F$ a basis for
   159		$\ker(L)^\perp$, and $L^\perp$ as in Definition~\ref{def:Lperp}. Then
   160		$\ker(L^\perp) = \ker(L)^\perp$.
   161	\end{lemma}
   162	\begin{proof}
   163		\uses{def:Lperp, def:cl-canonical, lem:canonical-complement}
   164		Set $S = \mathrm{span}(F) = \ker(L)^\perp$ and $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$;
   165		by Lemma~\ref{lem:canonical-complement} every $v \in V$ decomposes uniquely
   166		as $v = v^S + v^T$, and by definition $L^\perp v = v^T$. If
   167		$L^\perp v = 0$ then $v = v^S \in S = \ker(L)^\perp$. Conversely, if
   168		$v \in S$ then $v^T = 0$, so $L^\perp v = 0$.
   169	\end{proof}

    65	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`, paper `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:231-384`.
    66	-/
    67	private def prefixMap (k n : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) :
    68	    (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin k → K) :=
    69	  { toFun := fun x i => x ⟨i.1, lt_of_lt_of_le i.2 hk⟩
    70	    map_add' := by

    77	/-- The rank of a prefix restriction used by the pivot characterization. -/
    78	private noncomputable def prefixRank {n : ℕ} (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K))
    79	    (k : ℕ) (hk : k ≤ n) : ℕ :=
    80	  Module.finrank K (W.map (prefixMap k n hk))
    81	
    82	/--
    83	The non-pivot coordinate set of `W`, defined by the rank-increase
    84	characterization of pivots.  This is the basis-free encoding approved for
    85	`def:canonical-complement` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:84-110`;
    86	the paper's Gaussian-elimination presentation is
    87	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:303-320`.
    88	-/
    89	noncomputable def canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
    90	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : Finset (Fin n) :=
    91	  Finset.univ.filter fun j =>
    92	    prefixRank W (j.1 + 1) (Nat.succ_le_of_lt j.2) =
    93	      prefixRank W j.1 j.2.le
    94

    99	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:342-373`.

   102	theorem isCompl_registerSubmodule_canonicalComplement {n : ℕ}
   103	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) :
   104	    IsCompl W (registerSubmodule K (canonicalComplement W)) := by
   105	  sorry

   109	`def:cl-canonical` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:133-145`,
   110	originating at `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:375-384`.

   112	noncomputable def canonicalProjOfKernel {n : ℕ}
   113	    (W : Submodule K (Fin n → K)) : (Fin n → K) →ₗ[K] (Fin n → K) := by

   245	              pauliOperatorDistanceB P S w W ≤ deltaQld a b ε P.m P.d P.q) := by

+import Mathlib
+import MIPStarRE.LDT.Basic.ParametersBase

+/-!
+# Finite-field bases and the fixed binary representation
+
+The Pauli basis test uses fields of size `2^k` for odd `k`, together with a
+chosen self-dual normal basis over `ZMod 2`.  This file records that choice as
+data, while exposing Mathlib's basis and algebra-trace APIs for later proofs.
+
+## References
+
+The declarations correspond to `def:admissible-size`, `def:subfields-kappa`,
+`def:subfield-trace`, and `def:binary-representation` in
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:182-232` and `298-315`.
+Their paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:433-502,653-728`.
+-/
+
+open scoped BigOperators
+
+namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
+
+/-- `IsAdmissibleSize q` is the predicate `q = 2^k` for an odd exponent.
+This is `def:admissible-size` in the blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:210-212`, with paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:662-667`.
+-/
+def IsAdmissibleSize (q : ℕ) : Prop := ∃ k : ℕ, Odd k ∧ q = 2 ^ k
+
+/--
+A fixed finite-field model records the carrier and the chosen coding of its
+elements by `Fin q`.  The algebra structure and stored basis data make explicit
+the paper's once-and-for-all self-dual normal-basis convention; they are
+deliberately part of the model rather than quantified afresh by the soundness
+theorem.  This is the Lean carrier for `def:binary-representation`, blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-728`.
+-/
+structure FixedFieldModel (q : ℕ) extends MIPStarRE.LDT.FieldModel q where
+  /-- Scalar restriction from `ZMod 2` to the chosen field. -/
+  algebra : Algebra (ZMod 2) K
+  /-- Dimension of the chosen basis over the prime subfield. -/
+  basisDim : ℕ
+  /-- The chosen basis dimension is odd, as required for a self-dual normal basis
+  over the binary field. -/
+  basisDimOdd : Odd basisDim
+  /-- The admissible field-size relation for the chosen basis dimension. -/
+  basisCard : q = 2 ^ basisDim
+  /-- The chosen basis of `K` over `ZMod 2`. -/
+  basis : Module.Basis (Fin basisDim) (ZMod 2) K
+  /--
+  The inherited coding of `K` is the natural binary encoding of the stored
+  basis coordinates.  This field records the source's `downsize` convention
+  rather than allowing an unrelated permutation of `Fin q`.  It is the
+  coordinate clause of `def:binary-representation` in
+  `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`, with paper origin
+  `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:669-680`.
+  -/
+  representation_natural :
+    ∀ v : Fin basisDim → ZMod 2,
+      (toFieldModel.equiv (basis.equivFun.symm v)).val =
+        ∑ i : Fin basisDim, if v i = 1 then 2 ^ i.1 else 0
+  /-- Self-duality of the chosen basis with respect to the field trace. -/
+  selfDual : ∀ i j, Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K (basis i * basis j) =
+    if i = j then 1 else 0
+  /-- Normality of the chosen basis, recorded by a Frobenius generator. -/
+  normal : ∃ α : K, ∀ i, basis i = α ^ (2 ^ i.1)
+
+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : Field F.K := F.toFieldModel.instField
+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : Fintype F.K := F.toFieldModel.instFintype
+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : DecidableEq F.K := F.toFieldModel.instDecidableEq
+instance {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : Algebra (ZMod 2) F.K := F.algebra
+
+/-- The fixed binary representation of field elements (`def:binary-representation`).
+Blueprint: `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`; paper origin:
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-680`.
+-/
+noncomputable def binaryEquiv {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K ≃ Fin q :=
+  F.toFieldModel.equiv
+
+/-- The fixed binary representation obtained from the chosen basis coordinates. -/
+noncomputable def binaryRepresentation {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K ≃ Fin q :=
+  binaryEquiv F
+
+/--
+The coordinate map associated with a finite basis.  This is the `κ` of
+`def:subfields-kappa` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:182-208`,
+whose paper origin is `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:433-502`.
+-/
+noncomputable abbrev kappa {F K ι : Type*} [CommSemiring F] [Semiring K]
+    [Algebra F K] [Finite ι]
+    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K ≃ₗ[F] (ι → F) :=
+  b.equivFun
+
+/--
+Multiplication by `a` in basis coordinates, using Mathlib's
+`Algebra.leftMulMatrix`.  It is the multiplication table `K_a` in
+`def:subfields-kappa` (blueprint lines 196-199; paper
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`).
+-/
+noncomputable abbrev multiplicationTable {F K ι : Type*} [CommSemiring F]
+    [Semiring K] [Algebra F K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
+    (b : Module.Basis ι F K) : K →ₐ[F] Matrix ι ι F :=
+  Algebra.leftMulMatrix b
+
+/--
+The finite-field trace used by the Pauli phases.  This is a thin wrapper around
+Mathlib's basis-independent `Algebra.trace`, matching `def:subfield-trace` and
+Equation `eq:def-trace` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:217-232`
+(`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`).
+-/
+noncomputable abbrev binTrace (K : Type*) [CommRing K] [Algebra (ZMod 2) K] :
+    K →ₗ[ZMod 2] ZMod 2 :=
+  Algebra.trace (ZMod 2) K
+
+/-- The trace selected by a fixed model; this is the map denoted `tr` in the
+paper's `def:binary-representation`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:298-315`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:653-680`. -/
+noncomputable def fixedBinTrace {q : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q) : F.K → ZMod 2 :=
+  binTrace F.K
+
+/--
+The matrix-trace presentation of `fixedBinTrace`, a statement-level bridge to
+Equation `eq:def-trace`.  It is the trace assertion in `def:subfield-trace`,
+blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:217-232`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:481-502`.  It remains a proof
+obligation in stage 4.1.
+-/
+theorem fixedBinTrace_eq_matrixTrace {q ι : ℕ} (F : FixedFieldModel q)
+    (b : Module.Basis (Fin ι) (ZMod 2) F.K) (a : F.K) :
+    fixedBinTrace F a = (multiplicationTable b a).trace := by
+  sorry
+
+end MIPStarRE.QPBT

+/-!
+# The Pauli basis test
+
+This file supplies the finite question and answer alphabets, the typed
+conditionally-linear question sampler, and the Boolean win predicate for the
+Pauli basis test.  The quantitative soundness theorem is isolated in
+`Soundness.lean`.
+
+## References
+
+The source-facing nodes are `def:admissible`, `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
+and `def:pauli-win-predicate` in
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-367`; their paper origin is
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:908-1225`.

+
+open scoped BigOperators
+
+namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
+
+open MIPStarRE.LDT
+
+/-- An admissible Pauli-test parameter package with the paper's fixed
+self-dual-normal field identification.  This is `def:admissible` in
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
+-/
+structure AdmissibleParams where
+  q : ℕ
+  m : ℕ
+  d : ℕ
+  hd : 1 ≤ d
+  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
+  hdvd : m ∣ q
+  model : FixedFieldModel q
+
+/-- The positivity of the ambient dimension is a proof obligation implicit in
+the admissibility convention `def:admissible`, blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
+-/
+theorem AdmissibleParams.one_le_m (P : AdmissibleParams) : 1 ≤ P.m := by
+  sorry
+
+/-- The low-degree parameter view of an admissible Pauli-test package.  This is
+a Lean-only bridge supporting the statement closure; it is not an additional
+hypothesis of `thm:pauli`.  Blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
+-/
+def AdmissibleParams.toLdParams (P : AdmissibleParams) : LdParams where
+  q := P.q
+  m := P.m
+  d := P.d
+  k := 1
+  hm := P.one_le_m
+  hd := P.hd
+  hk := by decide
+  hq := P.hq
+  hdvd := P.hdvd
+  model := P.model
+
+/-- The scalar carrier associated with an admissible parameter package.  It is
+the fixed field carrier in `def:admissible`, blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:269-283`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
+-/
+abbrev PauliScalar (P : AdmissibleParams) := P.model.K
+
+/-- The six families of Pauli-test questions.  This is part of
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+inductive PauliType where
+  | point (W : PauliKind)
+  | aline (W : PauliKind)
+  | dline (W : PauliKind)
+  | pauli (W : PauliKind)
+  | pairW (W : PauliKind)
+  | pair
+  | ms (t : MsType)
+  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
+
+/-- The register blocks used by the Pauli question space.  These are the
+coordinates displayed in `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
+`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+abbrev PauliIndex (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
+  (((((Fin P.m ⊕ Fin P.m) ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m) ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Unit)
+
+/-- The ambient Pauli question coefficient space (`def:pauli-question-distribution`,
+blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).
+-/
+abbrev PauliSpace (P : AdmissibleParams) := PauliIndex P → PauliScalar P
+
+/-- The coefficient register indexed by the Boolean cube in
+`def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:908-945`.
+-/
+abbrev PauliRegister (P : AdmissibleParams) := Cube P.m → PauliScalar P
+
+/- The nested sum is the fixed register order
+`V_X ⊕ V_Z ⊕ V_I ⊕ V_V ⊕ V_{R_X} ⊕ V_{R_Z}` from the blueprint. -/
+/-- The `V_X` block of an ambient Pauli vector (`def:pauli-question-distribution`,
+blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`). -/
+def pauliXBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
+  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl i)))))
+
+/-- The `V_Z` block of an ambient Pauli vector in `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
+blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliZBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
+  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))))
+
+/-- The scalar block `V_I` of an ambient Pauli vector in
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliScalarBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
+  z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr ()))))
+
+/-- The direction block `V_V` of an ambient Pauli vector in
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliDirectionBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
+  fun i => z (.inl (.inl (.inr i)))
+
+/-- The `r_X` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliRXBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
+  z (.inl (.inr ()))
+
+/-- The `r_Z` scalar block in the Pauli question content from
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliRZBlock (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliScalar P :=
+  z (.inr ())
+
+/-- Select the basis-dependent point block from a Pauli question content in
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliPointBlock (W : PauliKind) (z : PauliSpace P) :
+    Fin P.m → PauliScalar P :=
+  match W with
+  | .X => pauliXBlock z
+  | .Z => pauliZBlock z
+
+/-- Read the low-degree register selected by a basis from an ambient Pauli
+vector.  Lean-only coordinate plumbing for `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
+blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliToLd (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind) (z : PauliSpace P) :
+    LdSpace P.toLdParams :=
+  fun i => match i with
+  | .inl (.inl j) => pauliPointBlock W z j
+  | .inl (.inr _) => pauliScalarBlock z
+  | .inr j => pauliDirectionBlock z j
+
+/-- Embed a low-degree vector into the basis-selected Pauli blocks, clearing the
+other basis and the two `r` registers.  This is Lean-only coordinate plumbing
+for `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def embedLd (P : AdmissibleParams) (W : PauliKind)
+    (u : LdSpace P.toLdParams) : PauliSpace P :=
+  fun i => match i with
+  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) =>
+      match W with
+      | .X => u (.inl (.inl j))
+      | .Z => 0
+  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) =>
+      match W with
+      | .X => 0
+      | .Z => u (.inl (.inl j))
+  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => u (.inl (.inr ()))
+  | .inl (.inl (.inr j)) => u (.inr j)
+  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
+  | .inr _ => 0
+
+/-- The type-4 projection retaining `V_X`, `V_Z`, `V_{R_X}`, and `V_{R_Z}` from
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper
+origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliSharedProjection (z : PauliSpace P) : PauliSpace P :=
+  fun i => match i with
+  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))) => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl j)))))
+  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))) => z (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inl (.inr j)))))
+  | .inl (.inl (.inl (.inr _))) => 0
+  | .inl (.inl (.inr _)) => 0
+  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
+  | .inr _ => z (.inr ())
+
+/-- The source level attached to each typed Pauli CL map.  This records the
+exact levels in items 1--5 of `def:pauli-question-distribution`: point, line,
+and diagonal maps have levels 1, 2, and 3, the Pauli map has level 0, and the
+shared projection has level 1.  Blueprint
+`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliCLLevel : PauliType → ℕ
+  | .point _ => 1
+  | .aline _ => 2
+  | .dline _ => 3
+  | .pauli _ => 0
+  | .pairW _ => 1
+  | .pair => 1
+  | .ms _ => 1
+
+/-- The typed CL dispatcher.  The point/line maps are the corresponding
+low-degree maps embedded in the selected basis block; Pair, Magic Square, and
+Pair/W types use the shared projection; Pauli/W is the zero-level map.  This
+is the direct finite-space form of `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
+blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+noncomputable def pauliCL (P : AdmissibleParams) (t : PauliType) :
+    PauliSpace P → PauliSpace P :=
+  match t with
+  | .point W => fun z => embedLd P W (ldPointCL P.toLdParams (pauliToLd P W z))
+  | .aline W => fun z => embedLd P W (ldALineCL P.toLdParams (pauliToLd P W z))
+  | .dline W => fun z => embedLd P W (ldDLineCL P.toLdParams (pauliToLd P W z))
+  | .pauli _ => fun _ => 0
+  | .pairW _ => pauliSharedProjection
+  | .pair => pauliSharedProjection
+  | .ms _ => pauliSharedProjection
+
+/-- Level assertions for the typed Pauli CL maps.  These are Lean-only
+proof obligations corresponding to the prose following `def:pauli-question-distribution`
+(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).
+-/
+theorem isCondLinear_pauliCL (P : AdmissibleParams) (t : PauliType) :
+    IsCondLinearOn (PauliScalar P) Finset.univ (pauliCLLevel t) (pauliCL P t) := by
+  sorry
+
+/-- A finite edge set for the typed Pauli question graph.  The self-loops and
+the displayed type-incidence families are the graph used by the sampler in
+`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint lines 285-329, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+def pauliEdges : Finset (Sym2 PauliType) :=
+  let loops := Finset.univ.image (fun t : PauliType => Sym2.mk t t)
+  let lineEdges :=
+    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
+      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.aline W)) ∪
+      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
+        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.dline W)) ∪
+      (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
+        Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pauli W))
+  let basisEdges :=
+    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
+      Sym2.mk (.point W) (.pairW W)) ∪
+      ({Sym2.mk (.point .X) (.ms (.var ⟨0, by decide⟩)),
+        Sym2.mk (.point .Z) (.ms (.var ⟨4, by decide⟩))} : Finset (Sym2 PauliType))
+  let pairEdges :=
+    (Finset.univ : Finset PauliKind).image (fun W =>
+      Sym2.mk (.pairW W) .pair)
+  let msEdges' :=
+    (Finset.univ : Finset (MsType × MsType)).filter (fun xy =>
+      Sym2.mk xy.1 xy.2 ∈ msEdges) |>.image (fun xy =>
+        Sym2.mk (.ms xy.1) (.ms xy.2))
+  loops ∪ lineEdges ∪ basisEdges ∪ pairEdges ∪ msEdges'
+
+/-- A Pauli question is a type together with a full ambient coefficient vector
+(`def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`; paper
+origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).
+-/
+abbrev PauliQuestion (P : AdmissibleParams) := PauliType × PauliSpace P
+
+/-- The ordered-edge subtype used by the Pauli question sampler.  This is
+the finite carrier underlying `graphDistribution pauliEdges`; it is Lean-only
+infrastructure for `def:pauli-question-distribution`, blueprint
+`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`.
+-/
+abbrev PauliEdge :=
+  {e : PauliType × PauliType // Sym2.mk e.1 e.2 ∈ pauliEdges}
+
+/-- The Pauli graph has a loop, so its ordered-edge subtype is nonempty.  This
+is a finite-carrier fact used only to instantiate the uniform source sampler
+for `def:pauli-question-distribution`; the graph itself is the source-facing
+object `pauliEdges` above (same blueprint and paper references).
+-/
+theorem pauliEdge_nonempty : Nonempty PauliEdge := by
+  refine ⟨⟨(.point .X, .point .X), ?_⟩⟩
+  simp [pauliEdges]
+
+/-- The finite support obtained by sampling an edge and a common ambient seed,
+then applying the endpoint CL maps.  This is the inlined typed-CL construction
+of `def:pauli-question-distribution` (blueprint lines 285-329; paper
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:964-1120`).
+-/
+noncomputable def pauliQuestionSupport (P : AdmissibleParams) :
+    Finset (PauliQuestion P × PauliQuestion P) :=
+  by
+    classical
+    exact
+      (Finset.univ.filter fun s : (PauliType × PauliType) × PauliSpace P =>
+          Sym2.mk s.1.1 s.1.2 ∈ pauliEdges).image (fun s =>
+        ((s.1.1, pauliCL P s.1.1 s.2), (s.1.2, pauliCL P s.1.2 s.2)))
+
+/-- The Pauli question distribution from `def:pauli-question-distribution`,
+blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:285-329`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1070-1120`.
+-/
+noncomputable def pauliQuestionDistribution (P : AdmissibleParams) :
+    Distribution (PauliQuestion P × PauliQuestion P) :=
+  by
+    classical
+    letI : Nonempty PauliEdge := pauliEdge_nonempty
+    exact
+      Distribution.map
+        (uniformDistribution (PauliEdge × PauliSpace P))
+        (fun s =>
+          ((s.1.1.1, pauliCL P s.1.1.1 s.2),
+            (s.1.1.2, pauliCL P s.1.1.2 s.2)))
+
+/-- The finite answer alphabet for the Pauli basis test.  Its constructors are
+the seven answer forms in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint lines 331-367,
+paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
+-/
+inductive PauliAnswer (P : AdmissibleParams) where
+  | value (a : PauliScalar P)
+  | alinePoly (a : Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
+  | dlinePoly (a : Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P)
+  | pairBits (a : ZMod 2 × ZMod 2)
+  | bit (a : ZMod 2)
+  | msTriple (a : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
+  | pauliOutcome (a : PauliRegister P)
+  deriving DecidableEq
+
+/-- A finite sum code used only to construct the `Fintype` instance for the
+answer alphabet in `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
+`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
+-/
+abbrev PauliAnswerCode (P : AdmissibleParams) :=
+  PauliScalar P ⊕
+    ((Fin (P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
+      ((Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → PauliScalar P) ⊕
+        ((ZMod 2 × ZMod 2) ⊕
+          (ZMod 2 ⊕ ((Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ PauliRegister P)))))
+
+/-- The constructor-preserving finite-code equivalence for `PauliAnswer`.
+Lean-only infrastructure for `def:pauli-win-predicate`, blueprint
+`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:331-367`, paper origin
+`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1126-1225`.
+-/
+noncomputable def pauliAnswerEquiv (P : AdmissibleParams) :
+    PauliAnswer P ≃ PauliAnswerCode P where
+  toFun
+    | .value a => .inl a
+    | .alinePoly a => .inr (.inl a)
+    | .dlinePoly a => .inr (.inr (.inl a))
+    | .pairBits a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a)))
+    | .bit a => .inr (.inr (.inr (.inr (.inl a))))

    60	  exact ⟨q, 1, hqPrime, by decide, by simp⟩

    24	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]\label{def:register-subspace}
    25		A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
    26		subset of the standard basis of $V$. Such a subspace is represented by an
    27		indicator vector $u \in \{0,1\}^s$, where $s = \dim(V)$, via
    28		$S = \mathrm{span}\{\hat{e}_i : u_i = 1\}$.
    29	\end{definition}
    30	
    31	\begin{definition}[Dot product and orthogonal subspace]\label{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    32		For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$ and
    33		$v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V = \F^n$, the \emph{dot product} is
    34		\[
    35			u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
    36		\]
    37		For a subspace $S$ of $V$, the \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
    38		\[
    39			S^\perp = \bigl\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0 \text{ for all } v \in S \bigr\}\;.
    40		\]
    41		The notation $S^\perp$ leaves the ambient space $V$ implicit.
    42	\end{definition}
    43	
    44	Over finite fields, orthogonality lacks some of the familiar properties it has
    45	over $\R$ or $\C$; for example, a nonzero subspace may be orthogonal to itself,
    46	as is $\mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ over $\F_2$. The following dimension identity
    47	nevertheless holds over every field.
    48	
    49	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:perp_perp}
    50		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    51		Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) = \dim(V)$, and
    52		\[
    53			(S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
    54		\]
    55	\end{lemma}
    56	\begin{proof}
    57		\uses{def:dot-product-orthogonal}
    58		The elements of $S^\perp$ are the solutions of a feasible linear system whose
    59		coefficient matrix has $\dim(S)$ linearly independent rows, so the solution
    60		space has dimension exactly $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$. Every $u \in S$ is
    61		orthogonal to every element of $S^\perp$, so $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
    62		Applying the dimension identity twice shows that
    63		$\dim\bigl((S^\perp)^\perp\bigr) = \dim(S)$, so the inclusion is an equality.
    64	\end{proof}
    65	
    66	\begin{definition}[Complementary subspaces]\label{def:complementary}
    67		Two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of a linear space $V$ form a pair of
    68		\emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
    69		\[
    70			S \cap T = \{0\}\;, \qquad S + T = V\;.
    71		\]
    72		In this case we write $V = S \oplus T$. Every $x \in V$ can be written
    73		uniquely as $x = x^S + x^T$ with $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$; we call $x^S$
    74		(resp.\ $x^T$) the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel to $T$} (resp.\
    75		onto $T$ parallel to $S$). The unique linear map $L : V \to V$ with
    76		$x \mapsto x^S$ is the \emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
    77	\end{definition}
    78	
    79	A subspace may have many complementary subspaces: in $\F_2^2$, the subspace
    80	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    81	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,
    82	one may nevertheless single out a \emph{canonical} complement.
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace.
    98		% Basis-independence made explicit here: the source defines F^perp through
    99		% a basis but does not assert dependence on it; uniqueness of the reduced
   100		% row echelon form gives dependence on span(F) alone.
   101		Although defined through the basis $F$, it depends only on
   102		$\mathrm{span}(F)$ and the ambient standard basis: two bases of the same
   103		subspace form the rows of row-equivalent matrices, which have the same
   104		reduced row echelon form and hence the same pivot set $J$. The presentation
   105		through Gaussian elimination, adopted by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, makes the
   106		canonical complement efficiently computable. If $S$ is a register subspace
   107		spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the canonical complement of
   108		$\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its span coincides with
   109		$S^\perp$.
   110	\end{definition}
   111	
   112	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   113		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   114		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   115		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   116		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   117		\[
   118			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   119		\]
   120	\end{lemma}
   121	\begin{proof}
   122		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   123		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   124		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   125		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   126		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   127		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   128		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   129		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   130		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   131	\end{proof}

   182	\begin{definition}[Coordinate map and multiplication tables]\label{def:subfields-kappa}
   183		% The source lets k range over all integers; the extension field exists

   185		Let $q$ be a prime power and $k \ge 1$ an integer, so that $\F_q$ is a

   188		Fix a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{q^k}$ over $\F_q$. The bijection
   189		$\kappa_q : \F_{q^k} \to \F_q^k$ associated with this basis is
   190		\[
   191			\kappa_q : a \mapsto (a_i)_{i=1}^k\;, \qquad
   192			\text{where } a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i\;.
   193		\]
   194		The map $\kappa_q$ is an isomorphism of $\F_q$-vector spaces; in particular
   195		$\kappa_q(a + b) = \kappa_q(a) + \kappa_q(b)$ for all $a, b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   196		Moreover, multiplication by a fixed element corresponds to a linear map:
   197		for every $a \in \F_{q^k}$ there is a matrix $K_a \in \Mat_k(\F_q)$, the
   198		\emph{multiplication table of $a$ with respect to $\{e_i\}$}, such that
   199		$\kappa_q(ab) = K_a\, \kappa_q(b)$ for all $b \in \F_{q^k}$.
   200		The map extends coordinatewise to vectors, matrices, and sets: for
   201		$v = (v_1, \dots, v_n) \in \F_{q^k}^n$ set
   202		$\kappa_q(v) = (\kappa_q(v_i))_{i=1}^n \in \F_q^{kn}$; for
   203		$M = (M_{i,j}) \in \Mat_{m,n}(\F_{q^k})$ let
   204		$\chi_q(M) \in \Mat_{mk,nk}(\F_q)$ be the block matrix whose $(i,j)$-th
   205		block is $K_{M_{i,j}}$; and for a set $S$ of vectors put
   206		$\kappa_q(S) = \{\kappa_q(v) : v \in S\}$. When $q = p$ is the field
   207		characteristic, the subscript is omitted and we write $\kappa$ and $\chi$.

   259			      $\tr_{q^k \to q}(xy) = \kappa_q(x) \cdot \kappa_q(y)$;
