   216	\subsection{Linear spaces}
   217	\label{sec:linear-spaces}
   218	
   219	Linear spaces considered in the paper generally take the form $V = \F^n$ for a
   220	finite field $\F$ and integer $n \geq 1$.
   221	In particular, when we write ``let $V$ be a linear space'', unless explicitly
   222	stated otherwise we always mean a space of the form $\F^n$.
   223	Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \ldots, \hat{e}_n\}$ denote the standard basis of $V$, where for
   224	$i \in\{ 1, 2, \ldots, n\}$,
   225	\begin{equation*}
   226	  \hat{e}_i = (0, \ldots, 0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)
   227	\end{equation*}
   228	has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere.
   229	We write $\End(V)$ to denote the set of linear transformations from $V$ to
   230	itself.
   231	\begin{definition}[Register subspace]
   232	  A \emph{register subspace} $S$ of $V$ is a subspace that is the span of a
   233	  subset of the standard basis of $V$.\footnote{The use of the term ``register''
   234	    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often
   235	    partitioned into ``registers'' containing a few qubits each.}
   236	  We often represent such a subspace as an indicator vector $u\in \{0,1\}^s$,
   237	  where $s=\dim(V)$, such that if $\{\hat{e}_1,\ldots,\hat{e}_s\}$ is the standard basis of
   238	  $V$ then $S = \text{span}\{\hat{e}_i|\,u_i=1\}$.
   239	\end{definition}
   240	
   241	\begin{definition}
   242	  Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_i\}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$.
   243	  For two vectors $u = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i \hat{e}_i$, $v = \sum_{i=1}^n v_i \hat{e}_i$ in $V$,
   244	  define the \emph{dot product}
   245	  \begin{equation*}
   246	    u \cdot v = \sum_{i=1}^n u_i v_i \in \F\;.
   247	  \end{equation*}
   248	  Let $S$ be a subspace of $V$. The \emph{subspace orthogonal to $S$ in $V$} is
   249	  \begin{equation*}
   250	    S^\perp \,=\, \big\{ u \in V : u \cdot v = 0
   251	    \text{ for all }  v \in S \big\}\;.
   252	  \end{equation*}
   253	  Although the notation $S^\perp$ does not explicitly refer to $V$, the ambient
   254	  space will always be clear from context.
   255	\end{definition}
   256	
   257	We note that over finite fields, the notion of orthogonality does not possess
   258	all of the same intuitive properties of orthogonality over fields such as $\R$
   259	or $\C$; for example, a non-zero subspace $S$ may be orthogonal to itself (e.g.\
   260	$\mathrm{span} \{ (1,1) \}$ over $\F_2$).
   261	However, the following remains true over all fields.
   262	
   263	\begin{lemma}
   264	  \label{lem:perp_perp}
   265	  Suppose $S$ is a subspace of $V$. Then $\dim(S) + \dim(S^\perp) =
   266	  \dim(V)$, and 
   267	  \begin{equation*}
   268	    (S^\perp)^\perp = S\;.
   269	  \end{equation*}
   270	\end{lemma}
   271	
   272	\begin{proof}
   273	  The statement about the dimensions follows from the fact that vectors in $S^\perp$ are
   274	  the solution to a feasible linear system of equations with $\dim(S)$ linearly
   275	  independent rows; this implies that the solution space has dimension exactly
   276	  $\dim(V) - \dim(S)$.
   277	  Next, we argue that $S \subseteq (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   278	  Let $u \in S$.
   279	  Since all vectors $v \in S^\perp$ are orthogonal to every vector in $S$,
   280	  in particular $u$, this implies that $u \in (S^\perp)^\perp$.
   281	  By dimension counting, it follows that $(S^\perp)^\perp = S$.
   282	\end{proof}
   283	
   284	\begin{definition}\label{def:complementary}
   285	  Given a linear space $V$, two subspaces $S$ and $T$ of $V$ are said to form a
   286	  pair of \emph{complementary subspaces} of $V$ if
   287	\begin{equation*}
   288	  S \cap T = \{ 0 \}, \quad S + T = V\;.
   289	\end{equation*}
   290	In this case, we write $V = S \oplus T$.
   291	Any $x\in V$ can be written as $x = x^S + x^T$ for $x^S \in S$ and $x^T \in T$
   292	in a unique way.
   293	We refer to $x^S$ (resp.~$x^T$) as the \emph{projection of $x$ onto $S$ parallel
   294	  to $T$} (resp.~\emph{onto $T$ parallel to $S$}).
   295	We call the unique linear map $L: V \to V$ that maps $x \mapsto x^S$ the
   296	\emph{projector onto $S$ parallel to $T$}.
   297	\end{definition}
   298	
   299	A given subspace may have many different complementary subspaces: consider the
   300	example of $S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1) \}$ in $\F_2^2$.
   301	Different complementary subspaces include $T = \mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and
   302	$T' = \mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$.
   303	It is convenient to define the notion of a \emph{canonical complement} of a
   304	subspace $S$, given a basis for $S$.
   305	
   306	\begin{definition}
   307	  \label{def:canonical-complement}
   308	  Let $E$ be the standard basis of linear space $V = \F^n$.
   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.
   311	  The \emph{canonical complement $F^\perp$ of $F$} is the set of $n-m$ independent
   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary
   315	  fields, transform the $m\times n$ matrix $(a_{i, j})$ to reduced row echelon
   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.
   317	  Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices of the leading $1$ entry in each row
   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.
   319	  The canonical complement is defined as $F^\perp = \{ \hat{e}_j : j \not\in J \}$.
   320	\end{definition}
   321	
   322	
   323	\begin{remark}
   324	We emphasize that the canonical complement $F^\perp$ is a \emph{set} (rather than
   325	a subspace), and it is defined with respect to a \emph{set} of linearly
   326	independent vectors $F$. While there are equivalent ways of defining
   327	a canonical complement of a \emph{subspace} in a basis-independent manner, 
   328	we use this particular definition because it makes it clear that
   329	the canonical complement of a set $F$ is efficiently computable. 
   330	\end{remark}
   331	
   332	\begin{remark}
   333	  Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V$.
   334	  Suppose subspace $S$ is a register subspace of $V$ spanned by
   335	  $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$.
   336	  Then it is not hard to verify that the canonical complement of $\hat{E}_{0}$ is
   337	  $\hat{E}\setminus \hat{E}_0$ and the span of the canonical complement coincides with
   338	  $S^\perp$.
   339	\end{remark}
   340	
   341	
   342	\begin{lemma}
   343	  \label{lem:canonical-complement}
   344	  Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors $F = \{v_1,\ldots,v_m \}
   345	  \subseteq V$ and let $F^\perp$ be the canonical complement of $F$ as defined
   346	  in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   347	  Let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$.
   348	  Then
   349	  \begin{equation*}
   350	   \qquad S + T = V\;,  S \cap T = \{ 0 \} \;.
   351	  \end{equation*}
   352	\end{lemma}
   353	
   354	\begin{proof}
   355	To show the first item, we must show that every vector in $V$ can be
   356	written as a sum of an element of $S$ and an element of $T$. To do
   357	this, let $A = (a_{i, j})$ be the $m\times n$ matrix over $\F$ whose
   358	rows are the vectors $v_i$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.
   359	  Write $A = U B$ where $U$ is invertible and $B$ is in reduced row echelon
   360	  form.
   361	  Let $J$ be the set of column indices of the leading 1 entries in
   362	  $B$, as in Definition~\ref{def:canonical-complement}.  
   363	  Now, the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span the subpsace $S$, and the restriction of
   364	  these rows to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   365	  span $\F^m$. Thus, for any vector $u \in V$, there is some linear
   366	  combination $v$ of rows of $B$ such that $u$ and $v$ agree
   367	  restricted to the columns in $J$. In other words, there exists $v
   368	  \in S$ such that $u_j = v_j$ for all $j \in J$. Hence, $u = v + w$
   369	  for $w \in T$, where $T$ is the canonical complement.
   370	  This shows $S + T = V$.
   371	  Counting dimensions shows that necessarily $S\cap T =
   372	  \{0\}$.
   373	\end{proof}

   653	\subsubsection{Bit string representations}
   654	\label{sec:ff-representations}
   655	
   656	As mentioned at the end of \Cref{sec:tms}, we sometimes treat the
   657	inputs and outputs of Turing machines as representing elements of a finite
   658	field, or a vector space over a finite field.
   659	We discuss some important details about bit representations of finite field
   660	elements and arithmetic over finite fields.
   661	
   662	In the paper we only consider fields $\F_{2^k}$ where $k$ is odd. 
   663	
   664	\begin{definition}\label{def:admissible-size}
   665	  A field size $q$ is called an \emph{admissible} field size if $q=2^k$ for odd
   666	  $k$.
   667	\end{definition}
   668	
   669	Elements of $\F_2$ are naturally represented using bits. 
   670	To represent elements of $\F_{2^k}$ as binary strings we require the
   671	specification of a basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   672	Given a basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^k$ of $\F_{2^k}$, every element $a \in \F_{2^k}$
   673	has a unique expansion $a = \sum_{i=1}^k a_i e_i$ and can be represented as the
   674	$k$-bit string corresponding to $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$.
   675	Note that we omitted the subscript $2$ of $\downsize$ as it maps to the linear
   676	space over the prime subfield $\F_2$.
   677	Thus the \emph{binary representation} of $a \in \F_{2^k}$ is defined as the
   678	natural binary representation of $\downsize(a) \in \F_2^k$ (which in turn is the
   679	\emph{$\F_2$-representation of $a$}).
   680	Throughout the paper we freely associate between the binary representation of a
   681	field element $a \in \F_{2^k}$ and its $\F_2$-representation,
   682	although---technically speaking---these are distinct objects.
   683	
   684	Given the representations $\downsize(a), \downsize(b)$ of $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$, to
   685	compute the binary representation of $a+b$ it suffices to compute the addition
   686	bit-wise, modulo $2$.
   687	Computing the multiplication of elements $a, b$ requires the specification of
   688	the multiplication tables $\{K_{e_i} \in \Matrix_k (\F_2)\}_{i=1}^k $ for the
   689	basis $\{e_i\}$.
   690	Given representations $\downsize(a) = (a_i)_{i=1}^k$, $\downsize(b) =
   691	(b_i)_{i=1}^k$ for $a, b \in \F_{2^k}$ respectively, the representation
   692	$\downsize(ab)$ of the product $ab$ is computed as
   693	\begin{equation}
   694	  \label{eq:eq-mult}
   695	  \downsize(ab) = \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \, \downsize \bigl( e_i b \bigr) =
   696	  \sum_{i=1}^k \, a_i \bigl( K_{e_i}\, \downsize (b) \bigr)\;.
   697	\end{equation}
   698	Thus, using our representation for field elements, efficiently performing finite
   699	field arithmetic in $\F_{2^k}$ reduces to having access to the multiplication
   700	table of some basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$.
   701	
   702	The following fact provides an efficient deterministic algorithm for computing a
   703	self-dual normal basis for $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the corresponding
   704	multiplication tables for any odd $k$.
   705	
   706	\begin{lemma}
   707	  \label{lem:efficient_basis}
   708	  There exists a deterministic algorithm that given an odd integer $k > 0$,
   709	  outputs a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$ and the
   710	  multiplication tables of the basis in $\poly(k)$ time.
   711	\end{lemma}
   712	
   713	\begin{proof}
   714		The algorithm of Shoup~\cite[Theorem 3.2]{shoup1990new} shows that for prime
   715	  $p$, an irreducible polynomial in $\Fp[X]$ of degree $k$ can be computed in
   716	  time $\poly(p, k)$.
   717	  Then, the algorithm of Lenstra~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{lenstra1991finding} shows
   718	  that given such an irreducible polynomial, the multiplication table of a
   719	  normal basis of $\F_{p^k}$ over $\Fp$ can be computed in $\poly(k,\log p)$
   720	  time.
   721	  Finally, the algorithm of Wang~\cite{wang1989algorithm} shows that for odd $k$
   722	  and a multiplication table $K$ of a normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over $\F_2$, a
   723	  multiplication table $K'$ for a self-dual normal basis of $\F_{2^k}$ over
   724	  $\F_2$ can be computed in $\poly(k)$ time.
   725	  Putting these three algorithms together yields the claimed statement.
   726	\end{proof}

   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

   971	  \cup \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair\}\;,

   973	where $\type^\ms$ is the question type set of the Magic Square game defined in
   974	Section~\ref{sec:ms}.

  1073	\paragraph{Conditional linear functions for the Pauli basis test.}
  1074	The CL functions corresponding to the Pauli basis test question distribution are
  1075	parameterized by the parameter tuple $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$.
  1076	Let $V^\pauli$ denote the linear space $(\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m
  1077	\times (\F_q)^2$.
  1078	The space $V^\pauli$ is decomposed into a direct sum of the following register
  1079	subspaces: $V_\xpt,V_\zpt$ (which are $m$-dimensional), $V_\coord$ (which is
  1080	$1$-dimensional), $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is $m$-dimensional), and
  1081	$V_{\rxpt},V_{\rzpt}$ (which are $1$-dimensional).
  1082	We identify elements of $V^\pauli$ as tuples $(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1083	\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q \times \F_q^m \times (\F_q)^2$.
  1084	We define CL functions $L_\tvar: V^\pauli \to V^\pauli$ for every type $\tvar
  1085	\in \type^\pauli$:
  1086	\begin{enumerate}
  1087	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Point,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1088	  = L_\Point(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\Point$ is the $1$-level CL function defined in
  1089	  \Cref{eq:cl-ptf}.\footnote{The range $V_{\xpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus
  1090	    V_{\dir{}}$ or $V_{\zpt} \oplus V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ of $L_\Point$ is
  1091	    embedded in $V^\pauli$ in the natural way.
  1092	    The same convention is used also in Item 2 and 3 for $L_\ALine$ and
  1093	    $L_\DLine$.}
  1094	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\ALine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1095	  = L_\ALine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\ALine$ is the $2$-level CL function defined in
  1096	  \Cref{eq:cl-alnf}.
  1097	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\DLine,W}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)
  1098	  = L_\DLine(u_W,s,v)$ where $L_\DLine$ is the $3$-level CL function defined in
  1099	  \Cref{eq:cl-dlnf}.
  1100	\item For $\tvar \in \type^\ms \cup \{\Pair, (\Pair,X), (\Pair,Z) \}$,
  1101	  $L_{\tvar}(u_\xpt,u_\zpt,s,v,r_\xpt,r_\zpt) =
  1102	  (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,0,0,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, i.e., it projects onto $V_\xpt \oplus
  1103	  V_\zpt \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$.
  1104	  Thus $L_{\tvar}$ is a $1$-level CL function.
  1105	  
  1106	\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, define $L_{\Pauli,W} = 0$ as the identically $0$
  1107	  function.
  1108	  Thus it is a $0$-level CL function.
  1109	
  1110	\end{enumerate}
  1111	We note that the maps $L_{\Point,W}, L_{\ALine,W}, L_{\DLine,W}$ act as the zero function
  1112	on $V_{\overline{W}} \oplus V_{\rxpt} \oplus V_{\rzpt}$ where $\overline{W} = X$
  1113	if $W = Z$ and $\overline{W} = Z$ if $W = X$.
  1114	
  1115	The question distribution of $\game^\pauli$ is thus a typed CL distribution on
  1116	$\type^\pauli \times V^\pauli \times \type^\pauli \times V^\pauli$ where
  1117	$(\tvar_\alice,x_\alice,\tvar_\bob,x_\bob)$ is sampled by first uniformly
  1118	sampling an edge $(\tvar_\alice,\tvar_\bob)$ from the graph $G^\pauli$ defined
  1119	in Figure~\ref{fig:type-graph-pauli}, sampling a uniformly random $z \in
  1120	V^\pauli$, and then setting $x_w = L_{\tvar_w}(z)$ for $w \in \AB$.

  1229	We describe an honest, value-$1$ PCC strategy for the Pauli basis test.
  1230	
  1231	
  1232	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pauli-completeness}
  1233	  The Pauli basis test $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ has a value-$1$ SPCC strategy.
  1234	\end{lemma}
  1235	
  1236	\begin{proof}
  1237	  We begin by specifying the value-$1$ strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, E)$.
  1238	  The state is
  1239	  \begin{equation*}
  1240	    \ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\;.
  1400	  we can write the $(\Point, W)$ measurement as follows: 
  1401	  \begin{equation*}
  1402	  E^{(\Point,W),\, y}_{[\tr(\,\cdot\, r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}]}
  1403	  = \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(y)r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}]} \otimes I
  1404	  = E^{(\Pair, W), \omega}_{a_{\overline{w}}} \otimes I.
  1405	  \end{equation*}
  1406	  As a result, due to the consistency of the $(\Pair, W)$ measurement, the
  1407	  consistency check is passed with probability~$1$.
  1408	  On the other hand, if $\gamma \neq 0$, then the strategy passes the Magic
  1409	  Square check by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1410	  As for the consistency check in Item~\ref{item:magic-square-consistency}, we
  1411	  can write the $(\Point, X)$ measurement as follows:
  1412	  \begin{equation*}
  1413	  E^{(\Point,X),\, y}_{[\tr(\,\cdot\, r_X) = a_{\overline{w}}]}
  1414	  = \tau^X_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(y)r_X) = a_{\overline{w}}]} \otimes I
  1415	  = E^{\Variable_1,\, \omega}_{a_{\overline{w}}} \otimes I,
  1416	  \end{equation*}
  1417	  where the last step is by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1418	  As these measurements are consistent, this test is passed with
  1419	  probability~$1$.
  1420	\end{proof}

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}
  1446	
  1447	We provide a proof of \Cref{thm:pauli} in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
  1448	
  1449	
  1450	The strategies described in the proof of \Cref{lem:pauli-completeness} and in the conclusion of \Cref{thm:pauli} are described in terms of qudit Pauli measurements and maximally entangled states defined over $q$-dimensional qudits. 
  1451	However, it is more convenient for our application of the Pauli basis test to
  1452	instead deal with \emph{qubits}.
  1453	In particular, we use the Pauli basis test in the ``introspection game'' of
  1454	Section~\ref{sec:introspection}, where the players are commanded to sample
  1455	questions according to a sampler $\sampler$ of a normal form verifier.
  1456	By definition of normal form verifier, $\sampler$ is a sampler over $\F_2$, and
  1457	therefore it is natural to use a test for qubit Pauli measurements.
  1458	
  1459	Since we use field sizes $q$ that are powers of $2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-binary}
  1460	shows that the conclusions of \Cref{thm:pauli} can also be described in terms of
  1461	testing for maximally entangled states over qubits and qubit Pauli measurements.
  1462

  1470	\label{cor:pauli-binary}

     5	/-!
     6	# The Magic Square game
     7	
     8	The Magic Square component is represented by finite constraint and variable
     9	question types, the incidence graph, and the two corresponding answer forms.
    10	Its rigidity theorem is outside the stage-4.1 statement closure; only the game
    11	carrier is needed here.
    12	
    13	## References
    14	
    15	This file formalizes `def:ms-game` in
    16	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, from
    17	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    18	-/
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    21	
    22	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    23	
    24	/-- A Magic Square question is either a row/column constraint or a cell
    25	variable.  This is `def:ms-game`, blueprint lines 188-203, paper origin
    26	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    27	-/
    28	inductive MsType where
    29	  | constraint (i : Fin 6)
    30	  | var (j : Fin 9)
    31	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    32	
    33	/-- The cell incident to a constraint and one of its three positions in
    34	`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    35	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    36	-/
    37	def msConstraintVars (i : Fin 6) (j : Fin 3) : Fin 9 :=
    38	  ⟨if i.val < 3 then i.val * 3 + j.val else i.val - 3 + j.val * 3, by
    39	    by_cases h : i.val < 3 <;> simp [h] <;> omega⟩
    40	
    41	/-- The exceptional Magic Square parity, equal to one only on the final
    42	constraint.  Blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`; paper
    43	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    44	-/
    45	def msParity (i : Fin 6) : ZMod 2 :=
    46	  if i.val = 5 then 1 else 0
    47	
    48	/-- The 18 constraint-variable incidence edges of the Magic Square graph in
    49	`def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    50	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    51	-/
    52	def msEdges : Finset (Sym2 MsType) :=
    53	  (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin 6 × Fin 3)).image (fun ij =>
    54	    Sym2.mk (.constraint ij.1) (.var (msConstraintVars ij.1 ij.2)))
    55	
    56	/-- The Magic Square incidence graph has an edge, as required by the
    57	nonempty-support API of `graphDistribution`.  This is the finite carrier fact
    58	used to instantiate `def:ms-game`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
    59	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    60	-/
    61	theorem msEdges_nonempty : msEdges.Nonempty := by
    62	  refine ⟨Sym2.mk (.constraint 0) (.var (msConstraintVars 0 0)), ?_⟩
    63	  exact Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨(0, 0), Finset.mem_univ _, rfl⟩
    64	
    65	/-- A Magic Square answer is a parity triple or a single cell bit, as prescribed
    66	by `def:ms-game`, blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`,
    67	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    68	-/
    69	inductive MsAnswer where
    70	  | triple (β : Fin 3 → ZMod 2)
    71	  | bit (γ : ZMod 2)
    72	  deriving DecidableEq
    73	
    74	/-- A finite code for the two Magic Square answer constructors.  This is
    75	Lean-only carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
    76	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    77	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    78	-/
    79	abbrev MsAnswerCode := (Fin 3 → ZMod 2) ⊕ ZMod 2
    80	
    81	/-- The constructor-preserving code equivalence for `MsAnswer`; Lean-only
    82	finite-carrier infrastructure for `def:ms-game`, blueprint
    83	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
    84	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
    85	-/
    86	noncomputable def msAnswerEquiv : MsAnswer ≃ MsAnswerCode where
    87	  toFun
    88	    | .triple β => .inl β
    89	    | .bit γ => .inr γ
    90	  invFun
    91	    | .inl β => .triple β
    92	    | .inr γ => .bit γ
    93	  left_inv := by intro x; cases x <;> rfl
    94	  right_inv := by
    95	    intro x
    96	    cases x <;> rfl
    97	
    98	noncomputable instance : Fintype MsAnswer :=
    99	  Fintype.ofEquiv MsAnswerCode msAnswerEquiv.symm
   100	
   101	instance : Inhabited MsAnswer := ⟨.bit 0⟩
   102	
   103	/-- The Magic Square consistency predicate.  Constructor mismatches are
   104	rejected, as required by `def:ms-game` (blueprint lines 188-203; paper
   105	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`).
   106	-/
   107	def msWinPredicate :
   108	    MsType → MsType → MsAnswer → MsAnswer → Bool
   109	  | .constraint i, .constraint j, .triple β, .triple β' =>
   110	      decide (i = j ∧ β = β')
   111	  | .var i, .var j, .bit γ, .bit γ' =>
   112	      decide (i = j ∧ γ = γ')
   113	  | .constraint i, .var j, .triple β, .bit γ =>
   114	      decide
   115	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   116	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   117	  | .var j, .constraint i, .bit γ, .triple β =>
   118	      decide
   119	        ((∑ k : Fin 3, β k) = msParity i ∧
   120	          ∃ k : Fin 3, msConstraintVars i k = j ∧ β k = γ)
   121	  | _, _, _, _ => false
   122	
   123	/-- The Magic Square game as a finite `Game`.  This is `def:ms-game` in
   124	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:188-203`, paper origin
   125	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:512-610`.
   126	-/
   127	noncomputable def msGame : Game where
   128	  QuestionA := MsType
   129	  QuestionB := MsType
   130	  AnswerA := MsAnswer
   131	  AnswerB := MsAnswer
   132	  μ := graphDistribution msEdges msEdges_nonempty
   133	  μ_prob := by sorry
   134	  decide := msWinPredicate
   135	
   136	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

    97	noncomputable def chiIndex (P : LdParams) (s : ScalarQ P) : Fin P.m := by
    98	  letI : NeZero P.m := ⟨by

    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99

   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.

   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.

   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal

   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}

   512	\subsection{The Magic Square game}
   513	\label{sec:ms}
   514	
   515	We recall the \emph{Magic Square game} of Mermin and
   516	Peres~\cite{mermin1990simple,peres1990incompatible,aravind2002simple}.
   517	The Magic Square game is a simple self-test for EPR pairs (it tests for two of
   518	them). In addition, it allows one to test that a pair of observables
   519	\emph{anticommutes}.
   520	Here we use it as a building block to construct the quantum low-degree test. 
   521	
   522	There are several formulations of the Magic Square game; here we present it as a
   523	\emph{binary constraint satisfaction} game~\cite{cleve2014characterization}.
   524	In this formulation of the game (denoted by $\game_\MS$) there are $6$ linear
   525	equations defined over $9$ variables that take values in $\F_2$.
   526	The variables correspond to the cells of a $3 \times 3$ grid, as depicted in
   527	Figure~\ref{fig:ms}.
   528	Five of the equations correspond to the constraint that the sum of the variables
   529	in each row and the first two columns must be equal to $0$, and the last
   530	equation requires that the sum of the variables in the last column must be equal
   531	to $1$.

   549	
   550	The question set $\type^\ms$ of the Magic Square game is the following:
   551	\begin{equation*}
   552	  \begin{split}
   553	    \type^\msc & = \{ \Constraint_i : i = 1, 2, \ldots, 6\}\;,\\
   554	    \type^\msv & = \{ \Variable_j : j = 1, 2, \ldots, 9\}\;,\\
   555	    \type^\ms & = \type^\msc \cup \type^\msv\;.
   556	  \end{split}
   557	\end{equation*}
   558	The questions $\Constraint_i$ for $i \in \{1,2,3\}$ correspond to the three row
   559	constraints, the questions $\Constraint_4$, $\Constraint_5$ correspond to the first
   560	two column constraints, and question $\Constraint_6$ corresponds to the third
   561	column constraint.
   562	
   563	In the Magic Square game, the verifier first samples a constraint $\Constraint_i
   564	\in \type^\msc$ uniformly at random, and then samples $\Variable_j$, one of the
   565	three variables in the row or column corresponding to $\Constraint_i$, uniformly
   566	at random.
   567	One player is randomly assigned to be the $\Constraint$ player, and the other is
   568	assigned to be the $\Variable$ player.
   569	The $\Constraint$ player is sent the question $\Constraint_i$ and is expected to
   570	respond with three bits $(\beta_{v_1}, \beta_{v_2}, \beta_{v_3}) \in \F_2^3$,
   571	where $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ are the indices of the three variables corresponding to
   572	$\Constraint_i$.
   573	The $\Variable$ player is given question $\Variable_j$ and is expected to
   574	respond with a single bit $\gamma \in \F_2$.
   575	The players win if the $\Constraint$ player's answers satisfy the equation
   576	associated with $\Constraint_i$, and $\gamma = \beta_j$.
   577	More precisely, the verifier samples an edge of the type graph (see Section~\ref{sec:types}) $G^\ms$
   578	in Fig.~\ref{fig:type-graph-ms}, sends one endpoint to a random player, and the
   579	other endpoint to the other player.

   612	The following theorem records the self-testing (also known as \emph{rigidity})
   613	properties of the Magic Square game.
   614	Its self-testing properties
   615	are crucial to the Pauli basis test.
   616	In particular, it is used to enforce anticommutation relations between certain
   617	pairs of operators.
   618	We will refer to this theorem in the proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test (\Cref{thm:pauli} below) in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}.
   619	
   620	\begin{theorem}[Rigidity of the Magic Square game]
   621	  \label{thm:ms-rigidity}
   622	
   623	
   624	Let $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ be a strategy that succeeds in the Magic Square game $\game^{\MS}$ with probability $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_A \otimes \mH_B$ is a state.    901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.

   929	For a set $V$, we write $\C^V$ for the complex vector space of dimension $|V|$.
   930	The space $\C^V$ is endowed with a canonical orthonormal basis
   931	$\{\ket{x}\}_{x\in V}$.
   932	By ``a quantum state on $V$'' we mean a unit vector
   933	\begin{equation*}
   934	  \ket{\psi}_V \in \complex^V\;.
   935	\end{equation*}
   936	If $V = \bigoplus_{i=1}^k V_k$ is the direct sum of subspaces $V_k$ over $\F$,
   937	then $\complex^V$ can be identified with $\bigotimes_{i=1}^k
   938	\complex^{V_i}$, by the identification of $\ket{x_1 \oplus \dots \oplus
   939	  x_k}$ with $\ket{x_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \ket{x_k}$.
   940	As a special case, if $\{e_i\}$ is a basis of $V$ the decomposition $V =
   941	\bigoplus_{i=1}^k ( \F e_i)$ yields the tensor product decomposition $\C^V =
   942	\bigotimes_{i=1}^k \C^{\abs{\F}}$.
   943	We sometimes refer to the spaces $\C^{\abs{\F}}$ as the ``qudits'' of $\C^V$ (or
   944	of a state on it).

   946	\begin{definition}
   947	  \label{def:EPR}
   948	  For a linear space $V$ over a finite field $\F$, define the \EPR state on $\C^V
   949	  \otimes \C^V$ by
   950	  \begin{equation*}
   951	    \ket{\EPR}_V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\abs{V}}} \sum_{x\in V}\ket {x}\otimes \ket{x}\;.
   952	  \end{equation*}

   957	\subsection{Measurements and observables}
   958	
   959	Quantum measurements are modeled as positive operator-valued
   960	measures (POVMs).
   961	A POVM consists of a set of positive semidefinite operators $\{ M_a \}_{a\in S}$
   962	indexed by outcomes $a\in S$ that satisfy the condition $\sum_a M_a = I$. If the latter condition is relaxed to $\sum_a M_a \leq I$ then we refer to $\{M_a\}$ as a \emph{sub-measurement}.
   963	We sometimes use the same letter $M$ to refer to the collection of operators
   964	defining the POVM.
   965	The probability that the measurement returns outcome $a$ on state $\ket{\psi}$
   966	is given by
   967	\begin{equation*}
   968	  \Pr(a) = \bra{\psi} M_a \ket{\psi}\;.
   969	\end{equation*}
   970	A POVM $M=\{M_a\}$ is said to be \emph{projective} if each operator $M_a$ is a
   971	projector ($M_a^2 = M_a$). This automatically implies that operators
   972	$M_a, M_b$ for distinct outcomes $a \neq b$ are orthogonal ($M_a M_b =
   973	M_b M_a = 0$). An \emph{observable} is a unitary matrix.
   974	A \emph{binary observable} is an observable $O$ such that $O^2 = \Id$, i.e.\ $O$
   975	has eigenvalues in $\{-1,1\}$.
   976	
   977	We follow the convention that subscripts of the measurement index
   978	the outcome and superscripts of the measurement are used to index different
   979	measurements.
   980	For example, we use $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$ to represent a measurement indexed by $x$
   981	whose outcome consists of two parts $a$ and $b$.
   982	In this case, by slightly abusing the notation, we use $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$
   983	to denote
   984	\begin{equation*}
   985	  M^x_a = \sum_b M^x_{a,\, b}\;, \quad M^x_b = \sum_a M^x_{a,\, b}\;.
   986	\end{equation*}
   987	For any $x$, $\{M^x_a\}$ and $\{M^x_b\}$ are POVMs sometimes referred to as the
   988	``marginals'' of $\{M^x_{a,\, b}\}$.
   989	
   990	\begin{definition}
   991	  \label{def:bracket}
   992	  Let $\{M^x_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a family of POVMs indexed by $x\in \cal{X}$.
   993	  Let $f:A\to B$ be an arbitrary function.
   994	  We write $\bigl\{ M^x_{[f(\cdot)=b]} \bigr\}$ for the POVM derived from
   995	  $\{M^x_a\}$ by applying the function $f$ before returning the outcome.
   996	  More precisely,
   997	\begin{equation*}
   998	  M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]} = \sum_{a : f(a)=b} M^x_a\;.
   999	\end{equation*}
  1000	If $b$ is not in the image of $f$, then we define $M^x_{[f(\cdot) = b]}$ to be
  1001	$0$. In cases where the outcome $a$ has a natural interpretation as a tuple $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$ we sometimes slightly abuse notation and write $M^x_{[a_i=b]}$ for some $i\in \{1,\ldots,k\}$ to denote 
  1002	\[ M^x_{[a_i=b]} \,=\,\sum_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k):\,a_i=b} M^x_{(a_1,\ldots,a_k)}\;.\]
  1003	\end{definition}

  1052	\subsection{Generalized Pauli observables}
  1053	\label{sec:generalized-pauli}
  1054	
  1055	
  1056	For prime number $p$, the generalized Pauli operators over $\Fp$ are a
  1057	collection of observables indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element
  1058	$a$ or $b$ of $\Fp$, with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1059	They are given by
  1060	\begin{equation}
  1061	  \label{eq:pauli-fp}
  1062	  \sigma^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \ket{j + a} \bra{j}\qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1063	  \sigma^Z(b) = \sum_{j \in \Fp} \omega^{bj} \ket{j} \bra{j}\;,
  1064	\end{equation}
  1065	where $\omega = e^{\frac{2\pi i}{p}}$, and addition and multiplication are over
  1066	$\Fp$.
  1067	These observables obey the ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1068	\begin{equation}
  1069	  \label{eq:twisted-fp}
  1070	  \forall a,b\in\Fp\;,\qquad \sigma^X(a)\, \sigma^Z(b) =
  1071	  \omega^{-ab} \,\sigma^Z(b)\,\sigma^X(a)\;.
  1072	\end{equation}
  1073	Similarly, over a field $\Fq$ with $q$ a power of $p$, we can consider a set of generalized Pauli
  1074	operators, indexed by a basis setting $X$ or $Z$ and an element of $\Fq$ and
  1075	with eigenvalues that are $p$-th roots of unity.
  1076	For $a, b\in\Fq$ they are given by
  1077	\begin{equation*}
  1078	  \qp^X(a) = \sum_{j \in \Fq} \ket{j+a}\bra{j} \qquad \text{and} \qquad
  1079	  \qp^Z(b)= \sum_{j \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(b j)} \ket{j}\bra{j}\;,
  1080	\end{equation*}
  1081	where addition and multiplication are over $\Fq$.
  1082	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $a, a' \in \Fq$, and $b \in \Fp$, powers of these
  1083	observables obey the relations
  1084	\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pauli-product-power}
  1085	  \bigl(\qp^W(a)\qp^W(a')\bigr) = \qp^W(a+a') \qquad \text{and}
  1086	  \qquad \bigl( \qp^W(a) \bigr)^b = \qp^W(a b) \;.
  1087	\end{equation*}
  1088	In particular, since $pa=0$ for any $a\in \Fq$ we get that that $(\qp^W(a))^p =
  1089	I$ for any $a\in\Fq$.
  1090	The observables obey analogous ``twisted commutation'' relations
  1091	to~\eqref{eq:twisted-fp},
  1092	\begin{equation}
  1093	  \label{eq:twisted-fq}
  1094	  \forall a, b \in \Fq\;, \qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) =
  1095	  \omega^{-\tr(a b)} \, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;.
  1096	\end{equation}
  1097	It is clear from the definition that all of the $\qp^X$ operators commute with
  1098	each other, and similarly all the $\qp^Z$ operators commute with each other.
  1099	Thus, it is meaningful to speak of a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^X$
  1100	operators, and a common eigenbasis for all $\qp^Z$ operators.
  1101	The common eigenbasis for the $\qp^Z$ operators is the computational
  1102	basis $\{\ket{j}\}_{j \in \F_q}$.
  1103	To map this basis to the common eigenbasis of the $\qp^X$ operators, one can
  1104	apply the Fourier transform
  1105	\begin{equation}
  1106	  \label{eq:fourier-f}
  1107	  F \,=\, \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_{a, b\in \Fq} \omega^{-\tr(ab)}
  1108	  \ket{a}\bra{b}\;.
  1109	\end{equation}
  1110	Explicitly, the eigenbases consist of the vectors $\ket{e_W}$ labeled by an
  1111	element $e \in \Fq$ and $W \in \{X, Z\}$, given by
  1112	\begin{equation*}
  1113	  \ket{e_X} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{q}} \sum_j \omega^{- \tr(e j)} \ket{j}\;, \qquad
  1114	  \ket{e_Z}   = \ket{e}\;.
  1115	\end{equation*}
  1116	We denote the POVM whose elements are projectors onto basis vectors of the
  1117	eigenbasis associated with the observables $\qp^W$ by $\{\qp^W_e\}_e$.
  1118	Then for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $a\in \Fq$, the observables $\qp^W(a)$ can be
  1119	written as
  1120	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1121	  \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b \in \Fq} \omega^{\tr(a b)} \qp^W_b\;.
  1122	\end{equation}
  1123	
  1124	To invert this relation, we first quote the following useful Fourier fact.
  1125	\begin{lemma}[Fact 3.2 of \cite{NW19}]
  1126	  \label{lem:cancellation}
  1127	  Let $V$ be a subspace of $\F^k$. For all $v \not\in V^\perp$, 
  1128	  \begin{equation*}
  1129	    \E_{u \sim V} \omega^{\tr(u \cdot v)} = 0\;,
  1130	  \end{equation*}
  1131	  where the expectation is over a uniformly random vector $u$ from $V$.
  1132	\end{lemma}
  1133	
  1134	We may now invert~\Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}:
  1135	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single}
  1136	  \E_{a\in \F_q} \omega^{-\tr(ab)} \qp^W(a) = \sum_{b'\in \F_q} \E_{a\in \F_q}
  1137	  \omega^{\tr(a(b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;,
  1138	\end{equation}
  1139	where the second step follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}.
  1140	
  1141	For systems with many qudits, we will consider tensor products of the operators
  1142	$\qp^W$.
  1143	Slightly abusing notation, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$ and $a \in \Fq^n$ we denote by
  1144	$\qp^W(a)$ the tensor product $\qp^W(a_1) \ot \dots \ot \qp^W(a_n)$.
  1145	These obey the twisted commutation relations
  1146	\begin{equation*}
  1147	  \forall a,b\in \Fq^n,\qquad \qp^X(a)\, \qp^Z(b) \,=\, \omega^{-\tr (a \cdot
  1148	    b)}\, \qp^Z(b)\, \qp^X(a)\;,
  1149	\end{equation*}
  1150	where $a \cdot b = \sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i b_i \in \Fq$.
  1151	For $W\in\{X,Z\}$ and $e \in \Fq^n$ define the eigenstates
  1152	\[ \ket{e_W} = \ket{(e_1)_W} \ot \dots \ot \ket{(e_n)_W}\;, \]
  1153	and associated rank-$1$ projectors $\qp^W_e$. Analogous versions of \Cref{eq:pauli-obs-proj-single}
  1154	and \Cref{eq:pauli-inversion-0-single} relate the multi-qubit observables
  1155	and projectors:
  1156	\begin{align}
  1157	  \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b \in \Fq^n} \omega^{\tr(a \cdot b)}
  1158	  \qp^W_b\;, \label{eq:pauli-obs-proj} \\
  1159	    \E_{a\in \F_q^n} \omega^{-\tr(a \cdot b)} \qp^W(a) &= \sum_{b'\in \F_q^n} \E_{a\in \F_q^n}
  1160	  \omega^{\tr(a\cdot (b'-b))} \qp^W_{b'} = \qp^W_b\;. \label{eq:pauli-inversion-0}
  1161	\end{align}
  1162	
  1163	Since we only consider finite fields $\F_q$ such that $q = 2^k$ the maximally
  1164	entangled state $\ket{\EPR_q}$ and the corresponding qudit Pauli
  1165	observables/projectors are isomorphic to a tensor product of maximally entangled
  1166	states $\ket{\EPR_2}$ and \emph{qubit} Pauli observables/projectors
  1167	respectively; this is shown in the next lemma.

  1169	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) gives a self-test for Pauli observables and
  1170	maximally entangled states over qubits.
  1171	
  1172	\begin{lemma}
  1173	  \label{lem:pauli-binary}
  1174	  For all admissible field sizes $q = 2^k$ and integers $L$, there exists
  1175	  an isomorphism $\phi: (\C^q)^{\otimes L} \to (\C^2)^{\otimes L k}$

     5	/-!
     6	# Generalized Pauli operators and EPR states
     7	
     8	The definitions here use finite matrix entries and rank-one projectors, so they
     9	are usable by the later game statements without introducing an abstract
    10	operator algebra.  The Fourier/orthogonality identities are retained as named
    11	proof obligations for subsequent stages.
    12	
    13	## References
    14	
    15	The source-facing nodes are `def:lin-reg`, `def:EPR`, `def:generalized-pauli`,
    16	and `lem:pauli-observable-expansion` in
    17	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:494-652`.  The paper origin is
    18	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:908-1161`.
    19	-/
    20	
    21	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    22	
    23	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    24	
    25	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    26	
    27	variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]
    28	  [Algebra (ZMod 2) K]
    29	
    30	/-- The two generalized Pauli bases used by the test in `def:generalized-pauli`,
    31	blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    32	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    33	-/
    34	inductive PauliKind where
    35	  | X
    36	  | Z
    37	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    38	
    39	/-- The binary character used for generalized Pauli phases; see
    40	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1081`.
    41	
    42	It is public because the Fourier expansion declarations below expose this
    43	character in their statement types. -/
    44	noncomputable def phaseSign (t : ZMod 2) : ℂ :=
    45	  if t = 0 then 1 else -1
    46	
    47	/--
    48	The shift operator `τ^X(a)`.  Blueprint `def:generalized-pauli`,
    49	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`; paper origin
    50	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    51	-/
    52	noncomputable def tauShift (a : K) : Op K :=
    53	  fun i j => if i = j + a then 1 else 0
    54	
    55	/--
    56	The phase operator `τ^Z(b)`, with the fixed binary trace in the phase.  It is
    57	the second operator of `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 529-571; paper
    58	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`).
    59	-/
    60	noncomputable def tauPhase (b : K) : Op K :=
    61	  fun i j => if i = j then phaseSign (binTrace K (b * j)) else 0
    62	
    63	/-- The single-qudit eigenvector coordinate used in the tensor-product basis;
    64	see `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1126-1161`. -/
    65	private noncomputable def singlePauliVec (W : PauliKind) (e x : K) : ℂ :=
    66	  match W with
    67	  | .Z => if x = e then 1 else 0
    68	  | .X =>
    69	      (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card K : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ * phaseSign (binTrace K (e * x))
    70	
    71	/--
    72	The normalized single/multi-qudit eigenvector for a Pauli basis label.  For an
    73	index type `ι`, the input `e : ι → K` labels the tensor-product basis vector.
    74	This is the vector form of `def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint
    75	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:550-570`, paper origin
    76	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`.
    77	-/
    78	noncomputable def pauliVec {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    79	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) (x : ι → K) : ℂ :=
    80	  ∏ i : ι, singlePauliVec W (e i) (x i)
    81	
    82	/--
    83	The rank-one projector onto `pauliVec W e`.  This is the projective measurement
    84	element `τ^W_e` in `def:generalized-pauli` (blueprint lines 562-570; paper
    85	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1101-1122`).
    86	-/
    87	noncomputable def pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    88	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    89	  Matrix.vecMulVec (pauliVec W e) (fun x => star (pauliVec W e x))
    90	
    91	/-- A compact operator-valued form of a generalized Pauli observable from
    92	`def:generalized-pauli`, blueprint `ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:529-571`, paper origin
    93	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1096`.
    94	-/
    95	noncomputable def tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    96	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) : Op (ι → K) :=
    97	  fun x y =>
    98	    ∏ i : ι,
    99	      match W with
   100	      | .X => tauShift (a i) (x i) (y i)
   101	      | .Z => tauPhase (a i) (x i) (y i)
   102	
   103	/--
   104	The EPR vector on a finite label space.  Blueprint `def:EPR`,
   105	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:513-523`; paper origin
   106	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`.
   107	-/
   108	noncomputable def eprState (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   109	    EuclideanSpace ℂ (V × V) :=
   110	  (EuclideanSpace.equiv (V × V) ℂ).symm
   111	    (fun p : V × V =>
   112	      if p.1 = p.2 then (Real.sqrt (Fintype.card V : ℝ) : ℂ)⁻¹ else 0)
   113	
   114	/-- The EPR vector is normalized on a nonempty finite carrier; see
   115	`def:EPR`, `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:946-955`. -/
   116	theorem eprState_norm (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] [Nonempty V] :
   117	    ‖eprState V‖ = 1 := by
   118	  sorry
   119	
   120	/--
   121	Fourier expansion of a generalized Pauli observable in the Pauli projectors.
   122	This is `lem:pauli-observable-expansion`, equations `eq:pauli-obs-proj` and
   123	`eq:pauli-inversion-0`, in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`;
   124	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   125	Both directions are deliberately left as proof-level obligations in stage 4.1.
   126	-/
   127	theorem tauObservable_eq_sum_pauliProj {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   128	    (W : PauliKind) (a : ι → K) :
   129	    tauObservable W a =
   130	      ∑ e : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • pauliProj W e := by
   131	  sorry
   132	
   133	/-- The inverse Fourier expansion of a Pauli projector
   134	(`lem:pauli-observable-expansion`), blueprint
   135	`ch11_qpbt_algebra.tex:638-652`, paper origin
   136	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1141-1161`.
   137	-/
   138	theorem pauliProj_eq_avg_tauObservable {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   139	    (W : PauliKind) (e : ι → K) :
   140	    pauliProj W e =
   141	      (Fintype.card (ι → K) : ℂ)⁻¹ •
   142	        ∑ a : ι → K, phaseSign (binTrace K (dotProduct a e)) • tauObservable W a := by
   143	  sorry
   144	
   145	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     4	/-!
     5	# Quantitative state and operator distances
     6	
     7	The blueprint uses asymptotic `approx` notation.  The skeleton records the
     8	corresponding squared norm functionals explicitly, leaving universal-constant
     9	estimates to later proof stages.
    10	
    11	## References
    12	
    13	These are `def:state-distance` and `def:povm-distance` in
    14	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-220`; the paper origin is
    15	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    16	-/
    17	
    18	open scoped BigOperators
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    21	
    22	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    23	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    24	
    25	/--
    26	Squared Euclidean distance between pure states.  Blueprint `def:state-distance`
    27	(`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:171-179`), paper origin
    28	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    29	-/
    30	noncomputable def stateDistSq {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι]
    31	    [DecidableEq ι]
    32	    (ψ φ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    33	  ‖ψ - φ‖ ^ 2
    34	
    35	/--
    36	Average squared state-dependent distance between two operator families.  This
    37	is `def:povm-distance` in `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:203-210`,
    38	with paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`.
    39	-/
    40	noncomputable def opFamilyDistSq {X α ι : Type*}
    41	    [Fintype α] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
    42	    (μ : Distribution X) (M N : X → α → Op ι)
    43	    (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : ℝ :=
    44	  avgOver μ (fun x =>
    45	    ∑ a : α, ‖applyOperatorToState (M x a - N x a) ψ‖ ^ 2)
    46	
    47	end MIPStarRE.QPBT

     6	/-!

     8

    10	states are vectors in `EuclideanSpace`, and POVMs use the project's matrix
    11	`Measurement` structure.
    12	
    13	## References
    14	
    15	The source-facing nodes are `def:game`, `def:povm-conventions`,
    16	`def:tensor-product-strategy`, and `def:tensor-product-value` in
    17	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:47-82` and `8-26`.

    20	
    21	open scoped BigOperators Matrix ComplexOrder
    22	
    23	namespace MIPStarRE.QPBT
    24	
    25	open MIPStarRE.LDT
    26	open MIPStarRE.Quantum
    27	
    28	/--
    29	A finite two-player one-round game with a probability distribution on question
    30	pairs and a Boolean decision predicate.  This is `def:game` in
    31	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:51-59`, with paper origin
    32	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:10-24`.
    33	-/
    34	structure Game where
    35	  QuestionA : Type
    36	  QuestionB : Type
    37	  AnswerA : Type
    38	  AnswerB : Type
    39	  [questionAFintype : Fintype QuestionA]
    40	  [questionBFintype : Fintype QuestionB]
    41	  [answerAFintype : Fintype AnswerA]
    42	  [answerBFintype : Fintype AnswerB]
    43	  [questionADecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionA]
    44	  [questionBDecidableEq : DecidableEq QuestionB]
    45	  [answerADecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerA]
    46	  [answerBDecidableEq : DecidableEq AnswerB]
    47	  μ : Distribution (QuestionA × QuestionB)
    48	  μ_prob : μ.IsProbability
    49	  decide : QuestionA → QuestionB → AnswerA → AnswerB → Bool
    50	
    51	attribute [instance] Game.questionAFintype Game.questionBFintype
    52	  Game.answerAFintype Game.answerBFintype Game.questionADecidableEq
    53	  Game.questionBDecidableEq Game.answerADecidableEq Game.answerBDecidableEq
    54	
    55	/--
    56	The marginal of a joint POVM obtained by post-processing its answer pair.  This
    57	is the POVM convention of `def:povm-conventions` in
    58	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; the post-processing operation
    59	is the already formalized `Measurement.postprocess`, with paper origin
    60	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
    61	-/
    62	noncomputable def marginalLeft {α β d : Type*}
    63	    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    64	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    65	    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement α d :=
    66	  M.postprocess Prod.fst
    67	
    68	/-- The right marginal of a joint POVM, obtained using `Prod.snd` in
    69	`def:povm-conventions`, `blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`,
    70	paper origin `references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
    71	-/
    72	noncomputable def marginalRight {α β d : Type*}
    73	    [Fintype α] [Fintype β] [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq β]
    74	    [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    75	    (M : Measurement (α × β) d) : Measurement β d :=
    76	  M.postprocess Prod.snd
    77	
    78	/-- Projectivity of every effect in a POVM (`def:povm-conventions`, blueprint
    79	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:8-26`; paper origin
    80	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:68-72`). -/
    81	def Measurement.IsProjective {α d : Type*} [Fintype α] [Fintype d] [DecidableEq d]
    82	    (M : Measurement α d) : Prop :=
    83	  ∀ a, IsProj (M.effect a)
    84	
    85	/--
    86	The tensor-product strategy of `def:tensor-product-strategy` in
    87	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69` (paper origin
    88	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`).
    89	-/
    90	structure Strategy (G : Game) where
    91	  ιA : Type
    92	  ιB : Type
    93	  [ιAFintype : Fintype ιA]
    94	  [ιBFintype : Fintype ιB]
    95	  [ιADecidableEq : DecidableEq ιA]
    96	  [ιBDecidableEq : DecidableEq ιB]
    97	  ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (ιA × ιB)
    98	  ψ_norm : ‖ψ‖ = 1
    99	  A : G.QuestionA → Measurement G.AnswerA ιA
   100	  B : G.QuestionB → Measurement G.AnswerB ιB
   101	
   102	attribute [instance] Strategy.ιAFintype Strategy.ιBFintype
   103	  Strategy.ιADecidableEq Strategy.ιBDecidableEq
   104	
   105	/-- The rectangular tensor placement used in strategy probabilities.  This is
   106	the finite-matrix realization of `def:tensor-product-strategy`, blueprint
   107	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:61-69`; paper origin
   108	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:26-38`.
   109	-/
   110	def heteroKron {ιA ιB : Type*} (A : Op ιA) (B : Op ιB) : Op (ιA × ιB) :=
   111	  Matrix.kronecker A B
   112	
   113	/- The Euclidean linear map is the shared action used by the value and distance
   114	functionals.  Keeping it at the Euclidean-space level avoids accidentally
   115	using the function-space supremum norm of `Matrix.mulVec`. -/
   116	/-- Apply a finite matrix to a Euclidean-space state.  This is the Hilbert-space
   117	action underlying `def:tensor-product-value`, paper
   118	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   119	noncomputable def applyOperatorToState {ι : Type*} [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι]
   120	    (M : Op ι) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι) : EuclideanSpace ℂ ι :=
   121	  Matrix.toEuclideanLin M ψ
   122	
   123	/-- The Born weight of an answer pair for a strategy.  Lean-only support for
   124	`def:tensor-product-value`, blueprint `ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, paper
   125	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:219-271`. -/
   126	private noncomputable def outcomeWeight {G : Game} (S : Strategy G)
   127	    (x : G.QuestionA) (y : G.QuestionB) (a : G.AnswerA) (b : G.AnswerB) : ℝ :=
   128	  let M : MIPStarRE.Quantum.Op (S.ιA × S.ιB) :=
   129	    heteroKron ((S.A x).effect a) ((S.B y).effect b)

   131	  (inner ℂ S.ψ acted).re
   132	
   133	/--

   135	probabilities.  This is `def:tensor-product-value` in
   136	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:71-82`, with paper origin
   137	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`.
   138	-/
   139	noncomputable def Strategy.value {G : Game} (S : Strategy G) : ℝ :=
   140	  avgOver G.μ (fun xy =>
   141	    ∑ a : G.AnswerA, ∑ b : G.AnswerB,
   142	      if G.decide xy.1 xy.2 a b then outcomeWeight S xy.1 xy.2 a b else 0)

   144	/--
   145	The tensor-product game value as a conditional supremum over all finite
   146	strategies.  The `sSup (Set.range ...)` form is the csSup formulation requested

   149	`references/qpbt-paper/06_nonlocal_games_and_mipstar.tex:40-57`; attainment is
   150	intentionally not asserted here.
   151	-/
   152	noncomputable def Game.value (G : Game) : ℝ :=
   153	  sSup (Set.range (fun S : Strategy G => S.value))
   154	
   155	end MIPStarRE.QPBT
